: Figure 1The architecture of MHWA.(Top)(Bottom) It is illustrated at a context-update timestep $t=1+m\cdot k$ .

The model processes an interleaved sequence of observation ( $o_{t}$ ) and action ( $a_{t}$ ) tokens.

At this specific strided step, the High-Level Manager consumes the downsampled history to infer a slowly varying global context $z^{ctx}$ , supervised by a skip-step prediction head $p^{high}_{o}$ that forecasts the observation at the next coarse step $\hat{o}_{t+k}$ . We refer to the original, complete sequence as the dense trajectory, in contrast to the downsampled input used by the manager.

The Low-Level Worker operates at the atomic resolution. It employs a Context-Aware Dynamic Routing mechanism where a Gating Network utilizes both the current dense input and the refreshed high-level context $z^{ctx}$ to dynamically route computation to a sparse subset of experts (MoE).

The worker’s output drives the world model heads ( $p_{o},p_{r},p_{d}$ ) and the critic head ( $h_{Q}$ ).

3

We propose the ulti-timescale ierarchical orld ction model (), an asymmetric dual-layer architecture for reducing compounding errors in tokenized autoregressive world models.

MHWA targets two interference modes: conceptual interference between hierarchy levels, and structural interference across heterogeneous dynamics modes.

It addresses the former by isolating a slow high-level context through gradient detachment, and the latter by using context-aware sparse routing in the low-level dynamics model.MHWAMHWA

3.1

We consider offline reinforcement learning as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) $\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma\rangle$ .

In visual RL, the agent observes high-dimensional observations $o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}$ rather than ground-truth states, and we treat the stacked observation history as the state representation.

Given a static dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ , where $\tau=(o_{1},a_{1},r_{1},\dots,o_{T},a_{T},r_{T})$ , the goal is to learn predictive transition and outcome models that support long-term return maximization.

Following tokenized world-action models, each observation is encoded into $K$ discrete visual tokens using a VQ-VAE tokenizer, reusing the pretrained tokenizer from JOWA.

These visual tokens are interleaved with executed action tokens to form a single autoregressive sequence.

Token, positional, and task embeddings are combined before both Transformers, retaining JOWA’s explicit task conditioning.

An autoregressive predictor processes this sequence and produces embeddings consumed by four heads:

(i) a next-observation token head $p_{o}$ ,

(ii) a reward head $p_{r}$ ,

(iii) a termination head $p_{d}$ , and

(iv) a Q-value head $h_{Q}$ trained with offline TD learning.

In MHWA, this predictor is implemented by the Low-Level Worker modulated by the High-Level Manager, as described in Sec. .

We refer to the components producing $(p_{o},p_{r},p_{d})$ as the and those producing $h_{Q}$ as the ; both world-modeling and TD/CQL critic losses back-propagate through the autoregressive predictor.

3.2

world-partaction-part

Standard autoregressive world models treat trajectories as uniform token sequences, where prediction errors may accumulate with rollout depth.

MHWA instead introduces temporal abstraction to infer global context less frequently, while preserving local dynamics prediction at the native token resolution.

3.2

MHWA is organized around the two interference modes above.

To mitigate , the high-level representation should capture slow-varying context without being dominated by low-level reconstruction noise.

To mitigate , the low-level model should avoid fitting heterogeneous dynamics with a single shared feed-forward parameterization.

Accordingly, MHWA retains the tokenized world-action interface and standard prediction heads, while replacing the monolithic autoregressive predictor with an asymmetric two-level hierarchy (Figure ):

(i) a High-Level Manager that infers slowly varying context at a reduced update frequency, and

(ii) a Low-Level Worker implemented as an autoregressive Transformer whose feed-forward sublayers are replaced by sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers.

The worker output drives the world-model heads $(p_{o},p_{r},p_{d})$ and the critic head $(h_{Q})$ .

The manager provides an isolated slow context channel, while the worker combines this context with the instantaneous state for dynamic expert routing.

This couples temporal abstraction with modular local prediction, directly targeting conceptual and structural interference in heterogeneous multi-game dynamics.conceptual interferencestructural interference

1

3.3

The High-Level Manager targets conceptual interference by learning a slow context representation on a strided temporal scale.

Let $x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the input embedding at atomic step $t$ , where $x_{t}$ represents either an observation ( $o_{t}$ ) or an action ( $a_{t}$ ) embedding because the input sequence interleaves observations and actions.

We introduce a high-level index $m$ , where each step corresponds to atomic timestamp $t=1+m\cdot k$ with stride factor $k$ ; we set $k=4$ .

At coarse step $m$ , the manager consumes the strided token sequence $\mathbf{X}^{(m)}_{slow}=(x_{1},x_{1+k},\dots,x_{1+m\cdot k})$ , a $k$ -fold temporal downsampling of the atomic sequence.

A causal Transformer encoder  computes:[]

36

$h^{high}_{m}=\text{Transformer}_{High}(\mathbf{X}^{(m)}_{slow})$ (1)

From $h^{high}_{m}$ , a trainable Context Projector produces a continuous context vector $z^{ctx}_{m}=\mathrm{Projector}(\mathrm{stopgrad}(h^{high}_{m}))$ , which parametrizes the slow-varying context of the current dynamics regime rather than acting as a discrete subgoal.

We broadcast $z^{ctx}_{m}$ to the Low-Level Worker and hold it constant for the subsequent window of $k$ atomic steps.

Stop-gradient is placed between the manager and the Context Projector, leaving the projector, router, and worker trainable under the low-level objectives.

Thus, the manager is trained through its own auxiliary objective instead of low-level gradients, preventing short-range prediction noise from overwriting the high-level context.

This is the main mechanism for controlling conceptual interference between hierarchy levels.Context Broadcasting and Gradient Isolation.

Temporal abstraction is implemented as a fixed token-level stride on the interleaved sequence.

This matches the tokenized world-action interface, where visual and action tokens are flattened into one stream.

The stride shortens the manager sequence for efficient slow-context inference, while the Low-Level Worker still handles fine-grained native-resolution prediction.

Although striding discards some tokens, VQ-VAE visual codes contain sufficient redundancy for coarse context inference.Implementation of Stride.

The stride $k$ sets the manager’s temporal sampling and prediction scale; the context-refresh interval $r$ is set to $k$ by default.

Unlike static temporal abstractions  that lock low-level policies or dynamics for fixed intervals, MHWA keeps the low-level routing mechanism operating at the atomic timescale $t$ .

The worker therefore remains locally reactive by conditioning on both the broadcast context and the instantaneous state.Distinction from Static Execution.[]

10

3.4

The Low-Level Worker targets structural interference.

In heterogeneous multi-game dynamics, a monolithic low-level FFN must model diverse visual patterns, action effects, and transition modes with shared parameters, which can entangle incompatible behaviors.

MHWA replaces these FFN sublayers with sparse MoE layers .

The routing mechanism conditions on both the broadcast high-level context and the instantaneous token state, allowing expert selection to reflect slow dynamics modes while remaining locally reactive.[, ]

31

32

Let $x_{t}$ denote the intermediate token representation in the residual stream at token position $t$ , and let $z^{ctx}_{m}$ be the broadcast high-level context for $m=\lfloor(t-1)/k\rfloor$ .

A gating projection $W_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d\times N}$ maps the concatenated input to routing logits:

$l_{t}=(x_{t}\oplus z^{ctx}_{m})W_{g},$ (2)

where $\oplus$ denotes concatenation and $N$ is the number of experts $\{E_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ .

We apply Top- $K$ sparse routing by selecting $\mathcal{T}_{t}=\mathrm{TopK}(l_{t},K_{\mathrm{route}})$ and computing masked Softmax weights.

We set $N=4$ ; $K_{\mathrm{route}}=2$ :

$w_{t,j}=\frac{\exp(l_{t,j})}{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{T}_{t}}\exp(l_{t,r})},\;j\in\mathcal{T}_{t};\qquad w_{t,j}=0,\;j\notin\mathcal{T}_{t}.$ (3)

The MoE output is:

$y_{t}=x_{t}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{t}}w_{t,j}\,E_{j}(x_{t}).$ (4)

Conditioning the gate on both $z^{ctx}_{m}$ and $x_{t}$ makes routing both mode-aware and locally reactive: the context term encourages specialization across slow-varying dynamics regimes, while the state term preserves sensitivity to instantaneous visual and action-dependent details.

This addresses structural interference by replacing a single shared low-level transformation with sparse, context-conditioned expert computation.

We use no capacity factor, token dropping, or truncation; all selected tokens are computed, and expert collapse is mitigated with an auxiliary load-balancing regularizer. We provide complete architectural and routing implementation details in Appendix .

B

3.5

We train the MHWA architecture jointly but with cross-level stop-gradient.

Accordingly, the total objective function comprises .

The first two ( $\mathcal{L}_{base},\mathcal{L}_{critic}$ ) are adopted from baseline JOWA .

The latter two ( $\mathcal{L}_{high},\mathcal{L}_{aux}$ ) are novel structural constraints introduced by MHWA, specifically designed to enforce hierarchical representation learning and dynamic expert specialization.four distinct components[]

5

Following standard autoregressive approaches, the Low-Level Worker transforms the input sequence into a final hidden representation $h_{t}$ . This representation is then used to predict the next discrete observation token $o_{t+1}$ , reward $r_{t}$ , and termination signal $d_{t}$ via standard Cross-Entropy loss. This ensures the model accurately simulates the environment’s local dynamics:1. Base World Model Objectives ( $\mathcal{L}_{base}$ ):

$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{base}=-\sum_{t}\Big[$ $\displaystyle\underbrace{\log p_{o}(o_{t+1}|h_{t})}_{\text{Observation}}+\underbrace{\log p_{r}(r_{t}|h_{t})}_{\text{Reward}}+\underbrace{\log p_{d}(d_{t}|h_{t})}_{\text{Termination}}\Big]$ (5)

For policy evaluation, we employ a distributional Q-function learned via Temporal Difference (TD) learning, augmented with a Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) penalty to mitigate value overestimation in offline regimes . The critic loss is defined as:2. Offline Critic Objectives ( $\mathcal{L}_{critic}$ ):[]

15

$\mathcal{L}_{critic}=\mathcal{L}_{TD}(\theta_{Q})+\alpha_{cql}\mathcal{L}_{CQL}(\theta_{Q})$ (6)

where $\mathcal{L}_{TD}$ minimizes the distributional Bellman error (using C51) and $\mathcal{L}_{CQL}$ penalizes Q-values on out-of-distribution actions.

A core challenge in hierarchical modeling is preventing the high-level representation from collapsing into a trivial identity mapping of low-level features or overfitting to transient, hard-to-predict details.

To encourage the High-Level Manager to distill slow-varying and semantically meaningful context, we introduce a skip-step predictive objective.

Concretely, an MLP projection head $p_{high}$ predicts the token at the next sampled position using only the corresponding high-level hidden state $h^{high}_{m}$ .

This skip-step gap acts as an information bottleneck, discouraging reliance on ephemeral noise and promoting representations that remain predictive across multiple token steps:3. High-Level Representation Learning ( $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ ):

$\mathcal{L}_{high}=-\sum_{m}\log p_{o}^{high}(o_{(m+1)k}\mid h^{high}_{m})$ (7)

To prevent expert collapse and ensure balanced resource utilization, we minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the batch-wise expert selection frequency $\hat{p}$ and the uniform distribution $\mathcal{U}$ :4. Routing Regularization ( $\mathcal{L}_{aux}$ ):

$\mathcal{L}_{aux}=D_{KL}(\hat{p}\parallel\mathcal{U})=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{exp}}\hat{p}_{i}\log\hat{p}_{i}+\text{const}$ (8)

where $\hat{p}_{i}=\frac{1}{B\cdot T\cdot K_{\mathrm{route}}}\sum_{b,t}\mathbb{I}(i\in\mathcal{T}_{b,t})$ represents the normalized selection ratio of expert $i$ within a batch, here $B$ denotes the batch size, $T$ denotes the number of routed token positions per sequence, $K_{\mathrm{route}}$ is the number of active experts per token.

Minimizing this objective maximizes the entropy of the routing distribution, enforcing a balanced load across the expert bank.

The final training objective aggregates the main generative tasks with these structural constraints:Total Objective:

$\mathcal{L}_{total}=\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{base}+\mathcal{L}_{critic}}_{\text{Main Task}}+\underbrace{\lambda_{h}\mathcal{L}_{high}}_{\text{Representation}}+\underbrace{\lambda_{a}\mathcal{L}_{aux}}_{\text{Regularization}}$ (9)

where $\lambda_{h}$ and $\lambda_{a}$ are hyperparameters governing the strength of the hierarchical and sparsity constraints, respectively. We set $\lambda_{h}=1$ , $\lambda_{a}=0.1$ .

4.3

To evaluate error accumulation under autoregressive rollout, we measure open-loop reconstruction quality over steps $t=5\ldots 8$ within the context window.

For each game, we sample held-out trajectory segments disjoint from the training data, condition each model on the first four ground-truth frames and corresponding actions, and then roll out from $t=5$ without injecting ground-truth observations.

Actions are kept fixed to the dataset actions, so differences in MSE/PSNR/SSIM against ground-truth frames reflect dynamics-modeling errors rather than policy differences.

As shown in Figure , the monolithic JOWA-70M baseline shows a marked deterioration as rollout depth increases, indicating that reducing capacity without architectural changes amplifies error accumulation even within the context window.

In contrast, MHWA-77M curbs error propagation and achieves predictive stability comparable to JOWA-150M.

A longer-horizon diagnostic from $t=5$ to $t=54$ further shows that MHWA outperforms the smaller monolithic baseline and remains comparable to the larger baseline; see Appendix .

The stride ablations show that the high-level context update frequency is a key factor.

Collapsing the hierarchy to $k=1$ causes the largest degradation among all variants, with a 62.1% relative IQM drop, indicating that temporal abstraction is central to MHWA’s benefit.

The default $k=4$ performs best in this 44M/6-game setting, while $k=2$ and $k=8$ remain lower but competitive, with relative IQM drops of 20.9% and 8.3%, respectively.

This suggests that insufficient abstraction is especially harmful, whereas overly coarse abstraction has a milder effect in this setting.Temporal abstraction.

The variant removes the manager, Context Projector, skip-step head, and $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ , retaining the task embedding and low-level MoE; its IQM is 0.445. Removing the state input to the router yields IQM 0.359.

The larger drop from removing state routing (36.3%) suggests that local state information is especially important for reactive fine-grained prediction.

The 21.1% drop from removing the manager pathway further indicates that trajectory-dependent context helps expert selection across slow-varying dynamics modes.Routing mechanism.MoE-only (w/o Manager)

Replacing the sparse MoE with a dense FFN at matched parameter count () reduces IQM to 0.450, corresponding to a relative IQM drop of 20.2%.

Removing the skip-step objective $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ yields a moderate drop (IQM: $0.564\rightarrow 0.503$ , 10.8%), suggesting that explicit high-level supervision helps the manager learn stride-level predictive context rather than short-range noisy features.

Removing the load-balancing regularizer $\mathcal{L}_{aux}$ causes a larger drop (IQM: $0.564\rightarrow 0.444$ , 21.3%), supporting its role in preventing expert collapse and maintaining stable specialization.High-level supervision and routing regularization.

The completed factorial ablation (Table ) shows that stop-gradient improves IQM both with $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ ( $0.533\rightarrow 0.564$ ) and without it ( $0.387\rightarrow 0.503$ ).

Without $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ , the manager has fixed weights but supplies trajectory-dependent hidden states to the trainable Context Projector. Replacing those states with zeros or Gaussian noise reduces IQM from 0.503 to 0.406 or 0.381 (Appendix ).Gradient isolation.

5

We introduced MHWA, a multi-timescale hierarchical world-action model that combines a strided, gradient-isolated high-level manager with a context-aware MoE low-level worker. The manager reduces how often global context must be inferred, while the worker remains reactive at the native token resolution and routes computation through specialized experts. On the 10% offline Atari benchmark, MHWA outperforms a matched three-seed JOWA-70M baseline, achieves numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M with 77M parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence, and shows competitive adaptation to held-out Atari games.

The current evidence is intentionally scoped. We evaluate primarily in discrete-action offline Atari with a pretrained tokenizer and fixed stride, and extending to adaptive temporal abstraction , continuous control, and broader domains remains future work.[]

Appendix B

The High-Level Manager is also a 4-layer, 8-head, 512-dimensional Transformer, but uses a dense MLP with expansion ratio 4 instead of MoE. Its output is detached before a trainable $512\rightarrow 512$ Context Projector and broadcast across the following stride window. Low-level losses train the Context Projector, router, and worker, while $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ trains the manager. Both Transformers receive the shared token, positional, and task embeddings. The tokenized interface uses 37 tokens per block, consisting of 36 visual tokens and one action token, with 8 blocks per sequence. The critic head uses one Q-head, MLP dimension 768, and dropout 0.01.

The Low-Level Worker is a 4-layer causal Transformer with 8 attention heads and embedding dimension 512. Each feed-forward sublayer is replaced by an MoE layer with $N=4$ experts and Top- $K=2$ routing. Each expert is a $512\rightarrow 2048\rightarrow 512$ GELU MLP. The routing gate is a bias-free linear projection over the concatenation of the current token state and the broadcast high-level context. We do not use token dropping or capacity truncation; all selected tokens are computed, and exactly two experts are active per token.

The full MHWA model contains 77.27M parameters, with approximately 60.49M parameters activated per forward pass including the tokenizer.

We count forward+backward FLOPs for the main experimental configurations using 8 frames and 296 tokens per sequence, with batch size 256. The count includes the complete forward graph, world-model, critic, and auxiliary losses, and backward computation. For MHWA, it includes both hierarchy levels, all four MoE layers, four stored experts with Top-2 routing, load balancing, and high-level observation prediction. Appendix C

We provide a simple formal view of when a strided context model can have a smaller one-step open-loop rollout-error bound than a flat model. This analysis is intended to isolate the core mechanism of MHWA, rather than to provide a general performance guarantee. We focus on open-loop state prediction under a fixed action sequence.

Let the latent state be $x_{t}=(s_{t},c_{t})$ , where $s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}$ denotes the fast state and $c_{t}\in\mathcal{C}$ denotes the slow context. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be any metric action space, either discrete or continuous. The true dynamics are

$s_{t+1}=f(s_{t},c_{t},a_{t}).$ (10)

In MHWA, at macro-step $m$ , the manager predicts a context $\hat{c}_{m}$ , which is held fixed for the next $k$ local steps, while the worker rolls out

$\hat{s}_{t+1}=\hat{f}(\hat{s}_{t},\hat{c}_{m},\tilde{a}_{t}),$ (11)

where $\tilde{a}_{t}$ denotes the action representation used by the model.

Assumptions.

We use the following standard assumptions for open-loop dynamics prediction.

There exist constants $L_{s},L_{c},L_{a}\geq 0$ such thatLipschitz continuity.

$d_{\mathcal{S}}\!\left(f(s,c,a),f(s^{\prime},c^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right)\leq L_{s}d_{\mathcal{S}}(s,s^{\prime})+L_{c}d_{\mathcal{C}}(c,c^{\prime})+L_{a}d_{\mathcal{A}}(a,a^{\prime}),$ (12)

where $d_{\mathcal{S}}$ , $d_{\mathcal{C}}$ , and $d_{\mathcal{A}}$ are metrics on the fast-state, context, and action spaces.

There exists $\rho\geq 0$ such thatSlow context drift.

$d_{\mathcal{C}}(c_{t},c_{t+1})\leq\rho.$ (13)

Therefore, for a local step $t=mk+j$ with $j\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}$ ,

$d_{\mathcal{C}}(c_{mk},c_{t})\leq j\rho.$ (14)

At each macro-step $m$ , the manager’s context prediction satisfiesManager context error.

$d_{\mathcal{C}}(c_{mk},\hat{c}_{m})\leq\beta_{H}.$ (15)

Assume the local dynamics model has one-step approximation errorLocal one-step modeling and interface error.

$d_{\mathcal{S}}\!\left(f(s,c,a),\hat{f}(s,c,a)\right)\leq\varepsilon_{f}.$ (16)

We further collect action-representation and latent/interface approximation errors into a single quantity $\eta$ :

$d_{\mathcal{S}}\!\left(f(s,c,a),\hat{f}(s,c,\tilde{a})\right)\leq\eta,\qquad\eta:=\varepsilon_{f}+L_{a}\delta_{a}+\delta_{x},$ (17)

where $L_{a}\delta_{a}$ bounds the error induced by action approximation and $\delta_{x}$ collects additional latent or interface approximation error. In continuous-action or continuous-latent settings, these terms need not arise from discretization and may be smaller when no discretization interface is used.

Derivation.

Define the open-loop rollout error

$e_{t}:=d_{\mathcal{S}}(s_{t},\hat{s}_{t}).$ (18)

For a local step $t=mk+j$ , we have

$\displaystyle e_{t+1}$ $\displaystyle=d_{\mathcal{S}}(s_{t+1},\hat{s}_{t+1})$ $\displaystyle=d_{\mathcal{S}}\!\left(f(s_{t},c_{t},a_{t}),\hat{f}(\hat{s}_{t},\hat{c}_{m},\tilde{a}_{t})\right).$ (19)

By the triangle inequality,

$\displaystyle e_{t+1}$ $\displaystyle\leq d_{\mathcal{S}}\!\left(f(s_{t},c_{t},a_{t}),f(\hat{s}_{t},\hat{c}_{m},a_{t})\right)+d_{\mathcal{S}}\!\left(f(\hat{s}_{t},\hat{c}_{m},a_{t}),\hat{f}(\hat{s}_{t},\hat{c}_{m},\tilde{a}_{t})\right).$ (20)

Applying the Lipschitz condition in Eq. () to the first term gives

12

$\displaystyle d_{\mathcal{S}}\!\left(f(s_{t},c_{t},a_{t}),f(\hat{s}_{t},\hat{c}_{m},a_{t})\right)$ $\displaystyle\leq L_{s}d_{\mathcal{S}}(s_{t},\hat{s}_{t})+L_{c}d_{\mathcal{C}}(c_{t},\hat{c}_{m}).$ (21)

Using the local error definition in Eq. (), Eq. () yields

17

20

$e_{t+1}\leq L_{s}e_{t}+L_{c}d_{\mathcal{C}}(c_{t},\hat{c}_{m})+\eta.$ (22)

It remains to bound the context mismatch. By the triangle inequality, slow context drift, and manager context error,

$\displaystyle d_{\mathcal{C}}(c_{t},\hat{c}_{m})$ $\displaystyle\leq d_{\mathcal{C}}(c_{t},c_{mk})+d_{\mathcal{C}}(c_{mk},\hat{c}_{m})$ $\displaystyle\leq j\rho+\beta_{H}.$ (23)

Substituting Eq. () into Eq. (), we obtain the MHWA one-step open-loop error bound

23

22

$e_{t+1}=e_{mk+j+1}\leq L_{s}e_{t}+\eta+L_{c}(\beta_{H}+j\rho).$ (24)

Comparison to a flat model.

For a controlled comparison, we match the local one-step error $\eta$ and isolate the effect of context inference. Let a flat model re-infer context at every step, with per-step context error bounded by $\beta_{F}$ . Its analogous error recursion is

$e^{F}_{t+1}\leq L_{s}e^{F}_{t}+\eta+L_{c}\beta_{F}.$ (25)

For matched current rollout error $e_{t}=e_{t}^{F}$ , MHWA has a one-step upper bound no larger than the flat model’s whenever

$\beta_{H}+j\rho\leq\beta_{F}.$ (26)

Since the worst case within a stride window is $j=k-1$ , a sufficient condition over the whole window is

$\beta_{H}+(k-1)\rho\leq\beta_{F}.$ (27)

This condition identifies when the strided context yields a one-step error bound no larger than the flat model’s.

Implications for transfer across settings.

The comparison above does not rely on discrete actions or tokenized latent interfaces: discrete-action Atari is one special case, while continuous actions and continuous latent interfaces are covered by the same metric-space formulation, with interface effects absorbed into $\eta$ . Likewise, in this narrow architectural sense, the comparison does not depend on whether the model is trained offline or online; it depends on the achieved error terms $(\beta_{H},\beta_{F},\eta,\rho)$ rather than on how they are learned.

F.1

The factorial ablation in Table  retains the manager, Context Projector, context-conditioned router, and stride- $k$ broadcasting in all four configurations. With $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ on, the manager is trained by high-level supervision and, when stop-gradient is off, also by low-level objectives. With $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ off, the manager is fixed-weight when stop-gradient is on and trained only by low-level objectives when it is off. The Context Projector, router, and worker remain trainable throughout. MoE-only removes the complete manager pathway and widens the low-level experts to match model size.

3

We train two additional information controls under the $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ -off, stop-gradient-on setting. Both preserve the fixed-weight manager, trainable Context Projector, worker, MoE, parameter count, and $k=4$ broadcasting. They replace the manager hidden state after stop-gradient with zeros or Gaussian noise during both training and evaluation. Zero input produces a learned constant context through the projector bias; Gaussian noise is scaled using batch RMS and varies across context blocks.

: Table 11Information controls for the fixed-weight manager pathway. All variants are separately trained in the 44M/6-game setting with $\mathcal{L}_{high}$ off and stop-gradient on.

The trajectory-conditioned hidden state improves IQM over both controls. Its Median HNS is close to that of the zero-input variant, while IQM captures the larger separation across the six-game score distribution.

F.2

Table  varies expert number, Top- $K$ , and expert-MLP expansion in the 44M/6-game setting. Let $r_{0}$ denote the default expansion ratio. The $N=2$ , Top-1 configuration doubles the expansion, while $N=8$ , Top-4 halves it to keep total expert parameters comparable to the default. The $N=4$ , Top-1 variant keeps the default expert bank; the $N=8$ , Top-2 variant keeps the default per-expert expansion.

12

: Table 12Expert configuration study. IQM HNS on the six-game ablation benchmark.

Four-expert Top-1 retains 96% of the default IQM, and the eight-expert alternatives retain 87–91%. The two-expert configuration shows the largest drop, reflecting the effect of coarser capacity partitioning.

For each configuration, we aggregate final-layer expert activation frequencies for the six games, fit PCA independently, and rank the 15 pairwise distances in the three-dimensional projection. Table  reports the rank of the Assault–Phoenix pair. This neighborhood is closest for both Top-2 configurations, while Top-1 reorganizes cross-task sharing. Under four-expert Top-1, Centipede–SpaceInvaders moves from the default’s 15th-ranked pair to the 6th-ranked pair; their raw returns are 8950.4 and 917.8, respectively, and the six-game Median HNS is 0.516. For two experts, the normalized usage vector has one effective degree of freedom.

13

: Table 13Routing neighborhoods across expert configurations. Rank of the Assault–Phoenix distance among 15 game pairs in each configuration’s PCA projection; rank 1 is the closest pair.

Experts $N$ Top- $K$ Assault–Phoenix distance rank4214114821844

F.3

The manager sampling stride $k$ determines the temporal spacing of its inputs and the high-level prediction scale. The context-refresh interval $r$ determines how often the projected context is refreshed for low-level routing. The default uses $k=r=4$ .

We first vary only $r$ at inference using the same checkpoint trained with $k=r=4$ . The manager retains its $k=4$ input spacing and maximum context length, with sliding-window refreshes at $r=2$ or $r=1$ . We then retrain with $k=4,r=2$ throughout training and evaluation, allowing the router and worker to adapt to the alternative schedule. Table  separates these results.

14

: Table 14Context-refresh schedules at fixed manager stride $k=4$ . The inference-only variants use the default checkpoint; the retrained variant uses $r=2$ during both training and evaluation.

: Table 15Per-game results after retraining with $k=4,r=2$ . Raw returns under the same 44M/6-game protocol.

After retraining, $r=2$ improves Carnival and Centipede and lowers returns on the other four games. The resulting aggregate performance is comparable to the default schedule, with a higher Median and a slightly lower IQM. Changing the refresh schedule redistributes game-level performance while preserving the manager’s learned temporal scale.

Appendix G

We further evaluate open-loop rollouts beyond the context window. Starting from four ground-truth context frames, each model autoregressively predicts frames from $t=5$ to $t=54$ while conditioning on the same action sequence. As shown in Figure , the result shows that MHWA exhibits smoother degradation than the smaller monolithic baseline and remains broadly comparable to the 150M baseline. Importantly, the most visible anomaly in JOWA-150M around $t=17$ is not a uniform collapse across games; it is mainly driven by a sharp fluctuation on DemonAttack at $t=17$ – $20$ , while the same game/timestep does not show a comparable spike for the other models. This diagnostic is intended to test the smoothness of error accumulation rather than to claim indefinitely stable long-horizon generation.

4

: Figure 4Long-horizon open-loop reconstruction diagnostic from $t=5$ to $t=54$ .

MHWA shows smoother long-horizon degradation than the smaller monolithic baseline and remains broadly comparable to, while being less affected by sharp fluctuations than, the 150M baseline; however, it does not eliminate eventual manifold departure.

Appendix H

Broader impacts.

This work studies offline model-based reinforcement learning and world modeling in Atari benchmark environments. A potential positive impact is improved compute efficiency for training world models, which may lower the resource barrier for research on sample-efficient decision making. The main risks are indirect: more capable model-based RL systems could eventually be used in domains where inaccurate rollouts, distribution shift, or unsafe planning decisions may cause harm. Our experiments are limited to benchmark video games and do not involve deployment, human-subject data, personal data, or safety-critical decision making. We therefore view the immediate societal risk of this work as limited, while noting that future applications of model-based RL in real-world control should require domain-specific safety evaluation, uncertainty estimation, and deployment safeguards.

Safeguards.

The paper does not release a high-risk foundation model, image/text generator, scraped dataset, personal dataset, or deployed decision-making system. The code release is intended for reproducing Atari benchmark experiments. The datasets used are public benchmark datasets, and the trained models operate in Atari-like simulated environments. As a result, we do not identify a need for special access restrictions beyond standard research-use documentation and citation of the underlying assets.

Existing assets and licenses.

We use the public version of the Atari replay data from RL Unplugged, which follows the DQN Replay data distribution used in prior offline Atari work. We cite the original DQN Replay Dataset, RL Unplugged, JOWA, and other baseline methods used for comparison. We also reuse the pretrained tokenizer interface from JOWA for a controlled comparison within the same tokenized world-action framework. Our supplementary code release will include instructions for obtaining the public datasets and pretrained components from their original sources, and users should follow the corresponding licenses and terms of use of those upstream assets. We do not introduce a new dataset.rlu-atari

item.title: 在梦里学会、在真局里赢：十英雄 MOBA 的连续 Dyna 闭环 ｜ Learning in Dreams, Winning in Reality: A Continuous Dyna Loop for a Ten-Hero MOBA
item.description:
一句话：策略只在世界模型里训练，真实游戏只负责出数据和做评估，胜率从 33.7% 提到 70.2%。

要点：

  • 世界模型覆盖一整局十英雄 MOBA：206 个单位、每个英雄每 tick 都行动、单局最长 6000 tick
  • 策略完全在冻结的世界模型里用 1400 tick 的自由推演回合训练，真实游戏不提供梯度
  • 异步连续 Dyna 闭环把「真实对局→世界模型训练数据」与「在线评估筛选策略」接起来：天辉方胜率 70.2%（421/600），纯想象训练为 0%，闭环前为 33.7%

为什么值得看：给出了没有大规模真机算力时的替代训练架构：世界模型负责学，真实环境只负责少量在线评估与锚定。

中文摘要：大多数世界模型是从内部评估的：预测损失、想象中策略的回报、帧看起来像不像。这篇改成从外部评估——只问策略在真游戏里赢不赢。作者为完整的十英雄 MOBA 学了一个结构化多智能体世界模型（206 个单位、每个英雄每 tick 行动、单局最长 6000 tick），策略完全在其中用 1400 tick 的自由推演回合训练，真实游戏既不给梯度，也不反复调用。真实对局只提供两样东西：策略自己打出的对局作为世界模型的训练数据，以及一个在线评估来挑选与锚定策略。把两者接成异步连续的 Dyna 闭环后，天辉方在从未参与任何决策的随机种子上赢下 70.2%（600 局中 421 局，95% 置信区间 66.4–73.7），而只在梦里训练时为 0%，闭环前为 33.7%。天灾方仍然一局未胜，作者并未隐藏这一点。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.AI（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.08033v1 [cs.AI] 06 Oct 2026

Learning in Dreams, Winning in Reality:

A Continuous Dyna Loop for a Ten-Hero MOBA

Jordy Kieto

Affiliation: Code, world models, policies, evaluation and videos:

https://github.com/JordyKieto/puffermoba-dyna

Affiliation: Figures notebook:

docs/moba/paper/figures.ipynb

Affiliation: Companion reports: ;

Imitation Learning for Autonomous Driving in CARLA

Affiliation:

Neural Simulator: Lightweight World Models for Continuous Interactive Environments

Abstract

World models are usually judged from the inside: by their prediction loss, by the return a policy earns in imagination, or by how convincing their frames look. We judge one from the outside. We learn a structured, multi-agent world model of a complete ten-hero MOBA (206 units, every hero acting every tick, games of up to 6,000 ticks), train a policy only inside it with 1,400-tick free-running imagined episodes, and measure that policy in the real game against the opponent the game ships with. The real game never provides a gradient. It provides two things: the policy’s own games as training data for the world model, and an online evaluation that selects and anchors the policy. With these, run as a continuous asynchronous Dyna loop, the policy wins 70.2% of real games as radiant (421 of 600; 95% CI 66.4–73.7) on seeds never used for any decision, up from 0% for dream training alone and 33.7% before the loop. It wins none as dire, and neither does the shipped opponent when it plays itself. Four findings explain the result. Model exploitation is invisible from inside the dream: every unanchored run collapsed within a few updates while no in-dream metric tracked the collapse. A world model that is accurate on its training corpus is badly wrong on the policy’s own games, and Dyna repairs it there, which is worth $+9.2$ points of real win rate with the policy recipe held fixed. Finally, the policy inherits its world model’s fidelity profile mechanic by mechanic: the model represents the macro game and not crowd control, cast timing or lethality, and the policy wins by map-wide pressure with almost no coordinated fighting.

A policy trained only in a learned simulator of a ten-hero MOBA wins most of its real radiant games, but only once real data repairs the simulator where the policy goes and real games keep the policy honest; what it learns, and fails to learn, follows the simulator’s fidelity, mechanic by mechanic.TL;DR.

The policy, trained only in the world model, in a real game against the shipped PufferNet, drawn by the game’s own client. The world-model debugger: the real game and the dream start from the same state and receive the same actions of all ten heroes; after 300 ticks of open loop, lines join each predicted hero to its true position. The paper is about the gap between these two panels.Figure 1: (a)(b)

1

Learned world models now render playable games  and train agents with a fraction of the real experience model-free methods need . The evidence behind that progress comes in two forms. Either the model is scored on its own terms (likelihood, frame fidelity, human preference), or an agent is trained with it, usually from short imagined rollouts branched off real states while real experience keeps flowing in. Neither form answers the question a practitioner faces when the real environment is slow, expensive or unsafe: [, , ]

1

2

3

[, , ]

4

5

3

if a policy learns by long, free-running imagination in a learned model, what does it actually learn, and does it survive contact with reality?

This report is the third in a line of work on that question. The first asked whether a policy can learn to drive from demonstrations ; the second whether a compact learned model can stand in for a simulator under continuous control . Here we close the loop: learn a world, teach an agent inside it, and judge the agent only in the real world.[]

6

[]

7

We pick a setting that stresses every weakness of a learned simulator. PufferLib’s MOBA  has 206 units (heroes, creep waves, neutral camps, towers), fifteen abilities with cooldowns, mana and crowd control, ten agents acting at every tick, and games that last thousands of ticks. Our policy trains on 1,400-tick imagined episodes. That is the regime model-based RL is designed to avoid: latent-imagination agents typically imagine 15 to 20 steps , and model-based policy optimisation keeps rollouts short precisely because model error compounds with horizon . We evaluate the way the question demands: real games, a fixed and strong opponent, seeds never touched by any decision, and confidence intervals.[]

8

[, ]

9

5

[, ]

10

11

The story in one paragraph.

Dream training alone wins nothing. Long episodes with a win reward and less reward for what the dream overpays (experience) bring the policy to a third of real radiant games. Then every attempt to train further collapses: real win rate drops to near zero within a handful of updates, at any learning rate we tried, while the dream reports steady progress. The cause is the oldest problem of learning in a model , exploitation, but in a form we could only see from outside: real kills and deaths fall in lockstep with real wins, because the policy is learning to stop fighting, while nothing measured inside the dream tracks it. Two remedies, applied together, turn the collapse into steady improvement. A continuous Dyna loop  retrains the world model on the policy’s newest real games, which repairs the model exactly where the policy goes; and a KL anchor ties the policy to the best real-game policy so far, an anchor that moves only when a candidate wins on fresh seeds. The resulting policy wins 70% of its real radiant games. When we look at it wins, we find that it plays the game its world model can represent: the macro game of lanes and towers, not the micro game of stuns, timed heals and burst kills.[]

12

[]

13

how

Findings.

Each is measured (Section ); the last is an inference supported by two independent measurements.

5

1.

A policy trained only on 1,400-tick dreams wins 70.2% of real radiant games. A ladder of policies evaluated on the same untouched games attributes the gain to its ingredients: 0%, 1.3%, 5.7%, 33.7%, 53.0%, 70.2%.Long free-running imagination can transfer.

2.

Over the collapse, dream reward, dream experience, dream deaths, policy entropy and update size all fail to track real wins ( $|r|\leq 0.37$ ); real kills and deaths track them ( $r=0.84$ , $0.82$ ). Online real-game evaluation is part of the method, not only of the reporting.Exploitation is invisible from inside the dream.

3.

On the policy’s own games, the pre-Dyna model predicts 1.79 $\times$ the real number of tower falls (it is well calibrated on its corpus) and is worse than predicting no change for hero and tower health. After Dyna, tower falls are within 16% and hero position error after 200 ticks drops 2.4 $\times$ . With the policy recipe held fixed, the Dyna-trained model is worth $+9.2$ points [3.5, 14.7] of real win rate.A world model is wrong where the policy goes, and Dyna repairs it there.

4.

Measured mechanic by mechanic on the policy’s games, the model reproduces towers, lanes and aggregate damage, and misses crowd control (17% of real stuns), cast timing and lethality (heroes die 2.4 $\times$ too rarely). The policy’s real play mirrors this: it takes more towers than the shipped net, but it groups 9% of the time (the net 54%), stuns before 7% of its kills (26%) and trades 3.3 deaths per kill.The policy inherits its world model’s fidelity profile.

Contributions beyond the findings.

A that treats the learned simulator as an experimental subject: paired real and imagined timelines on identical actions, a field-by-field decomposition of every unit, an event layer, and a batch mode that turns every view into a metric (Section ). An for dream-trained policies under repeated online selection, with seed sets whose biases are stated and an untouched holdout for reporting (Section ). And the system itself, released in full: the world model, the dream-PPO harness with an exact GPU port of the opponent, the asynchronous loop, every policy, log and video, at a whole-project cost of $382 in attributed cloud spend.world-model debugger

4.4

evaluation protocol

3

What we do not claim.

We do not claim the policy beats the shipped net at the game: the net wins every one of its own radiant games, in less than half the time. We make no claim about the dire side, where nothing wins. And we make no sample-efficiency claim: the loop played about 46,000 real games, most of them to choose checkpoints.

2

Learning inside a learned model.

Dyna  interleaves real experience, model learning and planning on simulated experience; our system is Dyna with the three processes running asynchronously and at scale. Ha and Schmidhuber  trained a controller entirely inside a learned dream and observed it exploiting the dream’s errors, which they countered by making the dream noisier. We meet the same exploitation in a much larger multi-agent world, show that it cannot be detected from inside the dream, and counter it with real data and real-game anchoring instead.[]

13

[]

12

Latent imagination and short horizons.

The Dreamer line , IRIS  and DIAMOND  learn behaviours from imagined rollouts of 15–20 steps started from real states, with real data collected throughout; multi-agent variants on StarCraft micromanagement follow the same design . MBPO  argues for short model rollouts on the grounds that error compounds with horizon, a long-standing observation . We work in the regime these methods avoid, 1,400-step free-running episodes in a ten-agent world, and report what it takes to make it transfer and what it costs.[, ]

9

4

[]

5

[]

3

[]

14

[]

10

[]

11

Generative interactive games.

GameNGen , Genie , DIAMOND’s game model  and Oasis  generate playable worlds and are judged by visual quality and human play. Our model is symbolic and full-state, small (0.66 M parameters), and judged by what an agent trained in it does in the real game.[]

1

[]

2

[]

3

[]

15

Model quality and control quality.

The objective mismatch of model-based RL  is that a model’s likelihood does not predict the controller’s performance; MuZero  sidesteps reconstruction altogether. We add a mechanistic version of the mismatch: fidelity measured per game mechanic, on the policy’s own state distribution, predicts of play the policy acquires.[]

16

[]

17

what kind

Regularising against exploitation.

Offline model-based RL penalises model uncertainty ; behaviour-regularised RL keeps the policy close to a reference , as RL from human feedback does with a KL term . Our anchor is such a reference, chosen and moved by real-game performance on fresh seeds: a cheap, online form of the same idea.[, ]

18

19

[]

20

[]

21

MOBA and RTS agents.

OpenAI Five  and AlphaStar  reached top human level by training in the real game at enormous scale. We study the opposite corner: no real gradients, a small model and a small budget.[]

22

[]

23

Evaluation practice.

We follow the advice of Henderson et al.  and Agarwal et al.  on seeds, intervals and selection, and adds untouched seed sets to keep repeated online selection from inflating the reported number.[]

24

[]

25

3

The game and the opponent.

We use the MOBA from PufferLib’s Ocean suite , unmodified (upstream commit ), wrapped so that every game is deterministic and every state can be captured and restored byte for byte (a restored state continues identically in 99 of 99 tests). Two teams of five heroes (support, assassin, burst, tank, carry) fight over three lanes of creep waves, neutral camps, 22 towers and two ancients; a game ends when an ancient falls, or at 6,000 ticks. Our policy controls all five heroes of one side. The other side is the , the policy PufferLib distributes for this game, run from the same code that recorded our data.[]

8

42f70d69shipped PufferNet

Data.

Every real game is stored as a seed plus actions and replayed into dense per-tick state, verified by state hash. Table  lists the corpora. The world model starts from 2,000 games of the shipped net, scripted bots and random play; by the end, 70% of all real games are the loop’s own policy playing.

1

Real-game data. 10,700 games and 234 GB in total. Ticks are counted where measured.Table 1:

Evaluation protocol.

A policy is only ever judged in the real game against the shipped net; the world model scores nothing. Because the loop selects checkpoints from real games, we separate the seeds used for selection from the seeds used for reporting (Table ). Every win rate in this paper comes from the untouched holdout sets, with 95% Wilson intervals, and Newcombe intervals for differences. A game that reaches the time limit counts as not won. Evaluation is deterministic: re-running four policies on the holdout reproduced every count exactly. The two selection sets are visibly optimistic, which is why they exist: the pre-loop policy that looked best on the per-update set (45%) wins 34% on the holdout, and the final anchor wins 74% on the gate set and 70% on the holdout.

2

Seed sets. Only the holdout sets are ever reported as win rates.Table 2:

4

4.1

The world model is a token model of the full game state. Each of the 206 units is one token carrying its position, health, mana, experience, ability and attack cooldowns, stun, slow and movement timers, alive and hit flags, and a $9\times 9$ patch of nearby walls; a global token carries the phases of the creep-wave, neutral-respawn and rescan clocks. At every tick the actions of all ten heroes enter as inputs. Two pre-LayerNorm transformer blocks mix the 207 tokens with full attention and a learned distance and team bias, a GRU per unit carries memory across ticks, and typed heads predict regression targets, events and classes (0.66 M parameters in total). We train it the way it will be used: autoregressively on its own predictions, in chunks of 16 ticks over spans of up to 4,096, with loss weights that decay along the rollout, plus a penalty on predicted tower deaths that do not happen, which calibrates tower falls. Training is federated across a fleet of A40 GPUs that average weights every 50 updates .[]

26

What is not learned.

Unit spawns (creep waves, neutral camps), creep constants, a hero’s level from its experience and the statistics that follow from level, counters and value clamps are supplied by hand-coded rules inherited from the first version of the model. Everything dynamic is learned: movement, fights, damage, healing, mana, cooldowns, stuns, experience, deaths with their same-tick respawn, and tower destruction. Every result includes the rules; no rule was added for any result reported here.

4.2

The policy is PufferLib’s MOBA policy (an encoder and a six-layer MinGRU), one network shared by the five heroes of a side, acting on the game’s own 510-byte egocentric observation. In the dream, observations are rebuilt from imagined state (byte-identical to the game’s on real states), and the opponent is the shipped net ported to the GPU (logits within $5\times 10^{-6}$ of the original). Our side is drawn at random in each imagined game. Episodes last 1,400 ticks; eight A40s averaging weights after every PPO update reach about 135,000 agent steps per second. The reward is the game’s own, reweighted: $\pm 100$ for winning or losing, shaping for tower damage and falls, champion kills and siege presence, the game’s experience reward halved because the dream overpays for farming, and, in the final configuration, no death penalty.

4.3

Four processes run concurrently and never wait for one another. A world-model fleet trains without stopping, drawing a quarter of every batch from the hundred most recent real games of the current policy and publishing a checkpoint every 200 updates (about seven minutes). A PPO fleet trains without stopping and swaps each new world model in at the same update on every rank. A collector plays the newest policy against the shipped net and streams the recorded games to the world model. An evaluator plays 60 real games per side for every new policy.

Anchoring and drift.

The policy’s loss includes $0.3\cdot\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\text{anchor}}\,\|\,\pi)$ , where the anchor is the best real-game policy so far. A policy that matches the anchor on the per-update seeds is played 300 games per side on the fresh seeds, and replaces the anchor if it wins at least nine more radiant games, about one standard error. If three consecutive evaluations fall to half the anchor’s wins, every rank restarts from the anchor.

4.4

Aggregate losses say a world model is wrong; they do not say where, when, about whom or about which mechanic, and those are the questions that decide what a policy trained inside it will learn. The debugger is built to answer them, and its design follows from treating the model as an experimental subject (Figure ).that

2

The real game and the dream start from the real state and receive the recorded actions of all ten heroes at every tick; after a short warm-up the dream runs open loop on its own predictions, so any difference between the two panels is the model’s own accumulated error with the agents’ choices held fixed. Every frame of the window is precomputed, so the whole game can be scrubbed, stepped and rewound instantly along a timeline that shows where in the game the model is running; divergence can be traced to the tick where it begins. Any of the 206 units can be decomposed field by field, real against model, with the unit ringed in both panels, so a global error becomes a statement about one unit, one field and one tick. An event layer makes the exploitable mechanics visible: ability casts (detected by cooldown resets), hero deaths (a same-tick jump to base at full health), tower falls, and key presses, which separate a key that was pressed from an ability that actually fired. A ghost overlay draws the true positions on the dream, and every divergence readout sits next to the error of predicting no change. Finally, everything the window shows comes from a programmable replay object, so each view becomes a batch metric over hundreds of windows. Sections  and  are built from that batch mode.samesame

5.3

5.6

Entity decomposition in the debugger, after 300 ticks of open loop on a real game of the policy (Dyna world model). The radiant support, field by field: the dream has its heal just cast (W cooldown 21; real 0) and has missed the stun it really cast (E cooldown 2; real 26). Over the window the dream fired 269 casts against 95 real ones. The mechanics result of Section  in a single tooltip.Figure 2:

5.6

5

5.1

Table  gives the holdout results. The final anchor wins 213 of 300 radiant games on the holdout and 208 of 300 on the second untouched set, 70.2% pooled [66.4, 73.7]. That is 37.3 points [29.6, 44.4] above the policy that started the loop and 18.0 points [10.3, 25.4] above the loop’s first run. The radiant side alone wins nothing: an untrained policy wins none of its 300 radiant games and takes 0.17 towers per game. Two baselines keep the number honest. The shipped net playing itself wins all 300 of its radiant games, in about 2,270 ticks; our policy wins 70% and needs about 5,540. And as dire, no policy wins: not ours, and not the shipped net against itself. Our dire play is barely better than random, losing in about 1,290 ticks where a random policy lasts 1,090 and the net 2,270.

3

Real games against the shipped net on the holdout seeds (300 per side). Game length in ticks.Table 3:

5.2

Before the anchor, training could not be continued. Two runs of the loop, at learning rates six-fold apart, rose to about 30 wins in 60 and then fell to between zero and eight within four to six updates, again and again, needing nine resets between them (Figure ). Lowering the learning rate shrank each update threefold and changed nothing about how many updates the collapse took. Over the collapse of the slower run, no quantity measured inside the dream tracked real performance (Figure , left): dream reward ( $r=0.23$ ), dream experience ( $0.29$ ), dream deaths ( $0.16$ ), our dream towers ( $-0.10$ ), policy entropy ( $-0.37$ ). The real game told a clear story. Real kills and real deaths fell together with real wins ( $r=0.84$ and $0.82$ ), and the games stretched to the time limit: the policy was learning to stop fighting. The dream’s death penalty, together with its overpayment for safe experience, made disengagement look good in imagination. An ablation from the same starting policy separates the remedies: removing the entropy bonus changes nothing, removing the death penalty delays the collapse by about ten updates, and a KL anchor to the starting policy prevents it. With both changes in the loop, the run never needed a reset and moved its anchor four times in 69 updates, from 53% to 70% on the holdout.

3

4

Real radiant wins out of 60 after every PPO update. Without an anchor the policy collapses repeatedly (grey lines: drift resets); with the death penalty removed and a KL anchor it holds and improves (green lines: a new anchor confirmed on fresh seeds).Figure 3:

During a collapse, nothing measured in the dream tracks real wins (left), while the policy’s real behaviour does: real kills (middle) and deaths (right) per hero and game against real wins, coloured by game length.Figure 4:

5.3

On its training corpus the pre-Dyna world model is a good model of towers: 71% precision on tower falls, with the predicted rate matching the real one. On the policy’s own games it is a poor one. We collected 100 real games of the final policy after every model we compare had been saved, so none trained on them, and ran each model open loop from many points in those games. The pre-Dyna model predicts 1.79 times the real number of tower falls at 29% precision, and after 200 ticks its errors in hero and tower health exceed those of simply predicting that nothing changes (Table , Figure ). This is the distribution the policy optimises against, and it is wrong in the policy’s favour. Training on the policy’s newest games repairs it: the Dyna world model predicts 1.16 times the real number of tower falls at 52% precision and cuts hero position error at 200 ticks from 22.8 to 9.7 cells.

4

5

World models on the final policy’s own real games (unseen by every model). Open-loop error after 200 ticks (300 windows) and tower falls over 128-tick windows (5,265 windows).Table 4:

Open-loop divergence from the real game on the policy’s own games, by horizon. The pre-Dyna model (pink) is worse than predicting no change (dotted) for hero and tower health; the Dyna models are better at every horizon.Figure 5:

What the repair is worth.

To isolate the world model from everything else the loop changed, we froze it and trained the same recipe from the same start (the loop’s first-run policy, 53% on the holdout) for 40 updates, twice per model with different seeds. In the pre-Dyna dream the policy ends at 49.0% [45.0, 53.0], slightly below where it started; in the Dyna-trained dream it ends at 58.2% [54.2, 62.0]. The world model alone is worth 9.2 points [3.5, 14.7] (Table , right).

5

5.4

Table  (left) evaluates one representative policy per stage of the project on the same holdout games. The rungs are separate experiments with their own seeds and lengths, so a rung’s step is what a change added in practice rather than a matched estimate; the matched estimate for the world model is the control on the right. Dream training with the game’s reward and short episodes wins nothing. Long episodes with a win reward produce the first wins, and the largest single step comes from halving the reward for experience, which the dream overpays. The Dyna loop and the anchor account for the rest.

5

Left: one change per rung, radiant wins on the holdout (the last rung pools both untouched sets). Right: the frozen-world-model control.Table 5:

5.5

We played 20 holdout games each with the final policy, the pre-loop policy and the shipped net on the radiant side, and recorded every hero at every tick (Table , Figure ). The policy does not win by teamwork. Its heroes are within eight cells of two others 9% of the time; the shipped net’s are 54% of the time. It takes about ten enemy towers per game, more than the net’s six, but most fall with fewer than one of our heroes nearby: creeps do the damage while heroes keep up the pressure. It trades lives freely, 3.3 deaths per kill. Its support casts its area heal as often as the net’s does, and the heal reaches 0.13 allies per cast against the net’s 0.83. Two heroes of ours on the same enemy do focus fire, but they are rarely on the same enemy. The occupancy maps say the rest: the net marches all five heroes down the middle lane and wins in under 2,300 ticks, while our policy spreads over every lane and the jungle and wins by attrition. The loop did not change this strategy; the pre-loop policy plays the same way and converts less of it.

6

6

Behaviour in real radiant games (20 holdout games each).Table 6:

Where the radiant heroes spend their time, over 20 games each: the pre-loop policy (left), the final policy (middle) and the shipped net (right). The net moves as one group down the middle lane; both dream-trained policies cover the whole map.Figure 6:

5.6

To see why the policy plays this way, we measured the world model mechanic by mechanic on the policy’s own games. Each event (an ability cast, a heal, a displacement such as a blink strike or a hook, the start of a stun or a slow, a hero death, a tower fall) is detected in the real game and in the dream and matched by hero within four ticks, over 64-tick open-loop windows. Table  sets the result beside the policy’s behaviour.

7

Fidelity of the Dyna world model per mechanic (precision / recall / predicted-to-real count, on the policy’s own games), beside the policy’s real behaviour.Table 7:

The pattern is one to one. What the dream represents well, the policy has learned and uses: towers fall at the right rate in the dream, and the policy is a better tower-taker than the net. What the dream lacks, the policy does not do: the dream has almost no stuns or slows and heals at the wrong moments, and the policy almost never sets up a kill with a stun or heals an ally in a fight. What the dream distorts, the policy exploits in the direction of the distortion: heroes in the dream survive fights that kill them in reality, and the policy over-extends. Aggregate quality hides all of this; the Dyna model is better on every aggregate measure, and the policy’s strategy did not change. Our reading is that a dream-trained policy’s competence is bounded by the fidelity of its world model, mechanic by mechanic.

This is an inference from two measurements, not yet an experiment. The test is an intervention: raise the dream’s fidelity for crowd control and lethality, or take those mechanics out of the real game, and check that stun-before-kill, ally healing and grouping move with it. Two observations do not fit the simplest version of the story. The policy casts abilities at the net’s rate although the dream over-fires them twofold, and the pre-loop policy already played the same macro strategy, which the loop sharpened rather than created.

6

Long imagination transfers if reality keeps it honest.

Short rollouts are the standard defence against compounding model error. We trained on 1,400-tick dreams and transferred anyway, but only behind two guardrails that live outside the dream: real data for the model, aimed where the policy goes, and real games that select and anchor the policy. Neither is visible from inside. The practical lesson is that a dream-trained policy needs an outside observer, and that the observer’s most informative signal is behavioural.

World models for control should be evaluated where the policy plays, per mechanic.

The pre-Dyna model looked good on its corpus and failed on the policy’s games; per-mechanic fidelity on the policy’s own data predicted the kind of play the policy would learn, and corpus loss did not. We suggest an event-level fidelity table on the target policy’s data, next to a persistence baseline, as a standard report for world models meant for policy learning.

The fidelity profile is also a research agenda.

The path beyond 70% is concrete: model crowd control, cast timing and lethality well enough that the dream rewards coordinated fights; teach defence, which no dream-trained policy here learned; and make the outside observer cheaper. Real kills and deaths track real wins at $r\approx 0.8$ , so a behavioural proxy measured on a few games per update could replace most of the 38,000 games the loop spent on selection.

On instruments.

Every mechanistic claim in this paper started as something seen in the debugger and became a number through its batch mode. For learned simulators, being able to ask which unit, which field, which tick and which mechanic is what turns a loss curve into an explanation.

7

All results are against one opponent, the shipped PufferNet, in a game that is lopsided under it; we claim that a dream-trained policy wins most radiant games, not that it is the better player. The dire side is unsolved. The loop runs are single seeds, and the headline is one policy’s score, the best of 13 policies ever evaluated on the holdout; the second untouched set reproduces it (69.3% against 71.0%). The matched control isolates the world model’s contribution at 9.2 points but not the remaining 12 between that control and the full loop, which differ in a refreshed model, a moving anchor, four times the GPUs and more updates. The world model contains hand-coded rules for spawns and level-derived statistics. The real game was used at scale for selection and data, about 46,000 games or roughly 0.2 billion real ticks against 0.5 billion imagined ones, so this is not a sample-efficiency result. Finally, two infrastructure incidents changed what ran: the first world-model fleet trained on one machine for most of its life after the others ran out of memory, and the collector stopped for two hours on a full disk; both are documented in the repository.

8

Everything is in the repository (): the deterministic game wrapper and the renderer that records the real client; the world model, dream PPO and arena; the loop, the evaluation service and the scripts that regenerate every number in this paper from the logs; and the figures notebook. Every evaluated policy is stored with its md5. A new anchor is reported by evaluating it on the two holdout sets and re-running two commands, which regenerate every table and figure.

https://github.com/JordyKieto/puffermoba-dyna

The whole project, including every failed direction, cost $382 in cloud spend attributed to it by machine identifier (279 machine-hours, 272 of them on GPUs), plus $214 of unattributed spend on the same account during the same period and about $100 before billing records begin. The expensive part was the world model, trained early on single H200s; the loop that produced the result ran on A40s at about $13 per hour and reached its best policy within about four hours of starting.

Acknowledgements

We thank the PufferLib authors for the MOBA environment and the shipped policy that served as our opponent.
