C.7

GameGoBench seeds were selected and separated from the training seeds before development of the task-construction pipeline, using stratified selection to cover rendering formats and implementation difficulties. Training and test data are strictly isolated from the seed stage onward: none of the 124 benchmark seeds, their derived specifications, queries, or trajectories enters any training set. The benchmark contains 47 2D, 22 2.5D, and 55 3D tasks, stratified into Easy, Medium, and Hard within each rendering format. The training and test seeds subsequently pass through the same specification and query-construction pipeline, which was not designed around the test set. Details of gameplay clustering and training-pool quotas are provided in Appendix .

C.2

Appendix D

The study evaluates task representations through fixed-teacher artifact comparisons and corpus utility through student fine-tuning. Direct queries are produced by DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp from source seeds, rewriting supported gameplay into self-contained browser-game requests without the multi-stage PRD. All 124 query identifiers match the PRD and task-specific conditions. Their median length is 227.5 tokens, close to 235 for task-specific queries; these are seed rewrites rather than PRD summaries. The held-out comparison evaluates the construction procedure without tuning it on GameGoBench.

Collecting high-quality teacher trajectories is the main cost of representation-level training comparisons. Each alternative query changes implementation decisions, tool interactions, execution feedback, and repairs, requiring a fresh sandbox rollout and subsequent student training. Repeating this process for direct queries and full PRDs at corpus scale would multiply the teacher-collection cost. We therefore compare all three representations through controlled artifact evaluations on the 124 held-out seeds, while concentrating large-scale trajectory collection and SFT on the task-specific queries. This design allocates teacher compute to the final training corpus and evaluates the representation choices under a shared teacher, scaffold, and interaction budget. The same confidential teacher is used for trajectory collection and the task-representation comparisons. In each comparison condition, the task input is the corresponding direct query, full PRD, or task-specific query; the compact condition does not additionally supply the full PRD or the three planning-stage outputs. The Base/MoE study additionally examines learning from a pretrained initialization.

The static analysis covers the same 124 GameGoBench tasks as the artifact comparisons. Paired text lengths measure compression, while an audit of 927 PRD clauses measures complete, partial, and absent expression in the task-specific queries. We report clause retention and density alongside artifact preferences on this shared task set. Downstream experiments evaluate the training utility of the collected corpus across model backbones.

Appendix E

E.1

The principal dense models are Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.8-27B, initialized from their corresponding instruction-tuned checkpoints. A separate Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE run is retained as an additional training study. All three runs apply SFT to all language-model parameters rather than using LoRA, while visual towers and aligners remain frozen. The final GameGoData corpus contains 55,060 trajectories, all of which are retained for both dense-model training runs after length filtering. The dense-model configurations and training counts are reported below.

The local training runs use NVIDIA H800 GPUs with approximately 80 GB per GPU, BF16 arithmetic, public random seed 42, and Linux. The dense runs use PyTorch 2.9.1+cu128, MS-SWIFT 4.4.0, Transformers 5.12.1, DeepSpeed 0.19.2, Megatron-Core 0.16.1, FlashAttention 2.8.3, and Transformer Engine 2.10.0. The training trajectories are converted directly into MS-SWIFT JSONL records with , , and . With , an over-length trajectory is removed as a whole rather than left- or right-truncated.messagestemplate=qwen3_5agent_template=qwen3_5padding_free=truetruncation_strategy=delete

Within each benchmark, all compared models use the same Code Arena scaffold, sandbox environment, and inference budget, as specified in the main text. For GameGoCoder and its matched base checkpoints, the inference settings are temperature $0.6$ , top- $p=0.95$ , at most 100 interaction steps, and a maximum of 65,536 generated tokens per model call. The dense models are served with vLLM in BF16 using tensor parallelism 8 and a 262,144-token context limit. Each model makes one generation attempt per query. The accompanying configurations specify training and inference settings.

E.2

Each dense model is trained for one epoch over its retained GameGo training subset. After length filtering, both the Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.8-27B runs contain 55,060 training trajectories. Both use fused AdamW, peak learning rate $1\times 10^{-5}$ , cosine decay to zero, 3% warm-up, $(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95)$ , $\epsilon=10^{-8}$ , weight decay $0.1$ , gradient clipping at $1.0$ , gradient checkpointing, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 with CPU-pinned optimizer offload. The effective global batch size is 8 and the maximum supported sequence length is 262,144 tokens.

The Qwen3.5 dense runs use 8 or 16 H800 GPUs across launches, reflecting resource allocation. Activation CPU offload supports long-context training. Checkpoints contain model, optimizer, scheduler, and RNG state. The final reported model is the last checkpoint of its corresponding SFT run.

E.3

The Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Base experiment uses 64 H800 GPUs with MS-SWIFT Megatron/Megatron-Core rather than DeepSpeed. Training runs for six epochs at sequence length 262,144 with 19,148 packed sequences. Tensor, pipeline, data, and expert parallelism are TP=8, PP=1, DP=8, and EP=8, with expert tensor parallelism ETP=1, context parallelism CP=1, and sequence parallelism enabled. The microbatch size is 1 and the global batch size is 128, corresponding to 16 microbatches per optimizer update on each data-parallel replica. The model has 256 routed experts and activates the top 8 experts per token.

The MoE run uses Adam with a linear learning-rate decay from $5\times 10^{-5}$ to $5\times 10^{-6}$ , no warm-up, $(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95)$ , $\epsilon=10^{-8}$ , weight decay $0.1$ , and gradient clipping at $1.0$ . Router computation uses FP32 with load-balancing coefficient $10^{-3}$ ; grouped GEMM, all-to-all dispatch, FlashAttention, fused cross entropy, and full uniform activation recomputation are enabled. Epoch checkpoints are checkpoint-149, -298, -447, -596, -745, and -894, with checkpoint-897 as the training endpoint. This run resumed from weights without restoring optimizer moments or RNG state. Restarted jobs preserve model weights and scheduler position and initialize fresh optimizer state.

E.4

The response-masked objective in the main text is implemented at message level. , , and tokens receive label $-100$ and contribute context only. Assistant thinking, assistant natural-language responses, and tool calls are supervised with their original token IDs. Tool calls are first serialized as assistant-side messages, whereas tool responses are serialized as messages. Consequently, the objective supervises the agent’s decisions and actions while preserving execution feedback as conditioning context.systemusertool_responsetool

E.5

We evaluate 413 ArtifactsBench-G tasks and 156 Cookie-Bench-G tasks using their official queries and evaluation pipelines, with Claude Sonnet 4.6 powering both verifier pipelines as in the main text. Each model generates one artifact for every query. Failed builds receive the score prescribed by the corresponding official evaluator. Table  reports task-level mean scores; comparisons with the corresponding base checkpoint use the same benchmark tasks. The reported values are task-level mean point estimates.

1

E.6

The main results use Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp and Qwen3.8-Max provide additional evaluations in Table . Each verifier configuration runs the two-stage protocol described in the main text: an interactive multimodal agent plays the game in a headless browser under step-driven execution, and a separate evaluation agent scores the resulting interaction trace. Each configuration collects its own observations. Requirements scores cover core concepts, input responsiveness, game loops, and query specifications; Quality scores use chronologically sampled frames to assess subject art, scene composition, and UI integration. Every model attempts 124 tasks, yielding $N_{\mathrm{repo}}$ React repositories, with counts from 117 to 124. Of these, $N_{\mathrm{render}}$ display a rendered page. The Execution Rate reported as Exec. in Table , called Render in the evaluation records, is $100N_{\mathrm{render}}/N_{\mathrm{repo}}$ . Tasks without a repository are excluded from this denominator; generated repositories that fail to render remain in it. This repository-conditioned rate measures rendering success; runtime behavior is additionally examined in the interactive traces. Repository availability and rendering success are separate stages. The three verifier configurations use the same generated repository sets and have identical Exec. scores. The main table retains Sonnet 4.6 results.

5

1

For verifier $j$ , the aggregate Overall score is $S_{j}=(\mathrm{Req}_{j}+Q_{j})/2$ , where $\mathrm{Req}_{j}$ and $Q_{j}$ are the aggregate Requirements and Quality scores. For each evaluated model, we report the cross-verifier mean $\bar{S}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{j=1}^{3}S_{j}$ and sample variance $s^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{3}(S_{j}-\bar{S})^{2}$ . These statistics summarize variation among the three verifier-level aggregate scores.

GameGoBench Overall scores under three verifiers. DS-Flash denotes DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp and Qwen denotes Qwen3.8-Max. Mean and variance are computed across the three verifiers from unrounded component scores; variance is in squared score points.Table 5:

The DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp and Qwen3.8-Max rankings have Spearman correlations of 0.964 and 0.976 with the Sonnet 4.6 ranking, respectively; their mean absolute Overall-score differences from Sonnet are 0.47 and 0.54 points. GameGoCoder 3.5 improves over its matched baseline by 17.85, 18.06, and 18.91 points under Sonnet, DeepSeek, and Qwen, respectively; the corresponding gains for GameGoCoder 3.8 are 2.76, 1.78, and 2.66 points. Thus, both matched-baseline improvements persist across all three verifiers, and the aggregate rankings remain similar. The three model families provide complementary automated evaluations with closely aligned aggregate rankings. The blinded human comparisons provide complementary evidence.

E.7

The trajectory analysis described in Figure  uses the same 124 GameGoBench query identifiers for each included model. Trajectories are aligned by , not by file order, and the three query groups contain 13, 40, and 71 tasks. We aggregate all assistant-generated content over turns for trajectory length, and report thinking length separately. Interaction steps count assistant turns with their resulting tool observations; simultaneous tool calls are retained as one step and their width is recorded independently. Build statistics count calls to and record the first and last build positions both in absolute steps and relative trajectory quartiles.

6

data_idbuild_project

For each model and metric, the supplementary analysis reports p10, p25, p50, p75, p90, p95, and p99 quantiles together with the interquartile range. Tool reliability is summarized at both the individual-call level and the per-trajectory level, while infrastructure failures are retained as a separate category rather than being silently treated as model errors. Most providers expose completion and reasoning usage directly; when usage is unavailable, we estimate the corresponding lengths with a common Qwen tokenizer. Those estimates support relative behavioral comparisons under a common tokenization scheme. The full per-query, tool-distribution, build-position, and group-stratified statistics are released as supplementary analysis artifacts.

Appendix F

The same six hired independent expert evaluators assess available playable artifact pairs from the 124 benchmark tasks; pair availability depends on the compared systems. For the model comparisons in Figure , both GameGoCoder variants are compared with the corresponding comparison models with model identities hidden. Each reviewer plays every eligible game from its start through the end of the playable experience before making a pairwise judgment. Sessions follow completion of the game rather than a fixed number of minutes. Reviewers select the first artifact, the second artifact, or a tie. The task-representation study reports 124 artifact pairs for each of its three comparisons. Reviewers assess fidelity, playability, and overall quality against the original seed. Table  pools their judgments across artifact pairs. Its win, tie, and loss counts are reviewer judgments rather than counts of distinct tasks, and the percentages use $W+T$ as the denominator. Full PRDs receive 69.0% preference against direct queries, while task-specific queries receive 85.7% against full PRDs and 86.6% against direct queries.

5

2

For the MoE checkpoint comparisons, all six reviewers assess each eligible artifact pair with checkpoint identities hidden. Table  includes only pairs for which both games are playable. Its $N$ values of 110, 108, and 123 count artifact pairs, while W/T/L pools reviewer judgments over those pairs. Epoch 2 receives preference scores of 0.852 against Base and 0.664 against the official post-SFT MoE checkpoint. Epoch 6 receives 0.807 against the official checkpoint. Each comparison uses its corresponding set of eligible playable pairs.

3

Both tables report W/T/L from the first system’s perspective and compute preference as $W/(W+L)$ , excluding ties. Each eligible artifact pair receives six judgments, which are pooled to obtain the reported preference. The MoE comparisons use the playable pairs listed in Table . Reviewer agreement is reported separately below.

3

Inter-reviewer agreement.

We report raw pairwise agreement among the six reviewers. For each evaluated artifact pair $i$ , let $n_{iW}$ , $n_{iT}$ , and $n_{iL}$ denote the numbers selecting a win, tie, and loss for the first system, with $n_{iW}+n_{iT}+n_{iL}=6$ . The fraction of the 15 reviewer pairs giving the same judgment is

$A_{i}=\frac{\sum_{c\in\{W,T,L\}}n_{ic}(n_{ic}-1)}{6\cdot 5}.$ (4)

Ties are retained as a separate judgment category. Averaged over the evaluated artifact pairs within each study, raw agreement is 82.5% for the model comparisons in Figure , 81.7% for the task-representation comparisons in Table , and 84.7% for the MoE checkpoint comparisons in Table . Each percentage summarizes the corresponding evaluation as a whole rather than every individual comparison row. These percentages report observed reviewer agreement across the three studies.

5

2

3

Appendix G

G.1

We analyze the stored PRDs and task-specific queries of all 124 GameGoBench tasks used in the artifact comparisons. Records are aligned by their original task identifiers across the PRD file and the query exports containing 40, 13, and 71 tasks. Three empty query fields in the exports are recovered from their archived gallery inputs and checked against the corresponding original query records. The analysis retains the fixed evaluation queries and records source hashes and recovery provenance.

Token lengths are measured with the Qwen3.5-27B tokenizer, with special tokens disabled and no chat template. We count the stored Markdown and serialized specifications. The first complete heading separates each PRD into its body and asset appendix. We compute retained length and compression for each matched task before aggregating. Table  reports medians of these per-task ratios alongside median text lengths.Deterministic Asset Execution Contract

6

G.2

Reference clauses are selected from PRD text before examining query coverage. A deterministic script extracts spans of 45 to 230 characters containing a condition or transition cue, prioritizing core mechanics and rule sections and using controls, progression, and other gameplay sections as a fallback. Asset, execution, feedback, color, shader, performance, and acceptance sections are excluded. Candidates are ordered by the SHA-256 hash of the task identifier and clause text, and up to eight are selected per task. The inventory is frozen before semantic annotation, with exact source paragraphs and clause hashes retained.

A single AI-assisted text audit reviews the 977 candidates and excludes 50 attribute lists, presentation or implementation requirements, and uninterpretable fragments, leaving 927 gameplay clauses across all 124 tasks. Each eligible clause is labeled when the query expresses the full dependency, including its stated conditions and parameters; when the mechanism is expressed with some conditions, values, or consequences unspecified; or when the dependency is unexpressed or contradicted. Complete and partial labels include exact query quotations. The scoring script checks source and query quotations, task alignment, and arithmetic. These semantic annotations are AI-assisted; the six independent expert evaluators separately judge the generated games.completepartialabsent

For task $s$ , the reference inventory $E_{s}$ contains its $n_{s}$ eligible clauses, and $K_{s}(q)$ counts the clauses labeled complete. We compute $R_{s}=K_{s}(q)/n_{s}$ , $D_{s}=1-R_{s}$ , and $G_{s}=R_{s}/r_{s}$ using the definitions in Appendix . Partial clauses are reported as a separate category, so $D_{s}$ includes both partial and absent clauses. Each reference clause is weighted equally. We report pooled clause percentages and medians of per-task coverage and density separately; all 124 tasks contribute to the medians, including tasks with zero complete coverage.

B

G.3

Median PRD and query lengths are 9,136 and 235 tokens. The median retained-length fraction is 2.26%, and median paired compression is $44.2\times$ ; compression relative to the PRD body is $21.6\times$ . Every query contains less than 5% of its full PRD’s tokens. Across the 927 eligible clauses, 112 are complete, 577 are partial, and 238 are absent. Median complete-clause coverage is 12.5%, and the median density gain is $3.79\times$ against full PRDs and $1.78\times$ against PRD bodies.

Text analysis of all 124 GameGoBench tasks. Lengths, coverage, and density gains are per-task medians; clause percentages pool the 927 eligible clauses. Compression is the median of paired token-count ratios. Complete coverage includes the clause’s stated conditions and parameters.Table 6:

The clause labels distinguish preserved mechanisms from complete specification detail. For example, the workshop-brawler query names an airborne dive strike, while the sampled PRD clause additionally specifies its velocity, damage, impact radius, and target-height restriction; this clause is labeled partial. The 56 tasks with no complete sampled clause contribute zero density gain. These text measurements characterize the same tasks whose generated games are compared in Table , connecting the analysis of execution requirements with artifact-level evaluation.

2

Appendix H

This appendix describes the implementation of the two pipelines used to construct tasks. The complete prompt specifications and routing policy will be released with the accompanying implementation upon acceptance, subject to applicable software licenses, as stated in the reproducibility statement. This release does not include GameGoData trajectories or their associated artifacts. The listings below record the canonical stage interfaces and the decisions that affect downstream execution. Both pipelines use three planning stages followed by canonical PRD compilation and task-adaptive query construction; downstream implementation executes the resulting query. They differ in the source envelope and the visual-asset contract.

H.1

The Image-Grounded Game Task Compiler accepts either an ordinary query or a record containing minimal text fields and at most five screenshots. The Text-Grounded Web-Game Task Compiler accepts an ordinary query or a web-game catalog record containing title, description, instructions, categories, and tags; it does not read screenshots or source URLs. In both cases, the execution order is:

In unattended batch production, both pipelines stop after Canonical + Compact and write one task-identifier/query record per input; execution is then run by the downstream trajectory-collection process. The three planning-stage outputs and the full PRD are internal construction representations; the task-specific query is the task description supplied for GameGoData collection. Each stage must emit its declared output before the next stage starts. The default revision budget is one revision per stage. Invalid JSON, failed schema checks, or failed asset-contract checks trigger this bounded revision; unresolved failures are retained as failed items rather than silently exported.

H.2

Stage 1 is the only stage that interprets the source record. It emits a self-contained, de-identified specification and does not prescribe the implementation architecture. The routing decisions are authoritative for all later stages:

•

exactly one primary category from the 20-category taxonomy, one finer-grained , and only implementation-relevant secondary tags. The output also lists archetype-specific required phases and a complete from entry to restart.Gameplay route:gameplay_archetypegameplay_flow_contract

•

for layered Canvas/SVG/Sprite interaction, for real 3D geometry under a fixed camera, and when play requires camera motion or free spatial observation. and concrete must agree with this choice.Rendering route:2d2.5d3dcamera_mobilitydimension_evidence

•

for a short fixed round and for non-interchangeable setup, progression, exploration, or multi-scene phases. The route is based on the required player journey, not on asset count or visual style.Scope route:compact_loopmulti_phase_journey

•

is selected only when the source contains explicit pixel-art evidence; otherwise the default is . The evidence is copied into .Asset route:procedural_pixelgenerated_hybridasset_production_evidence

For Steam inputs, screenshots are used only to record reliable ; uncertain visual inferences are separated and the source title, characters, locations, trademarks, and text are removed from the downstream request. For WebGame inputs, the visual plan is text-derived. The text-grounded pipeline therefore additionally emits , semantic visual anchors, and separate environment/entity/UI/typography color roles. These fields constrain later visual choices rather than adding unsupported style identity.image_only_factsvisual_evidence_level

H.3

Stage 2 consumes only the approved Stage-1 output and the de-identified source context. The pipeline loads a rendering overlay corresponding to the selected rendering branch and a gameplay profile selected by the primary category and archetype. The gameplay router always provides a core gameplay lens; it may additionally provide combat, level-flow, game-feel, or audio guidance when the approved seed contains the corresponding evidence. These lenses focus attention on failure-prone implementation relations and are explicitly forbidden from introducing new product requirements.

The deterministic skill policy is shared by the two pipelines. Stage 1 receives the routing-observer lens. Stage 2 starts with ; it adds for combat-oriented evidence, for spatial categories, 3D tasks, or multi-phase journeys, for action/arcade/rhythm-like categories, and when audio or mood is supported by the seed. Stage 2 is capped at four lenses. Stage 3 starts with and ; it may add for eligible 2D generated-hybrid tasks and when needed. The text-grounded pipeline additionally adds only when Stage 2 emits a concrete shader opportunity, and injects at most three technique metadata references. Skill selection is recorded per run and can be disabled for ablations.gameplay_coreaction_combatlevel_flowanimation_game_feelaudio_webart_bible_compactasset_source_gatesprite_pipelineaudio_webshader_fx

Stage 2 owns the canonical gameplay representation: , rules, controls, entities, progression, scene/state flow, camera and viewport contracts, feedback, implementation technology, and observable acceptance criteria. Stage 3 reads the approved seed and blueprint, loads the same rendering and gameplay routes, and owns only the executable asset plan. It maps each required scene, entity, UI element, transition, and feedback to a stable asset ID, source, dimensions, generation prompt or procedural construction, integration location, and scene coverage record. The text-grounded asset contract additionally supports project-owned inline shaders. Shader guidance is injected only when the blueprint contains an approved shader opportunity; at most three compact technique references are supplied, and the generated module must define its own uniforms, render state, performance bound, gameplay variation, and fallback.gameplay_flow_contract

H.4

Canonical compilation prevents later stages from redefining earlier decisions. Stage 1 owns product identity, source-derived constraints, routing, scope, and originality rules; Stage 2 owns gameplay and implementation; Stage 3 owns visual and audio realization. The compiler selects only these authoritative fields, replaces repeated prose with stable IDs and references, and removes the Stage-1 draft request once the blueprint has resolved it. For image-grounded assets, reference identity is redacted before downstream stages and graphic planning context is neutralized; for the text-grounded pipeline, shader contracts are reduced to executable project-owned modules rather than copied reference compositions.

Task-adaptive query construction recovers the authoritative rendering dimension, estimates semantic complexity from dependencies among player actions, states, and camera behavior, and checks the effect of removing each candidate clause. It retains a clause when removing it would change task identity, break the playable loop, make controls or space ambiguous, or remove a critical visual dependency. It deliberately leaves routine architecture, exhaustive counts, ordinary layout, and nonessential tuning open to the coding agent. The output is an English query plus an audit of preserved axes, protected risks, implementation freedom, complexity basis, and omitted detail.

H.5

The pipeline materializes structured outputs only after successful parsing and object-level checks. Required top-level fields are checked per stage; rendering branch consistency and cross-stage field ownership are enforced; Stage 3 additionally checks executable extensions, asset-source contracts, required asset IDs, prompt references, and complete scene coverage. A failed stage receives at most one bounded revision under the default configuration. For the text-grounded pipeline, inline shaders are rejected if they embed reference source code, leave unresolved Shadertoy interfaces, omit a fallback, or exceed their declared contract. After compaction and independent validation of query fidelity and execution freedom, the implementation handoff supplies the task-specific query to the coding agent. The three approved planning outputs are used to construct that query rather than concatenated into its execution request. The downstream process records the development trajectory and final game artifact, which are admitted under the checks in Appendix .

C.5

item.title: Player-1：用合成经验把电脑操作智能体练成游戏玩家 ｜ Player-1: Learning to Play from Synthetic Experience
item.description:
一句话：扩展动作空间 + 6044 条对局轨迹初始化 + 16 个合成环境做 RL，产出 9B 与 35B-A3B 两档。

要点：

  • 把电脑操作的动作空间扩到相对指针移动、持续按压与组合动作，贴近真实游戏手柄/键鼠操作
  • 用 6044 条精挑对局轨迹（动作、任务指令与视觉推理配对）做监督初始化
  • 自建 16 个合成 2D/3D 环境，具备程序化可验证奖励与随机化观测/控制动态，支持 PPO 多环境 RL

为什么值得看：要给 NPC 或自动化测试机器人做通用控制，这套「动作空间扩展 + 环境合成 + 可验证奖励」是可复用的最小闭环。

中文摘要：电脑操作智能体已经能看懂屏幕并执行键鼠动作，但游戏世界视觉丰富、机制多样，是迈向通用数字控制更难的下一级台阶。现有游戏智能体训练管线依赖大规模示范，覆盖的动态状态有限，可扩展的交互训练环境也不易获得。Player-1 提出一个后训练框架：先把动作空间扩展为相对指针移动、持续按压与组合动作；用 6044 条精挑的对局轨迹（录制动作、任务指令与视觉推理三件套）做监督初始化；再构建 16 个合成 2D/3D 环境，围绕跨游戏共享的控制需求设计，配备程序化可验证奖励与随机化观测和控制动态，从而支持多环境 PPO 强化学习。最终得到 Player-1-9B 与 Player-1-35B-A3B 两档模型，把「超越示范」作为训练目标。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.AI（English）

Player-1: Learning to Play from

Synthetic Experience

National University of Singapore ARC Lab, Tencent IEG Nanyang Technological UniversityMingyu Ouyang,

Yiran Wang,

Siyuan Hu,

Xingyilang Yin,

Huiqiang Sun,

Guangzhi Wang,

Junfu Pu,

Cheng Cheng,

Honghao Chen,

Ying Shan,

Mike Zheng Shou,

Hwee Tou Ng

Abstract

Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions.

However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control.

Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain.

We introduce , a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience.

We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions.

For supervised initialization, we fine-tune computer-use models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories that pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning.

We construct , sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around control demands shared across games.

Programmatically verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with PPO.

The resulting Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B improve MineDojo-300 success over their SFT policies by 27.8 and 17.7 percentage points, respectively.

Player-1-9B reaches 38.33% success compared with 12.63% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with further gains over SFT on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld.

Further analyses show that broader synthetic environment coverage improves transfer, while the use of composite actions that combine multiple keyboard and mouse inputs increases during RL.

We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience substantially improves game control beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.Player-1Player-1-Gym

1

Foundation models have developed broad capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and instruction following .

Computer-use agents bring these capabilities to digital interfaces, interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions .

Games offer a demanding next step toward general digital control: their visually complex environments and diverse mechanics require precise, sustained, and concurrent control under dynamic and rapidly changing visual feedback .(; ; )

OpenAI, 2024

Anthropic, 2025

Gemini Team, 2025

(; ; )

Wang et al., 2025a

Bai et al., 2025

Lu et al., 2026

()

Luo et al., 2026a

Recent game agents learn from large-scale gameplay demonstrations and interactive experience .

Yet demonstrations cover only a limited portion of the states an agent may encounter in open-ended tasks, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain.

Despite differences in appearance and rules, we find that many games share recurring control demands such as precise aiming, sustained movement, and coordinated inputs.

This motivates our central question:

(; ; ; )

Wang et al., 2025b

Magne et al., 2026

SIMA Team, 2025

Shi et al., 2026

Can synthetic experience advance game-control capabilities beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize to games outside the RL training suite?

Three challenges shape this approach.

First, gameplay demonstrations recorded with heterogeneous input conventions and temporal resolutions must be converted into a shared action space, and paired with task instructions and visual reasoning that reflect the player’s intent.

Second, learning beyond demonstrations requires feedback on states reached by the policy’s own actions, but implementing programmatic rewards across diverse commercial games is difficult to scale.

Third, experience from environments with different control demands, dynamics, and reward scales must be incorporated into a shared policy that generalizes beyond the training suite.

These challenges motivate our supervised initialization from curated demonstrations, followed by learning in controllable synthetic environments with verifiable rewards.

We present , a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience, as illustrated in Figure .

We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions.

Curated gameplay demonstrations pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning to initialize game control.

Vision-language models (VLMs) connect visual perception with language, supporting scene understanding and spatial grounding .

connects supervised initialization with learning from synthetic experience through a shared game-control action space.

We first extend computer-use actions to support dynamic game control, and initialize the policy using curated gameplay demonstrations.

3.1

We extend the computer-use action space for dynamic game control while retaining screenshot-conditioned decision making.

At turn $t$ , the policy receives task instruction $q$ , screenshot $I_{t}$ , and interaction history $C_{H}(h_{Section 3.2):

$(z_{t},\hat{a}_{t})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,I_{t},C_{H}(h_{

Here $z_{t}$ is reasoning and $\hat{a}_{t}$ the proposed action.

The game-control action space extends the base model’s computer-use actions with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions.

Relative pointer motion.

For the mouse actions, CUAs typically use normalized absolute coordinates to select visible targets by specifying their on-screen positions.

In game-play scenarios, to control the camera without a visible pointer, we extend this action space with relative displacements:

$\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{pointer}}=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{absolute}(x,y)\}}_{\text{Retained CUA coordinates}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\operatorname{relative}(\Delta x,\Delta y)\}}}_{\textbf{Relative-motion extension}}.$

Absolute coordinates satisfy $x,y\in[0,1000]$ , while relative displacements $\Delta x,\Delta y\in[-1000,1000]$ are normalized by screen width and height.

Positive $\Delta x$ denotes rightward motion, and positive $\Delta y$ denotes downward motion.

The resulting view rotation depends on the game’s camera gain.

Sustained inputs.

We extend taps and clicks with holds lasting one full control step of duration $\Delta t$ .

For a key or mouse button $b$ , the press or long-hold action space is

$\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{press}}(b)=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{tap/click}(b)\}}_{\text{Retained CUA taps/clicks}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\operatorname{hold}(b;\Delta t)\}}}_{\textbf{Sustained extension}}.$

Repeating holds across consecutive control steps sustains movement and interaction.

Composite actions.

We define a composite action as two or more compatible keyboard or mouse inputs executed concurrently within one control step.

The step action space is

$\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{step}}=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{wait}\}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{keyboard}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mouse}}}_{\text{Individual CUA inputs}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\textbf{input}_{1}\parallel\cdots\parallel\textbf{input}_{m}\}}}_{\textbf{Composite-action extension}}.$

Each $\text{input}_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{keyboard}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mouse}}$ ; $\parallel$ denotes concurrent execution and $m\geq 2$ .

These combinations support coordinated movement and combat that is crucial for game control.

For example, holding ‘W’ while tapping ‘Space’ enables running jumps, and pointer motion with a right-button hold and left-button click enables concurrent aiming and firing.

3.2

The extended action space in Section  defines the available controls, but the policy must learn when and how to use them.

In this section, we describe how we use SFT on a compact collection of curated gameplay demonstrations to initialize computer-use models for subsequent learning from synthetic experience.

3.1

Demonstration trajectory curation.

We curate 6,044 gameplay trajectories comprising 295,097 interaction turns from public datasets and in-house recordings, mapping recorded controls to the shared game-control action space defined in Section .

Controls are aligned to shared action intervals, and source-specific mouse calibration expresses relative inputs in normalized, pixel-equivalent coordinates.

After filtering incomplete or redundant recordings, we use a VLM to annotate the recorded actions with task instructions and per-turn visual reasoning.

For reasoning annotation, the VLM conditions on the task instruction, current and past observations, and the action target.

Figure  illustrates input coverage and an annotated demonstration.

Appendix  details the sources, alignment, calibration, and annotation procedures.(; ; ; )

3.3 Player-1-Gym

We construct , a suite of synthetic environments organized around control demands shared across games.

Programmatically verifiable rewards, together with randomized observations and control dynamics, support our multi-environment PPO training of the SFT-initialized policy.Player-1-Gym

Verifiable environment construction.

We identify recurring control demands across games and organize training tasks into five families: aiming, combat, driving, navigation, and UI interaction.

For example, aiming tasks require pointer-based or camera-relative target tracking, while combat tasks combine movement with attack timing.

Building upon our own shared 2D and 3D engines, reusable assets, and scene templates, we implement sixteen environments that require these forms of control through different game mechanics, viewpoints, and spatial layouts, as shown in Figure (a–b).

A unified runtime provides screenshot observations and executes the shared game-control action space.

This shared foundation facilitates extending the suite with new environments while maintaining consistent observation and action interfaces.

3

To provide verifiable training feedback, each environment defines game- and task-specific scoring rules over changing game states.

Score increments supply step-level rewards, providing dense and verifiable feedback without a learned judge, while privileged state is not exposed to the policy.

Environment randomization.

To further broaden training experience within each environment, we randomize four complementary dimensions in : : colors, lighting, and assets; : projection, placement, and initial orientation; : layouts, spawns, and task-specific configurations; and : input-response gains for camera rotation, movement, driving, and steering where applicable. All four dimensions are jointly randomized during training where supported.

Examples are provided in Figure (c).

C

Multi-environment reinforcement learning.

We jointly optimize the SFT-initialized policy with PPO across randomized environments with different control demands, dynamics, and reward scales.

To limit the effect of reward-scale differences on policy-update magnitudes, we apply to generalized advantage estimates (GAE):per-environment advantage normalization

$\widetilde{A}_{i,j}=\frac{A_{i,j}-\mu_{e}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{e}^{2}+\epsilon}},\quad\mu_{e}=\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}A_{i,j}}{N_{e}},\quad\sigma_{e}^{2}=\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}(A_{i,j}-\mu_{e})^{2}}{N_{e}-1}.$ (1)

Here $i$ indexes turns and $j$ response tokens.

For each environment $e$ , $\mathcal{S}_{e}$ contains its response-token indices in the rollout batch, with $N_{e}=|\mathcal{S}_{e}|$ .

We normalize each $A_{i,j}$ for $(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e}$ using the corresponding advantage mean $\mu_{e}$ and sample variance $\sigma_{e}^{2}$ .

Return-to-go targets accumulate rewards from subsequent turns, allowing later outcomes to inform earlier control decisions.

Appendix  further details reward construction, cross-turn credit, loss aggregation, and optimization.

4.1

Training setup.

We initialize Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B from their respective Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B backbones.

Both undergo two epochs of SFT on the full demonstration dataset with action-balanced sampling.

We then apply proximal policy optimization (PPO) in the sixteen-environment suite.

Both model sizes train on the full sixteen-environment suite with a budget of 200 RL steps. Each training step collects 256 episodes allocated equally across environments, with at most 50 interaction turns per episode.

More training details and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix .Player-1-Gym

D

Evaluation.

Besides in-domain evaluation of sixteen environments, we construct two evaluation suites: MineDojo-300, comprising 300 tasks from the MineDojo task collection in Minecraft, and ViZDoom-10, comprising ten maps from the twelve available maps in ViZDoom .

We also evaluate browser-game interaction on GameWorld , covering 170 tasks across 34 games.

Our standardized evaluation protocols use 8 trials per MineDojo task, 50 per ViZDoom map, and 3 per GameWorld task.

Appendix  details benchmark composition, metrics, and budgets.Player-1-Gym()

Generalization beyond the RL training suite.

The same policy improves performance on external games.

On ViZDoom-10, Player-1-9B increases scaled return from 0.4361 after SFT to 0.6922.

Player-1-35B-A3B achieves an overall scaled return of 0.7236, surpassing GameWAM, the strongest external baseline at 0.3938, by 83.7%.

On GameWorld’s $3\times 170$ episodes, progress rises from 31.43% to 34.45%.

Together, these results show that control experience acquired in transfers to first-person shooting and distinct browser games, beyond the synthesized environments for RL.

These gains support using synthetic experience to develop transferable control capabilities without reinforcement learning in each target game.Player-1-Gym

5.3

Figure  shows increased use of composite actions during RL.

Across Player-1-9B’s in-suite validation trajectories, the share of turns with composite actions rises from 64.7% at the start of RL to 85.4% and 93.2% after 50 and 100 RL steps, respectively.

This progressive increase occurs without an explicit reward for action composition, suggesting that task-driven RL reinforces coordinated inputs common to game control, such as aiming while firing or moving while adjusting the camera.

We presented , a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience.

Curated gameplay demonstrations initialize computer-use models in a shared game-control action space.

then provides sixteen synthetic environments organized around shared control demands, with verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics for multi-environment RL.

Evaluations on MineDojo-300, ViZDoom-10, and GameWorld demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience advances game-control capabilities beyond SFT, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.

Further analyses show improved transfer with larger training suites.

Together, these findings establish synthetic experience as an effective resource for learning transferable game control without online training in each target game.Player-1Player-1-Gym

Appendix A

A.1

Table  specifies the execution semantics of the actions introduced in Section .

For an observation of width $W$ and height $H$ , normalized absolute positions and relative displacements map to pixels as

5

3.1

$(x,y)\mapsto(xW/1000,yH/1000),\qquad(\Delta x,\Delta y)\mapsto(\Delta xW/1000,\Delta yH/1000).$

The origin is the upper-left corner, and positive displacement points right and down.

One movement uses either absolute or relative coordinates.

A key cannot be both held and tapped in the same step, nor can one mouse button be both held and clicked.

Game-control semantics.

Inputs in a composite action execute concurrently within one step; bindings are restricted to those supported by the environment.Table 5:

A.2

Relative motion requests input displacement, not a universal camera angle.

For per-pixel camera gain $g$ , requested yaw and pitch increments $\delta\psi$ and $\delta\phi$ have magnitudes

$|\delta\psi|=gW|\Delta x|/1000,\qquad|\delta\phi|=gH|\Delta y|/1000,$

before native camera limits; mouse displacement is not multiplied by action duration.

The seven mouse-controlled 3D environments use a nominal gain $g_{0}=0.00196$ radians per observation pixel by default. With Control randomization, the effective gain is $g=g_{0}L$ , where $L$ is defined in Appendix .

Observation geometry and camera constraints remain fixed within a checkpoint comparison. Benchmark-specific settings are given in Appendix .Player-1-Gym

C.2

E

A.3

SFT, RL, and evaluation all use two recent visual–action turns and two earlier action-only turns.

In the earlier action-only turns, screenshots are replaced by ; reasoning in all retained historical turns is replaced by .

The current screenshot and executed historical actions are retained.<image omitted><thinking omitted>

Appendix B

B.1

Both model sizes are trained with the collection in Figure : 6,044 trajectories and 295,097 turns from 2,544 source-qualified recording sessions and 172 games.

We approximate the sampled control hours, which equal the turn count $\times$ 200 ms, or 16.4 hours in total for the full annotated dataset.

9

Sources and game distribution of the 6,044 gameplay demonstrations used for SFT.

(a) Sources and scale, with sampled control hours.

(b) Game distribution.Figure 9:

Quality selection.

We automated validity, activity, and repetition checks that complement source-level and manual review of recording completeness, observation–action alignment, and sequence diversity.

The collection contains 5,360 gameplay trajectories with a total of 268,000 turns and 684 in-game UI trajectories with a total of 27,097 turns.

Action statistics.

Figure (a) counts the distribution of each action across all samples in the dataset.

Keyboard–mouse composites take precedence. Mouse-only turns are assigned by movement, click, hold, then scroll.

Inputs per step count each key tap/hold and mouse operation separately, with wait as one no-op.

Pointer-mode shares use all turns containing , including keyboard–mouse composites.

2

mouse_move

B.2

Temporal alignment.

For continuous gameplay, source timestamps define contiguous intervals of 150–250 ms, projected onto a 200-ms target grid using cumulative boundaries.

Relative input is summed within each source interval.

Keyboard presses shorter than 100 ms become taps, and longer presses become holds on overlapping target steps.

Mouse presses lasting at most 300 ms become clicks.

Each target summarizes compatible recorded inputs for concurrent execution within one control step.

UI trajectories also follow recorded operation boundaries.

Clicks retain their recorded targets, key sequences expand into individual presses, drags use start and endpoint controls with an explicit release, and scroll gestures become directional steps.

Execution uses the shared 200-ms action space.

Sampled control hours use target execution duration, while UI trajectories retain their recorded, operation-dependent timing.

Spatial alignment.

Native relative-mouse input scales vary across data sources and recording setups.

We therefore calibrate these inputs to pixel-equivalent displacements using freely moving GUI pointers from the same recording session.

The mapping also applies to pointer-locked recordings. Camera response is defined in Appendix .

For native-input sums $(r_{x},r_{y})$ , coefficients $(k_{x},k_{y})$ , and logical recording size $(W_{m},H_{m})$ , the normalized target is

A.2

$\Delta x=\operatorname{round}(1000k_{x}r_{x}/W_{m}),\qquad\Delta y=\operatorname{round}(1000k_{y}r_{y}/H_{m}).$

Mouse-move Calibration.

In-house and D2E calibration uses GUI windows with stable focus and geometry, aligned timestamps, and no pointer clipping or recentering.

For paired native input $r_{i}$ and pointer displacement $p_{i}$ , window and pooled session estimates are

$k_{i}=\frac{r_{i}^{\top}p_{i}}{r_{i}^{\top}r_{i}},\qquad\hat{k}=\frac{\sum_{i}r_{i}^{\top}p_{i}}{\sum_{i}r_{i}^{\top}r_{i}}.$

D2E uses window-equal estimates for a source-level coefficient; in-house coefficients are recording-specific.

Pixel2Play uses per-axis Huber regression over at least two stable, non-overlapping two-second GUI blocks.

Out-of-range projections are rejected rather than clipped to ensure the action quality. Table  lists the source mappings.

Source-specific mouse-action mapping.

Relative inputs use calibration coefficients bound to recording geometry; UI operations use absolute endpoints.Table 6:

B.3

We use Gemini 3.8 Flash to build reusable profiles of rules, roles, inputs, and examples for each game in the trajectory, and check them for recorded-control coverage and action validity.

It assigns goals from each profile, full-trajectory storyboard, and action timeline. The same game from different data sources should share the same assembled profile. For per-turn reasoning annotation, it re-uses the goal, fixed action target, and current and past frames.

C.1

By primary task, the sixteen environments comprise aiming (2), combat (5), driving (4), navigation (4), and UI interaction (1).

Tables  and  specify their tasks, score components, and API state fields.

Each environment defines a cumulative score $S_{e}(s)$ and supplies the increment $r_{e,t}=S_{e}(s_{t+1})-S_{e}(s_{t})$ as reward.

Reward computation and evaluation use privileged state, while the policy receives only screenshots and task/control text.

Figure  shows individual and joint Appearance, Camera, and Scene variation.

The parameters, distributions, and applicable environments for Appearance, Camera, Scene, and Control are specified in Table .

Specifically, appearance preserves collision geometry and functional roles; Scene varies layouts, spawns, and subsequent entity generation, potentially changing task difficulty.

Appearance and Camera are sampled at reset and fixed within each episode, with triangular modes at native values.

Background lightness and saturation, ambient intensity, and key-light intensity share one sampled quantile, and linked asset components receive compatible color changes.

Orthographic zoom is relative to the native view, including 2D platforming. Initial first-person point-of-view yaw/pitch is distinct from camera-rig pitch.

Control varies input response independently of camera projection and scene configuration.

For each supported response parameter $k$ , we independently sample

$c_{e,k}\sim\operatorname{Tri}(a_{e,k},1,b_{e,k}),\qquad c_{e,k}(t)=c_{e,k}(0)\quad\text{throughout the episode}.$ (2)

The control seed is independent of domain randomization. Separate parameter substreams set values at reset, unchanged through respawns.

The narrower chasing, platforming, and jump ranges preserve pursuit-speed and traversal constraints.

Appendix D

D.1

For supervised fine-tuning, both model sizes use token-level cross-entropy on the current turn’s reasoning and action, with the history in Appendix .

A.3

Action-balanced sampling.

In human gameplay recordings, some actions occupy only a small fraction of playing time but are critical for game progress.

For example, left mouse button inputs account for less than 1% of valid inputs in the original recordings, which are dominated by keyboard inputs and mouse movement.

In addition to selecting and filtering demonstrations for action coverage during data curation, we use action-balanced sampling to strengthen supervision for these infrequent but important actions.

We classify each turn by its current recorded action into overlapping pools: keyboard, mouse movement, click, hold, any mouse button, keyboard–mouse, movement–click, keyboard–click, and keyboard–movement–click.

Keyboard includes held and tapped keys; keyboard–mouse includes any mouse input, including scrolling.

Other contains the remaining turns, including wait and scroll-only actions.

Each draw selects a pool proportionally to its weight (1 for each control pool; 0.1 for Other), then samples a turn uniformly with replacement.

D.2

During RL, we use synchronous PPO with a dense critic initialized from Qwen3.5-9B for both actor sizes.

Before actor updates begin, the critic undergoes five warmup iterations under the same environment configuration.

Rollouts retain the observations, prompts, responses, masks, and behavior log probabilities used at generation, preserving the same conditioning during optimization.

Reward and cross-turn credit.

For turn $t$ in environment $e$ , we define the penalized step reward and undiscounted return-to-go as

$\widetilde{r}_{e,t}=r_{e,t}-p^{\mathrm{invalid}}_{e,t}-p^{\mathrm{length}}_{e,t},\qquad G_{e,t}=\sum_{u=t}^{T}\widetilde{r}_{e,u},$ (3)

where $r_{e,t}$ is the game-score increment (Appendix ) and $T$ the terminal turn.

Training curves average episode returns $G_{e,1}$ .

The penalties are

C.1

$p^{\mathrm{invalid}}_{e,t}=\mathbf{1}[\text{invalid action}],\qquad p^{\mathrm{length}}_{e,t}=\min\{1,\,0.005\max(0,n_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}}-64)\},$

where $n_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}}$ counts generated reasoning/prose tokens.

An invalid action executes the runtime’s wait fallback.

We apply no additional terminal-failure penalty or task-wise reward rescaling.

With $\gamma=\lambda=1$ , return targets are computed over complete trajectories, preserving cross-turn credit.

Advantage normalization and loss reduction.

We normalize advantages globally in GAE, then within environments using Equation (), with $N_{e}\geq 2$ and $\epsilon=10^{-8}$ ; critic return targets are unchanged.

For minibatch $\mathcal{B}$ , let $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ be turn $i$ ’s nonempty response-token set selected by the loss mask.

The clipped PPO loss averages within turns, then across turns:

1

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{policy}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}\ell^{\mathrm{PPO}}_{i,j}(\theta;\widetilde{A}_{i,j}).$ (4)

The critic uses the same reduction. Normalization is token-weighted within environments, whereas losses weight turns equally. Each environment therefore contributes in proportion to its included turns.

D.3

Table  summarizes the shared recipe for both model sizes. For each model size, the SFT stage uses 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs and takes approximately 24 hours, while a 200-step RL run uses 64 H200 GPUs and takes approximately 36 hours.

Both durations include validation.

Browser processes and contexts are reused across episodes to amortize startup costs.

Evaluation cost.

Our full MineDojo-300, ViZDoom-10, and GameWorld protocols allocate up to 3.14 million agent decision turns per model.

Our in-suite validation records average roughly 3,000 input tokens and 100 output tokens per turn, including visual context and generated reasoning.

Using these observed lengths as a workload proxy, a full-budget evaluation would cost approximately USD$110,000 at GPT-6 Astra’s standard API rates of USD$10 and USD$50 per million input and output tokens, respectively, before caching discounts.

Actual costs depend on model-specific tokenization, reasoning, and episode lengths.

Considering the estimated cost, our focus is mainly on representative released game-control and computer-use policies rather than proprietary API models.1, accessed Sep 24, 2026.11

https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra

E.1

We deploy JARVIS-VLA with its action-token decoder and two history entries to predict one action per decision.

UI-TARS-1.5-7B uses three previous screenshots, deterministic decoding, and a 400-token output limit. Its adapter maps pixel-coordinate actions to one benchmark interval, with drag and double-click unsupported.

NitroGen aggregates an 18-action chunk into six benchmark decisions (three native actions per decision), refreshing the image after each chunk.

GameWAM predicts 16 actions and executes eight before replanning, using its Minecraft checkpoint outside Doom and its ViZDoom checkpoint for Doom.

Open-P2P uses visual-only conditioning and session-specific recurrent state.

All temporal inference state is isolated between episodes.

Model inputs retain the released preprocessing for the best practice of each baseline: Minecraft is rendered at $864\times 480$ . We resize the screenshots to $640\times 360$ for JARVIS-VLA and UI-TARS, $256\times 256$ for NitroGen, $224\times 224$ for GameWAM, and $192\times 192$ for Open-P2P.

JARVIS-VLA and GameWAM retain their native degree-based Minecraft camera actions, while Open-P2P uses an adapter gain of $0.15$ degrees per raw mouse pixel.

一句话：扩展动作空间 + 6044 条对局轨迹初始化 + 16 个合成环境做 RL，产出 9B 与 35B-A3B 两档。

要点：

  • 把电脑操作的动作空间扩到相对指针移动、持续按压与组合动作，贴近真实游戏手柄/键鼠操作
  • 用 6044 条精挑对局轨迹（动作、任务指令与视觉推理配对）做监督初始化
  • 自建 16 个合成 2D/3D 环境，具备程序化可验证奖励与随机化观测/控制动态，支持 PPO 多环境 RL

为什么值得看：要给 NPC 或自动化测试机器人做通用控制，这套「动作空间扩展 + 环境合成 + 可验证奖励」是可复用的最小闭环。

中文摘要：电脑操作智能体已经能看懂屏幕并执行键鼠动作，但游戏世界视觉丰富、机制多样，是迈向通用数字控制更难的下一级台阶。现有游戏智能体训练管线依赖大规模示范，覆盖的动态状态有限，可扩展的交互训练环境也不易获得。Player-1 提出一个后训练框架：先把动作空间扩展为相对指针移动、持续按压与组合动作；用 6044 条精挑的对局轨迹（录制动作、任务指令与视觉推理三件套）做监督初始化；再构建 16 个合成 2D/3D 环境，围绕跨游戏共享的控制需求设计，配备程序化可验证奖励与随机化观测和控制动态，从而支持多环境 PPO 强化学习。最终得到 Player-1-9B 与 Player-1-35B-A3B 两档模型，把「超越示范」作为训练目标。

Abstract

Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions.

However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control.

Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain.

We introduce , a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience.

We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions.

For supervised initialization, we fine-tune computer-use models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories that pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning.

We construct , sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around control demands shared across games.

Programmatically verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with PPO.

The resulting Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B improve MineDojo-300 success over their SFT policies by 27.8 and 17.7 percentage points, respectively.

Player-1-9B reaches 38.33% success compared with 12.63% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with further gains over SFT on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld.

Further analyses show that broader synthetic environment coverage improves transfer, while the use of composite actions that combine multiple keyboard and mouse inputs increases during RL.

We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience substantially improves game control beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.Player-1Player-1-Gym

Recent game agents learn from large-scale gameplay demonstrations and interactive experience .

Yet demonstrations cover only a limited portion of the states an agent may encounter in open-ended tasks, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain.

Despite differences in appearance and rules, we find that many games share recurring control demands such as precise aiming, sustained movement, and coordinated inputs.

This motivates our central question:

Can synthetic experience advance game-control capabilities beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize to games outside the RL training suite?

Three challenges shape this approach.

First, gameplay demonstrations recorded with heterogeneous input conventions and temporal resolutions must be converted into a shared action space, and paired with task instructions and visual reasoning that reflect the player’s intent.

Second, learning beyond demonstrations requires feedback on states reached by the policy’s own actions, but implementing programmatic rewards across diverse commercial games is difficult to scale.

Third, experience from environments with different control demands, dynamics, and reward scales must be incorporated into a shared policy that generalizes beyond the training suite.

These challenges motivate our supervised initialization from curated demonstrations, followed by learning in controllable synthetic environments with verifiable rewards.

We present , a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience, as illustrated in Figure .

Curated gameplay demonstrations pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning to initialize game control.

then provides sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around recurring control demands across aiming, combat, driving, navigation, and UI interaction.

Programmatic game-state rewards and randomization of observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), yielding Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B.

3.1

We extend the computer-use action space for dynamic game control while retaining screenshot-conditioned decision making.

At turn $t$ , the policy receives task instruction $q$ , screenshot $I_{t}$ , and interaction history $C_{H}(h_{Section 3.2):

$(z_{t},\hat{a}_{t})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,I_{t},C_{H}(h_{

Here $z_{t}$ is reasoning and $\hat{a}_{t}$ the proposed action.

The game-control action space extends the base model’s computer-use actions with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions.

Relative pointer motion.

For the mouse actions, CUAs typically use normalized absolute coordinates to select visible targets by specifying their on-screen positions.

In game-play scenarios, to control the camera without a visible pointer, we extend this action space with relative displacements:

$\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{pointer}}=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{absolute}(x,y)\}}_{\text{Retained CUA coordinates}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\operatorname{relative}(\Delta x,\Delta y)\}}}_{\textbf{Relative-motion extension}}.$

Absolute coordinates satisfy $x,y\in[0,1000]$ , while relative displacements $\Delta x,\Delta y\in[-1000,1000]$ are normalized by screen width and height.

Positive $\Delta x$ denotes rightward motion, and positive $\Delta y$ denotes downward motion.

The resulting view rotation depends on the game’s camera gain.

Sustained inputs.

We extend taps and clicks with holds lasting one full control step of duration $\Delta t$ .

For a key or mouse button $b$ , the press or long-hold action space is

$\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{press}}(b)=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{tap/click}(b)\}}_{\text{Retained CUA taps/clicks}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\operatorname{hold}(b;\Delta t)\}}}_{\textbf{Sustained extension}}.$

Repeating holds across consecutive control steps sustains movement and interaction.

Composite actions.

We define a composite action as two or more compatible keyboard or mouse inputs executed concurrently within one control step.

The step action space is

$\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{step}}=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{wait}\}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{keyboard}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mouse}}}_{\text{Individual CUA inputs}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\textbf{input}_{1}\parallel\cdots\parallel\textbf{input}_{m}\}}}_{\textbf{Composite-action extension}}.$

Each $\text{input}_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{keyboard}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mouse}}$ ; $\parallel$ denotes concurrent execution and $m\geq 2$ .

These combinations support coordinated movement and combat that is crucial for game control.

For example, holding ‘W’ while tapping ‘Space’ enables running jumps, and pointer motion with a right-button hold and left-button click enables concurrent aiming and firing.

3.2

The extended action space in Section  defines the available controls, but the policy must learn when and how to use them.

In this section, we describe how we use SFT on a compact collection of curated gameplay demonstrations to initialize computer-use models for subsequent learning from synthetic experience.

3.1

Demonstration trajectory curation.

We curate 6,044 gameplay trajectories comprising 295,097 interaction turns from public datasets and in-house recordings, mapping recorded controls to the shared game-control action space defined in Section .

Controls are aligned to shared action intervals, and source-specific mouse calibration expresses relative inputs in normalized, pixel-equivalent coordinates.

After filtering incomplete or redundant recordings, we use a VLM to annotate the recorded actions with task instructions and per-turn visual reasoning.

For reasoning annotation, the VLM conditions on the task instruction, current and past observations, and the action target.

Figure  illustrates input coverage and an annotated demonstration.

Appendix  details the sources, alignment, calibration, and annotation procedures.(; ; ; )

3.3 Player-1-Gym

We construct , a suite of synthetic environments organized around control demands shared across games.

Programmatically verifiable rewards, together with randomized observations and control dynamics, support our multi-environment PPO training of the SFT-initialized policy.Player-1-Gym

Verifiable environment construction.

We identify recurring control demands across games and organize training tasks into five families: aiming, combat, driving, navigation, and UI interaction.

For example, aiming tasks require pointer-based or camera-relative target tracking, while combat tasks combine movement with attack timing.

Building upon our own shared 2D and 3D engines, reusable assets, and scene templates, we implement sixteen environments that require these forms of control through different game mechanics, viewpoints, and spatial layouts, as shown in Figure (a–b).

A unified runtime provides screenshot observations and executes the shared game-control action space.

This shared foundation facilitates extending the suite with new environments while maintaining consistent observation and action interfaces.

3

To provide verifiable training feedback, each environment defines game- and task-specific scoring rules over changing game states.

Score increments supply step-level rewards, providing dense and verifiable feedback without a learned judge, while privileged state is not exposed to the policy.

Environment randomization.

To further broaden training experience within each environment, we randomize four complementary dimensions in : : colors, lighting, and assets; : projection, placement, and initial orientation; : layouts, spawns, and task-specific configurations; and : input-response gains for camera rotation, movement, driving, and steering where applicable. All four dimensions are jointly randomized during training where supported.

Examples are provided in Figure (c).

C

Multi-environment reinforcement learning.

We jointly optimize the SFT-initialized policy with PPO across randomized environments with different control demands, dynamics, and reward scales.

To limit the effect of reward-scale differences on policy-update magnitudes, we apply to generalized advantage estimates (GAE):per-environment advantage normalization

$\widetilde{A}_{i,j}=\frac{A_{i,j}-\mu_{e}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{e}^{2}+\epsilon}},\quad\mu_{e}=\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}A_{i,j}}{N_{e}},\quad\sigma_{e}^{2}=\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}(A_{i,j}-\mu_{e})^{2}}{N_{e}-1}.$ (1)

Here $i$ indexes turns and $j$ response tokens.

For each environment $e$ , $\mathcal{S}_{e}$ contains its response-token indices in the rollout batch, with $N_{e}=|\mathcal{S}_{e}|$ .

We normalize each $A_{i,j}$ for $(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e}$ using the corresponding advantage mean $\mu_{e}$ and sample variance $\sigma_{e}^{2}$ .

Return-to-go targets accumulate rewards from subsequent turns, allowing later outcomes to inform earlier control decisions.

Appendix  further details reward construction, cross-turn credit, loss aggregation, and optimization.

4.1

Training setup.

We initialize Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B from their respective Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B backbones.

Both undergo two epochs of SFT on the full demonstration dataset with action-balanced sampling.

We then apply proximal policy optimization (PPO) in the sixteen-environment suite.

Both model sizes train on the full sixteen-environment suite with a budget of 200 RL steps. Each training step collects 256 episodes allocated equally across environments, with at most 50 interaction turns per episode.

More training details and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix .Player-1-Gym

D

Evaluation.

Besides in-domain evaluation of sixteen environments, we construct two evaluation suites: MineDojo-300, comprising 300 tasks from the MineDojo task collection in Minecraft, and ViZDoom-10, comprising ten maps from the twelve available maps in ViZDoom .

We also evaluate browser-game interaction on GameWorld , covering 170 tasks across 34 games.

Our standardized evaluation protocols use 8 trials per MineDojo task, 50 per ViZDoom map, and 3 per GameWorld task.

Generalization beyond the RL training suite.

The same policy improves performance on external games.

On ViZDoom-10, Player-1-9B increases scaled return from 0.4361 after SFT to 0.6922.

Player-1-35B-A3B achieves an overall scaled return of 0.7236, surpassing GameWAM, the strongest external baseline at 0.3938, by 83.7%.

On GameWorld’s $3\times 170$ episodes, progress rises from 31.43% to 34.45%.

Together, these results show that control experience acquired in transfers to first-person shooting and distinct browser games, beyond the synthesized environments for RL.

These gains support using synthetic experience to develop transferable control capabilities without reinforcement learning in each target game.Player-1-Gym

We presented , a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience.

Curated gameplay demonstrations initialize computer-use models in a shared game-control action space.

then provides sixteen synthetic environments organized around shared control demands, with verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics for multi-environment RL.

Evaluations on MineDojo-300, ViZDoom-10, and GameWorld demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience advances game-control capabilities beyond SFT, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.

Further analyses show improved transfer with larger training suites.

Together, these findings establish synthetic experience as an effective resource for learning transferable game control without online training in each target game.Player-1Player-1-Gym

Quality selection.

We automated validity, activity, and repetition checks that complement source-level and manual review of recording completeness, observation–action alignment, and sequence diversity.

The collection contains 5,360 gameplay trajectories with a total of 268,000 turns and 684 in-game UI trajectories with a total of 27,097 turns.

Action statistics.

Figure (a) counts the distribution of each action across all samples in the dataset.

Keyboard–mouse composites take precedence. Mouse-only turns are assigned by movement, click, hold, then scroll.

Inputs per step count each key tap/hold and mouse operation separately, with wait as one no-op.

Pointer-mode shares use all turns containing , including keyboard–mouse composites.

B.2

Temporal alignment.

For continuous gameplay, source timestamps define contiguous intervals of 150–250 ms, projected onto a 200-ms target grid using cumulative boundaries.

Relative input is summed within each source interval.

Keyboard presses shorter than 100 ms become taps, and longer presses become holds on overlapping target steps.

Mouse presses lasting at most 300 ms become clicks.

Each target summarizes compatible recorded inputs for concurrent execution within one control step.

UI trajectories also follow recorded operation boundaries.

Clicks retain their recorded targets, key sequences expand into individual presses, drags use start and endpoint controls with an explicit release, and scroll gestures become directional steps.

Execution uses the shared 200-ms action space.

Sampled control hours use target execution duration, while UI trajectories retain their recorded, operation-dependent timing.

Spatial alignment.

Native relative-mouse input scales vary across data sources and recording setups.

We therefore calibrate these inputs to pixel-equivalent displacements using freely moving GUI pointers from the same recording session.

The mapping also applies to pointer-locked recordings. Camera response is defined in Appendix .

For native-input sums $(r_{x},r_{y})$ , coefficients $(k_{x},k_{y})$ , and logical recording size $(W_{m},H_{m})$ , the normalized target is

A.2

$\Delta x=\operatorname{round}(1000k_{x}r_{x}/W_{m}),\qquad\Delta y=\operatorname{round}(1000k_{y}r_{y}/H_{m}).$

Mouse-move Calibration.

In-house and D2E calibration uses GUI windows with stable focus and geometry, aligned timestamps, and no pointer clipping or recentering.

For paired native input $r_{i}$ and pointer displacement $p_{i}$ , window and pooled session estimates are

$k_{i}=\frac{r_{i}^{\top}p_{i}}{r_{i}^{\top}r_{i}},\qquad\hat{k}=\frac{\sum_{i}r_{i}^{\top}p_{i}}{\sum_{i}r_{i}^{\top}r_{i}}.$

D2E uses window-equal estimates for a source-level coefficient; in-house coefficients are recording-specific.

Pixel2Play uses per-axis Huber regression over at least two stable, non-overlapping two-second GUI blocks.

Out-of-range projections are rejected rather than clipped to ensure the action quality. Table  lists the source mappings.

Appendix D

D.1

For supervised fine-tuning, both model sizes use token-level cross-entropy on the current turn’s reasoning and action, with the history in Appendix .

A.3

Action-balanced sampling.

In human gameplay recordings, some actions occupy only a small fraction of playing time but are critical for game progress.

For example, left mouse button inputs account for less than 1% of valid inputs in the original recordings, which are dominated by keyboard inputs and mouse movement.

In addition to selecting and filtering demonstrations for action coverage during data curation, we use action-balanced sampling to strengthen supervision for these infrequent but important actions.

We classify each turn by its current recorded action into overlapping pools: keyboard, mouse movement, click, hold, any mouse button, keyboard–mouse, movement–click, keyboard–click, and keyboard–movement–click.

Keyboard includes held and tapped keys; keyboard–mouse includes any mouse input, including scrolling.

Other contains the remaining turns, including wait and scroll-only actions.

Each draw selects a pool proportionally to its weight (1 for each control pool; 0.1 for Other), then samples a turn uniformly with replacement.

D.2

During RL, we use synchronous PPO with a dense critic initialized from Qwen3.5-9B for both actor sizes.

Before actor updates begin, the critic undergoes five warmup iterations under the same environment configuration.

Rollouts retain the observations, prompts, responses, masks, and behavior log probabilities used at generation, preserving the same conditioning during optimization.

Reward and cross-turn credit.

For turn $t$ in environment $e$ , we define the penalized step reward and undiscounted return-to-go as

$\widetilde{r}_{e,t}=r_{e,t}-p^{\mathrm{invalid}}_{e,t}-p^{\mathrm{length}}_{e,t},\qquad G_{e,t}=\sum_{u=t}^{T}\widetilde{r}_{e,u},$ (3)

where $r_{e,t}$ is the game-score increment (Appendix ) and $T$ the terminal turn.

Training curves average episode returns $G_{e,1}$ .

The penalties are

C.1

$p^{\mathrm{invalid}}_{e,t}=\mathbf{1}[\text{invalid action}],\qquad p^{\mathrm{length}}_{e,t}=\min\{1,\,0.005\max(0,n_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}}-64)\},$

where $n_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}}$ counts generated reasoning/prose tokens.

An invalid action executes the runtime’s wait fallback.

We apply no additional terminal-failure penalty or task-wise reward rescaling.

With $\gamma=\lambda=1$ , return targets are computed over complete trajectories, preserving cross-turn credit.

Advantage normalization and loss reduction.

We normalize advantages globally in GAE, then within environments using Equation (), with $N_{e}\geq 2$ and $\epsilon=10^{-8}$ ; critic return targets are unchanged.

For minibatch $\mathcal{B}$ , let $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ be turn $i$ ’s nonempty response-token set selected by the loss mask.

The clipped PPO loss averages within turns, then across turns:

1

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{policy}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}\ell^{\mathrm{PPO}}_{i,j}(\theta;\widetilde{A}_{i,j}).$ (4)

The critic uses the same reduction. Normalization is token-weighted within environments, whereas losses weight turns equally. Each environment therefore contributes in proportion to its included turns.

Evaluation cost.

Our full MineDojo-300, ViZDoom-10, and GameWorld protocols allocate up to 3.14 million agent decision turns per model.

Our in-suite validation records average roughly 3,000 input tokens and 100 output tokens per turn, including visual context and generated reasoning.

Using these observed lengths as a workload proxy, a full-budget evaluation would cost approximately USD$110,000 at GPT-6 Astra’s standard API rates of USD$10 and USD$50 per million input and output tokens, respectively, before caching discounts.

Actual costs depend on model-specific tokenization, reasoning, and episode lengths.

Considering the estimated cost, our focus is mainly on representative released game-control and computer-use policies rather than proprietary API models.1, accessed Sep 24, 2026.11
