一句话：不再逐场景优化，直接把 4DGS 属性排成编解码器友好的 2D 图，秒级压到 1/40。

要点：

  • 把 4DGS 压缩从「逐场景优化问题」改成通用后训练框架，直接复用现有图像与视频编解码器
  • 按高斯重要性做自适应量化，重新分配码率，同时保持与现有 codec 完全兼容
  • 利用 4DGS 的统计特性做运动与重要性感知的打包，把属性重排成编解码友好的 2D 图；压缩率超 40 倍且只需数秒

为什么值得看：动态 3DGS 的存储是部署死穴，能直接吃现成 codec、还能秒级完成，才谈得上流式加载与在线分发。

中文摘要：4D 高斯泼溅能实时高质量渲染动态场景，但存储开销高得难以部署。现有压缩方法多把压缩当成逐场景优化问题，泛化性差，也无法满足低延迟压缩的场景。TETRIS-4DGS 改用通用后训练框架：直接借助成熟的图像与视频编解码器，先按重要性水平对高斯做自适应量化，从而细化码率分配，并保持与现有 codec 完全兼容；再利用 4DGS 的统计特性，提出运动与重要性感知的打包方式，把高斯属性重排成对编解码器友好的 2D 图。实验显示它能在数秒内完成压缩、达到 40 倍以上的压缩率，同时保持较高质量。对需要把动态高斯内容分发到端侧的应用，这种「不训练、只用 codec」的路线工程成本最低。

TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of

4D Gaussian Splatting

Chengzhen Wu

Abstract

4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead.

Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required.

In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a for 4DGS to address these issues.

Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps.

Our approach can achieve over in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.generalized post-training compression framework40× compression rate

4D Gaussian Splatting, 4D Gaussian Splatting Compression, Post-Training Compression

Index Terms:

I Introduction

With photorealistic and fast rendering, dynamic Gaussian Splatting is a promising pathway toward free-viewpoint video, enabling immersive visual applications. Existing paradigms for dynamic Gaussian Splatting can be categorized into three classes: per-frame 3DGS methods , deformable Gaussians with canonical space , and 4D Gaussian representations .

Practical deployment of dynamic Gaussians requires both efficient rendering and lightweight representation. The former makes canonical-space deformable Gaussians less practical, since neural inference for deformation slows down rendering. The latter makes per-frame 3DGS less attractive due to its large storage footprint. 4D Gaussian representations—exemplified by 4DGS —offer a more favorable balance between rendering efficiency and model compactness.[, ]

11

4

[, ]

13

16

[, ]

15

9

[]

15

While striking a balance, 4D Gaussian still suffer from its raw data volume, highlighting the need for effective compression. One line of work reduces the number of parameters per primitive by modifying the representation for compression, as in MEGA and CSTG. However, introducing neural networks into the representation enable memory-efficient representation but increases rendering complexity. Another line of work achieves compression by pruning low-contribution primitives, such as 4DGS-1K and the masking strategy in CSTG. These methods require costly pruning-score computation and fine-tuning.

Despite their effectiveness in terms of rate-distortion performance, these methods still treat compression as a scene-specific optimization tightly coupled with 4D Gaussian training. This tight coupling demands costly re-training when the content is not generated using the same training pipeline and becomes impractical for low-latency compression.

: Fig. 1Targeting the 4DGS representation which balances model compactness and rendering efficiency, we exploit the unequal importance and spatial-temporal properties of 4D Gaussians and propose a post-training compression method for 4DGS that fully leverages existing image and video codecs.

We target 4DGS  representation and aim to achieve strong rate–distortion performance for 4DGS compression with short encoding and decoding time. As shown in Fig. , we propose , an efficient post-training compression scheme for 4DGS that packs Gaussians into different blocks like Tetris.

The key principle behind the scheme is to leverage off-the-shelf standard image and video codecs that are widely available across devices for efficient compression.[]

15

1

TETRIS-4DGS

4DGS attributes that affect primitive positions are seen as distortion-sensitive and encoded with lossless image codecs, while the remaining majority, distortion-robust attributes are encoded with lossy video codecs. To efficiently compress the latter, we introduce two techniques: 1) importance-based adaptive quantization, and 2) motion- and importance-aware packing. The former achieves adaptive bit allocation across primitives with different importance scores, without modifying the existing video codec implementation.

Unlike existing time-consuming importance calculation methods, we train a generalizable importance estimator that predicts importance scores in a feed-forward pass.

Guided by the motion statistics and importance of 4DGS, our packing method first partitions primitives into groups and then places primitives from the same group into spatially contiguous regions.

This produces codec-friendly 2D attribute maps that can be efficiently compressed by standard video codecs.

Our method achieves over compression ratio while maintaining high visual quality, with only for encoding and for decoding a 300-frame dynamic scene, offering a strong rate–distortion–runtime trade-off.40 $\times$ 12s2s

II Related Works

II-AGaussians Primitives Pruning

Existing methods typically address primitive redundancy by pruning Gaussians based on per-point importance metrics, which are mainly obtained in two ways:

(1) leveraging rendering kernels to calculate each primitive’s rendering contribution or uncertainty ; and

(2) learning per-point scores or masks through rate–distortion optimization .

While effective in improving RD performance, these methods incur substantial computational overhead and GPU memory consumption, limiting their practicality.

More recently, an MPEG contribution  proposed predicting per-point importance from Gaussian features using a generalized MLP, achieving competitive RD performance with reduced runtime.

However, both this method and prior approaches categorize Gaussians into only two groups—pruned or retained—overlooking the fact that Gaussians can be more finely stratified into multiple importance levels to further exploit redundancy.[, , , ]

2

3

17

[]

12

[]

14

II-B4D Gaussian Compression

Even though 4D Gaussian representations achieved favorable balance between model compactness and rendering efficiency, it still suffers from significant storage overhead.

To mitigate this issue, MEGA  enlarges each Gaussian’s influence range via entropy-constrained deformation, reducing the number of primitives, and replaces spherical harmonics with a color predictor for decoding. 4DGS-1K  ranks 4D Gaussians by spatial–temporal variation, pruning up to 80% of primitives to lower storage and proceeds fine-tuning to recover quality. CSTG  prunes Gaussians using learnable per-point masks and compresses attributes with residual vector quantization.

Though effective in terms of RD performance, these methods still tightly couple optimization with compression, lacking generalizability to pre-generated Gaussian models and making them unsuitable for low-latency compression.[]

III Method

: Fig. 2Overview of the proposed 4DGS generalized post-training compression framework. For encoding, a per-point importance score is first derived from the input 4DGS through the importance estimator, based on which Gaussian attributes are adaptively scaled and quantized. Attributes are then packed to 2D maps according to their importance level and motion property, making them amendable for subsequent image and video coding. During decoding, attributes are obtained from the bitstreams and rescaled to their original value, restoring the 4DGS data for further rendering.

In order to achieve strong rate–distortion–runtime trade-off on the 4DGS  representation, we propose Importance-Based Adaptive Quantization (Sec. ) and Motion- and Importance-Aware Packing (Sec. ) for 4DGS compression. Fig.  illustrates the overall workflow of our method.[]

15

III-B

III-C

2

III-APreliminary

Each 4DGS  primitive is defined by the following attributes: (i) 4D mean vector $\mu_{4D}=(\mu_{x},\mu_{y},\mu_{z},\mu_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{4}$ ; (ii) 4D rotation $R_{4D}$ , parameterized by a pair of isotropic quaternions, $q_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}$ and $q_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}$ ; (iii) 4D scaling factor $s_{4D}=(s_{x},s_{y},s_{z},s_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{4}$ ; (iv) spatial and temporal spherical harmonics (SH) $sh\in\mathbb{R}^{3(k_{v}+1)^{2}(k_{t}+1)}$ with view degrees of freedom $k_{v}$ and time degrees of freedom $k_{t}$ ; (v) opacity $o\in[0,1]$ . Given the above attributes, the covariance matrix $\Sigma_{4D}$ of a 4DGS can be constructed as:[]

15

$\Sigma_{4D}=R_{4D}S_{4D}S_{4D}^{T}R_{4D}^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}U&V\\

V^{T}&W\end{pmatrix},$ (1)

where $U\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ , $V\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 1}$ , and $W\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 1}$ represent the decomposed sub-matrices of the covariance.

For rendering, 4D Gaussians are projected into 3D space, where $\Sigma_{3D}=U-\frac{VV^{T}}{W}$ denotes the 3D covariance matrix and $\sigma(t)=e^{-\frac{(t-\mu_{t})^{2}}{2W}}$ models the temporal decay of opacity. Furthermore, the 3D centers of Gaussians are defined as $\mu_{3D}(t)=\mu_{3D}+(t-\mu_{t})\frac{V}{W}$ , approximating Gaussian trajectories as uniform linear motions. Following the projection of 4DGS into 3D space, differentiable rasterization is applied to the projected 3D Gaussians to synthesize the final image.

According to the above formulation, the spherical harmonics and opacity of 4DGS are distortion-robust for they do not affect the Gaussian position, whereas the remaining attributes influence their positions to some extent. Our work focuses on efficiently compressing the former group—which constitutes the majority of attribute channels—using lossy video codecs, as these attributes contain greater redundancy.

III-BImportance-Based Adaptive Quantization

While current pruning-based methods reduce the primitive redundancy among 4DGS, they treat all surviving Gaussians equally. This binary approach is inefficient for primitives of borderline importance: pruning them degrades quality, yet storing them at full precision wastes bits. These primitives should be treated in a more delicate way, for which we propose importance-based adaptive quantization.

We assign each Gaussian attribute a specific bit width and then uniformly quantize it using its per-channel minimum and maximum values, where we propose an importance-guided attribute rescaling. Specifically, each Gaussian is associated with an importance score $\phi\in(0,1)$ , predicted by a generalized importance score estimator, which is described in the following paragraph. We then divide the importance score $\phi$ into $L$ importance levels $l$ :Importance-Based Adaptive Quantization for Attributes:

$l(\phi)=\begin{cases}0,&\phi\in(0,\phi_{\mathrm{thres}}),\\

1+\left\lfloor(L-1)\cdot\dfrac{\phi-\phi_{\mathrm{thres}}}{1-\phi_{\mathrm{thres}}}\right\rfloor,&\phi\in[\phi_{\mathrm{thres}},1),\end{cases}$ (2)

where $l\in\{0,1,2,...,L-1\}$ denotes the assigned importance level and $\phi_{\mathrm{thres}}$ denotes a preset score threshold which will be explained later.

With the importance level of each primitive determined, we define the corresponding attribute rescale ratio $\hat{\phi}_{L}$ as:

$\hat{\phi}_{l}=\begin{cases}0,&l=0,\\[6.0pt]

\phi_{l}^{\max},&l\in\{1,2,...,L-2\},\\[6.0pt]

1,&l=L-1,\end{cases}$ (3)

where $\phi_{l}^{\max}$ denotes the maximum score value of level $l$ importance scores.

Next, the distortion-robust Gaussian attributes $A$ are multiplied by their respective rescale ratios $\hat{\phi}_{l}$ before quantization, forming adjusted attribute value $A^{\prime}$ :

$A^{\prime}=A\cdot\hat{\phi}_{l}$ .

During decoding, the original attribute values will be restored by dividing their own rescale ratio:

$\hat{A}=\hat{A}^{\prime}/\hat{\phi}_{l}$ .

Through this process, while Gaussian attributes share the same per-channel quantization range and bit width, the value ranges of attributes from less important Gaussians are narrowed down, equivalent to being quantized at a lower precision. When combined with subsequent video coding, this strategy plays a role analogous to the rate–distortion optimization process in video codecs, while requiring no major modifications to existing codec architectures.

It is worth noting that Gaussians assigned to the lowest importance level are permanently discarded, as their attributes are multiplied by zero and can no longer be restored. This process is equivalent to pruning and can be controlled by adjusting a predefined lowest importance ratio, which in turn determines the corresponding score threshold $\phi_{\mathrm{thres}}$ .

We now explain how to train a generalized score estimator to predict the aforementioned importance score $\phi$ . The score estimator we propose takes features that describe each primitive’s spatial and temporal properties as input, and outputs a per-point predicted importance score.Generalized Importance Score Estimator:

We extract seven feature types from each 4D primitive: the average KNN distance $d$ , computed at the midpoint of its uniform linear motion; the 4D Gaussian scales $(s_{x},s_{y},s_{z},s_{t})$ ; the 4D volume $V=s_{x}s_{y}s_{z}s_{t}$ ; the opacity $\alpha$ ; the color anisotropy $A$ , defined as the ratio of color variance to squared mean over $M$ sampled directions on the bounding sphere; the motion magnitude $v$ ; and the lifespan $T$ , measured as the temporal interval where the opacity decay $\sigma(t)$ exceeds a threshold $\tau$ .

Given the resulting 10-channel feature set $\{d,s_{x},s_{y},s_{z},s_{t},V,\alpha,A,v,T\}$ and the $K$ nearest neighbors of each Gaussian, we standardize each feature both globally across all features and locally within its neighborhood, and concatenate the resulting features to feed into the score estimator.

With the input of the score estimator prepared, we then obtain the corresponding supervision by training per-point importance scores in a rate-distortion optimization manner on the training dataset. Specifically, we assign a sigmoid function constrained importance score $\phi^{s}\in(0,1)$ to each Gaussian. Based on the score, we proceed simulation of importance-based adaptive quantization, where the quantization step size $\Delta$ is defined as:

$\Delta(\phi^{s})=\frac{\Delta_{0}}{\phi^{s}}$ (4)

Here, $\Delta_{0}$ denotes the base quantization step size. Through this design, Gaussians have their quantization step size adjusted according to their respective importance score, effectively simulating the possible perturbation caused by adaptive quantization. Additionally, the least important Gaussian attributes will all be quantized to zero to faithfully simulate the effect of discarding them.

Quantization is simulated using a straight-through estimator (STE) to enable gradient propagation, as quantization is inherently a discrete operation.

For optimization, we introduce a rendering quality loss to preserve representation accuracy, as defined in Eq. (), and a sparsity loss to encourage smaller importance scores, defined in Eq. (). The two terms formulate a rate–distortion joint training objective, enabling to learn rate–distortion–efficient importance scores as supervisions.

5

6

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{render}}=\lVert\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{gt}}\rVert_{1}+\lambda_{\mathrm{dssim}}\big(1-\mathrm{SSIM}(\mathbf{I},\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{gt}})\big).$ (5) $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sparcity}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\phi_{i}^{s},$ (6)

With both the input features and supervision scores prepared, we train a lightweight MLP as a score estimator on the training scenes. Once trained, the estimator generalizes well to unseen scenes, producing accurate and robust importance scores efficiently to guide importance-based adaptive quantization.

III-CMotion- and Importance-Aware Packing

Based on 4D primitives’ predicted importance and their spatial-temporal properties, we propose Importance-based Packing and Motion-Aware Packing to make 4DGS attributes more amendable for existing codecs.

During importance-based adaptive quantization, the distortion-robust Gaussian attributes are rescaled.

Therefore, attributes at different importance levels exhibit distinct statistical distributions. This necessitates separate handling when reorganizing 4DGS attributes into 2D attribute maps for image and video coding.

Specifically, we apply Morton sorting to the trajectory centers $\overline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{3D}$ of 4DGS within each importance level, evaluated at the time of maximum opacity. After obtaining the 1D Morton order for each level, we concatenate them into a unified 1D ordering. Based on this ordering, we reorganize 4DGS attributes into a 2D pixel grid using row-major layout, which balances packing efficiency and spatial locality.

Finally, the reorganized 2D maps of distortion-sensitive attributes are compressed using PNG. For distortion-robust attributes, higher-order SH maps are concatenated into a multi-frame video, while opacity and zeroth-order SH maps form single-frame videos; both are compressed using HEVC via FFmpeg.

Through this design, Gaussians of different importance levels are placed in separate regions, allowing less important attributes’ region to be smoother and easier for video codes to encode. It is worth noting that the importance map, doesn’t have to be encoded and transmitted for restoring the rescaled attribute values. Instead, thanks to the reorganization method described above, it suffices to store and transmit only the coordinates of the $L-2$ pixels that mark the boundaries between the $L-1$ regions in the importance map, along with the $L-1$ regions corresponding rescale ratio $\hat{\phi}_{l}$ .Importance-based Packing:

: Fig. 3Example histograms of one sh channel’s distribution.N

To exploit the spatial-temporal characteristics of 4DGS for compression, we analyze the motion statistics of 4D primitives and observe a Laplacian-like distribution: most Gaussians exhibit near-zero motion, while only a small fraction move rapidly. Further analysis reveals a consistent difference in attribute distributions between these two groups. For example, Fig.  shows that the high-order spherical harmonics coefficients (sh) of dynamic Gaussians lie in a significantly narrower range than those of near-static ones. This is because dynamic Gaussians are observed under fewer stable view directions, which suppresses high-frequency angular variations. This observation generalizes to other attribute channels like zero-order spherical harmonics and the imaginary parts of both quaternions.

Based on this observation, we partition 4DGS into , whose motion magnitudes along all axes are below a threshold $v_{\text{th}}$ , and , where at least one axis exceeds this threshold.

We then apply motion-aware packing by processing these two groups independently. Each group is reorganized into separate attribute maps and quantized using group-specific minimum and maximum values, while sharing the same bit width. As dynamic Gaussians occupy a smaller value range, this strategy effectively increases quantization precision, leading to improved rate-distortion performance without additional cost.Motion-Aware Packing:

IV-AExperiment Settings

For training, we select three representative scenes in the MeetRoom dataset to reconstruct 4DGS and derive per-point importance scores, serving as the supervision targets for the importance score estimator. For evaluation, we conduct experiments on the Neural 3D Video dataset, using the initial 300 frames of each scene for all evaluations.Datasets:[]

7

8

We adopt the official implementation of 4DGS to train 4DGS models on the two datasets. Notably, we do not employ the extremely redundant temporal spherical harmonics proposed in the original work. Instead, we use 48 channel spherical harmonics following Inria 3DGS  and are able to reproduce the reported rendering quality.

After obtaining the per-point importance scores as supervision, we train an MLP-based score estimator, whose layer dimensions are [256, 128, 64, 64, 32], to regress importance values.

We set the number of importance levels $L$ to 5 in our experiments.Implementation Details:[]

15

[]

5

Post-training compression for 4DGS remains largely unexplored, and no dedicated baselines currently exist. To enable a comprehensive evaluation, we compare our method against two categories of approaches.

We include D-FCGS , a post-training compression framework designed for dynamic Gaussian representations that operates on per-frame 3DGS sequences rather than 4DGS. We further adapt representative 3D or 4D compression methods to the post-training setting to compress the same 4DGS data for fair comparison. Specifically, we consider 4DGS-1K PC, adapted from 4DGS-1K  by removing the post-pruning fine-tuning stage, and SOGS , which we extend to 4DGS by sorting 4D Gaussians into 2D image layouts using its proposed sorting strategy.

We also compare with approaches that integrate compression into the reconstruction pipeline, including MEGA , 4DGS-1K , Spacetime Gaussians , and the original 4DGS  as a reference. These methods jointly optimize reconstruction and compression through end-to-end training or extensive per-scene fine-tuning, whereas our approach focuses on post-training compression without retraining.Baselines:(1) Post-training compression methods.[]

IV-BComparison with State-of-the-Art Methods

Table  reports rate–distortion (RD) performance in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, together with rendering FPS and encoding/decoding time on the Neural 3D Video dataset. Fig.  further shows PSNR–bitrate and encoding-time comparisons. Our method achieves superior RD performance over most post-training compression approaches while requiring substantially less encoding time. Compared with state-of-the-art optimization-based methods such as MEGA, our approach attains comparable RD performance while delivering significantly higher rendering FPS, as it avoids feature decoding during rendering. Moreover, our method is more flexible across devices with different GPU memory budgets, since the MLP-based importance prediction does not require processing all Gaussians simultaneously, unlike rendering-based scoring methods. Qualitative results in Fig.  further demonstrate that our method preserves visual quality comparable to the 4DGS baseline while achieving a $33\times$ compression ratio.

To assess the effectiveness of our method, we perform ablation studies on the Neural 3D Video dataset focusing on the following three components:

We assess our score estimator based on pruning guidance effectiveness, GPU memory usage, and computational time.

We first compare our generalized importance score with the spatiotemporal variation score proposed in 4DGS-1K, which requires rendering all training views and computing importance from opacity and lifespan. Fig.  shows the PSNR–pruning ratio curves, where our approach achieves better performance using an efficient, generalizable importance estimator. Next, we evaluate the flexibility of our method in terms of GPU memory usage and computational efficiency in Table , using the Coffee Martini scene with approximately 4.5 million primitives. While 4DGS-1K incurs high GPU memory consumption by loading all active primitives into the rendering pipeline simultaneously, our method allows for flexibly adjusting the input feature batch size to match available device memory. In terms of runtime, our approach completes in 4 seconds, whereas 4DGS-1K requires approximately 3 minutes due to the need to render all training views.

In this section, we evaluate the rate-distortion performance improvements achieved by the proposed importance-based adaptive quantization, as well as the effect of simulating this strategy during the supervision training of the generalized score estimator. The RD comparisons are presented in Fig. . To assess the effectiveness of adaptive quantization, we compare two settings with different numbers of importance levels: $L=2$ (Ours w/o Adaptive Quantization) and $L=5$ (Ours). Our method achieves an approximate 12% bitrate reduction at the highest bitrate point with no PSNR drop, indicating that it effectively removes redundancy among Gaussians while maintaining quality.Importance-Based Adaptive Quantization for Attributes:

6(b)

Furthermore, we analyze the contribution of adaptive quantization simulation during supervision training. When adaptive quantization is not simulated during training (i.e., only pruning is simulated with $L=2$ ), but adaptive quantization is still applied during post-training processing with $L=5$ , a noticeable degradation in rendering quality is observed. This behavior suggests that simulating adaptive quantization during training leads to importance scores that are more robust to adaptive quantization at compression time, thereby alleviating the quality loss introduced by this process.

Our separate packing strategy maintains the same quantization bit width for both dynamic and near-static Gaussians. As a result, dynamic Gaussian attributes are quantized with higher precision without introducing additional bit width due to their reduced value range. We further assign a higher QP to the high-order spherical harmonics of dynamic Gaussians when encoded with video codecs to optimize bitrate allocation. This leads to a clear improvement in RD performance, as demonstrated in Fig. .Motion-Aware Packing:

6(b)

V Conclusion

This paper introduces a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS that achieves competitive rate-distortion performance with minimal encoding and decoding time.

Through importance-based adaptive quantization and motion- and importance-aware packing, guided by a lightweight and generalizable importance estimator, we effectively exploit redundancy in the 4DGS representation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach delivers a strong rate–distortion trade-off with very short runtime and high flexibility across GPU memory constraints.

item.title: RDCompGS：把 3DGS 压缩当成率失真优化问题 ｜ RDCompGS: Rate–Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs
item.description:
一句话：把高斯属性映射成 2D 图后用可微率估计联合优化，BD-Rate 平均降 37.8%（HEVC）/49.3%（JPEG XL）。

要点：

  • 在把高斯属性排成 2D 图交给图像编解码器时，显式引入可微率估计模型，让码率与渲染失真一起进优化目标
  • 平均 BD-Rate 相对基线降低 37.84%（H.265/HEVC）与 49.31%（JPEG XL），渲染质量持平
  • 核心洞察是量化步长变大时率梯度幅值会衰减，需要按压缩条件动态调节率与失真的权重

为什么值得看：「压完画质崩」多半是压缩目标与渲染目标不一致，把率失真放进优化里最省事。

中文摘要：3DGS 渲染又快又好，但存储与传输代价高。把高斯属性映射到 2D 表示可以借用成熟的图像编解码器，问题是这样做之后率失真性能并不能自动对齐渲染质量——压缩优化的目标通常是降低表示误差，而不是降低渲染误差。RDCompGS 显式引入可微率估计模型，把估计码率与渲染失真一起纳入优化，并按不同压缩条件调节二者权重。作者还分析了量化步长增大时率梯度幅值会衰减这一现象，据此设计调整策略。在三个基准数据集上，方法在渲染质量持平的前提下取得平均 37.84%（H.265/HEVC）与 49.31%（JPEG XL）的 BD-Rate 降低；与剪枝结合时收益还能进一步叠加。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

RDCompGS: Rate–Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs

Huiping Ren

Shuai Wan

Luqian Bai

Zhang Chen

and Fuzheng Yang

†Huiping Ren, Shuai Wan and Luqian Bai are with the School of Electronics and

Information, Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi’an 710129, China

(e-mail: huiping_ren@mail.nwpu.edu.cn; swan@nwpu.edu.cn; Luqianbai@mail.nwpu.edu.cn).†thanks: †Zhang Chen is with the School of Electronics and Information,

Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi’an 710129, China, and also with the

Department of Computer Science, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR,

China (e-mail: chenzhang@mail.nwpu.edu.cn).†thanks: †Fuzheng Yang is with the School of Telecommunication Engineering,

Xidian University, Xi’an 710071, China

(e-mail: fzhyang@mail.xidian.edu.cn).†thanks:

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources.

Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs.

However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression.

To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding.

A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion.

The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions.

Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bjøntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.

3D Gaussian Splatting, 3DGS compression, rate-distortion optimization, image codecs.

Index Terms:

I Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  is an important approach for novel view synthesis. By representing scenes with explicit anisotropic 3D Gaussians and rendering them through $\alpha$ -blending, 3DGS achieves high rendering quality and real-time performance. 3DGS is an active research topic and is relevant to areas such as autonomous driving, multimedia interaction, virtual reality, cultural heritage digitization, and digital twinning .

However, representing a 3D scene with 3DGS typically requires millions of Gaussian primitives, leading to significant storage and memory overhead . Existing studies on 3DGS compression mainly focus on two aspects.[]

1

2

3

4

5

6

[, ]

8

The first aspect directly compresses the native 3D Gaussian representation. We broadly classify current approaches into Gaussian parameter and attribute compression , anchor-based compression , and Gaussian primitive compactification . These strategies are not mutually exclusive and are often combined to reduce redundancy.[, , , , , , , , ]

9

10

11

14

24

26

The second aspect converts 3DGS into 2D representations and compresses them using mature image codecs .

This direction enables 3DGS compression to directly leverage established coding standards and their existing software and hardware support, providing a practical solution for 3DGS storage and transmission.

As shown in Fig. , the general pipeline consists of 3DGS generation and compression. The scene is first represented by Gaussian primitives and then mapped into 2D representations for coding.[, , , , , ]

27

28

29

30

31

32

1

General pipeline for converting 3DGS into 2D representations and compressing them using image codecs.

Fig. 1:

However, in 3DGS compression through image codecs, Gaussian optimization is usually separated from subsequent coding. Specifically, Gaussian optimization evaluates attributes according to their contribution to rendered views, while

subsequent compression is performed considering both the coding distortion and the corresponding bit-rate as the cost. As the result, Gaussian representations with comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization even when their coding rates differ substantially. Therefore, the rate-distortion (R-D) performance cannot be optimized for compression if reducing the rendering distortion is the optimization goal. Since the actual bit-rate produced by the codec is also not differentiable, it is not feasible to be directly incorporated into Gaussian optimization.

Moreover, the balance between coding rate and rendering distortion changes across compression conditions. Therefore, applying a single rate constraint to all compression conditions cannot maintain an appropriate R-D trade-off, which limits the R-D performance after compression.

To address the above issues, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization in which Gaussian generation and subsequent coding are treated as a whole.

During Gaussian optimization, rendering distortion and the coding rate associated with subsequent compression are jointly optimized to improve the R-D performance after compression.

To incorporate the coding rate into Gaussian optimization, RDCompGS introduces differentiable rate estimation based on the statistical distribution of transformed coefficients and their quantization probabilities.

Different from prior approaches that optimize under a prescribed rate or distortion setting, the rate constraint adjustment model characterizes the relative strength of the estimated rate and rendering distortion and adjusts their balance across different compression conditions.

Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average BD-Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively, while maintaining comparable rendering quality.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows.

•

We consider Gaussian generation and subsequent coding as a whole for 3DGS compression and formulate the compression of Gaussian representations as an overall R-D optimization with respect to subsequent

coding.

•

Based on this formulation, we propose RDCompGS, which derives a differentiable estimate of the coding rate from transformed Gaussian attributes and introduces the rate constraint adjustment model to regulate the rate constraint under different coding conditions.

•

We validate RDCompGS on three benchmark datasets using both H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, showing consistent R-D improvements across different coding conditions. Additional experiments combining Gaussian pruning with image codec compression further confirm the effectiveness of RDCompGS.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows.

Section  presents the related work.

Section  introduces the proposed method. Section  reports the experimental results and analysis. Finally, Section  concludes this paper.

II

III

IV

V

II Related Work

Based on the Gaussian representation used during compression, we divide existing 3DGS compression methods into two types: compression of 3D Gaussian representations and compression of 3DGS with 2D representations.

II-ACompression of 3D Gaussian Representations

We broadly classify methods for compressing 3D Gaussian representations into Gaussian parameter and attribute compression, anchor-based compression, and Gaussian primitive compactification.

Gaussian parameter and attribute compression reduces storage by making the representation of individual Gaussians more compact while retaining the native 3D Gaussian structure.

Representative approaches include quantization, which reduces storage by lowering precision , entropy coding based on symbol probabilities to reduce the coded length , and spherical harmonics (SH) reduction .[, , , , ]

9

10

11

12

13

[, ]

14

15

[, ]

17

16

Anchor-based methods reduce 3DGS redundancy by organizing local Gaussians around sparse anchors while exploiting relationships among anchors and their associated attributes. Representative methods include Scaffold-GS , HAC , HAC++ , ContextGS , and CAT-3DGS , which exploit attribute prediction, contextual dependencies, hierarchical relationships, and spatial correlations for compression.[]

18

[]

19

[]

20

[]

21

[]

22

Gaussian primitive compactification reduces redundancy by controlling the number or distribution of Gaussians. Representative methods include PUP 3D-GS , LightGaussian , APNet , visibility-based geometry pruning , REFINE , and SPARE-GS . These methods exploit spatial sensitivity scores, global significance scores, view-dependent masks and Rasterization Weight Sampling, multi-view visibility, rendering-aware importance, and global budget allocation to reduce redundant Gaussians or regulate their spatial distribution.[]

23

[]

17

[]

3

[]

24

[]

25

[]

26

Although these methods effectively reduce redundancy in native 3D Gaussian representations, they mainly compress Gaussian primitives in their original representation form. Another direction incorporates 2D representations into 3DGS compression, enabling the use of established image codecs for compression.

II-BCompression of 3DGS with 2D Representations

We broadly divide existing 3DGS compression methods based on 2D representations according to when the 2D representation is introduced: during or after the Gaussian optimization process.

Methods that introduce 2D representations after Gaussian optimization adopt different mapping strategies.

LGSCV  first applies a 3D Morton scan to order Gaussian primitives and then uses a 2D Morton scan to map them into blockwise 2D maps, which are compressed using H.265/HEVC. To improve performance at medium and low bit-rates, it further applies Principal Component Analysis to SH coefficients and introduces MiniPLAS for local primitive permutation.

Zhu et al.  propose a Dual-Hilbert scan algorithm that uses a 3D Hilbert curve to preserve spatial locality and a 2D Hilbert curve to map the ordered Gaussian primitives into 2D grids for subsequent H.265/HEVC compression.

3DGCoding  sorts Gaussian primitives in z-order according to their positions, maps the quantized attributes onto 2D planes, and compresses the attribute planes of static Gaussians using lossless PNG and those of dynamic Gaussians using H.265/HEVC.

V sorts Gaussian primitives using Morton order, maps Gaussian attributes into video frames, and compresses them using H.264/AVC.[]

27

[]

28

[]

29

3[]

32

For methods that introduce 2D representations during Gaussian optimization, CodecGS  redesigns the explicit Gaussian representation using progressive tri-plane features and employs a multilayer perceptron to predict Gaussian attributes. The feature plane channels are then concatenated into frames and compressed using H.265/HEVC. Compared with CodecGS, SOG  retains explicit Gaussian attributes and directly organizes them into aligned 2D grids using Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS).[]

30

[]

31

Specifically, PLAS improves the local smoothness of the grids by constructing a smoothed target with a Gaussian filter and performing parallel blockwise assignments to update the arrangement of Gaussian primitives. The optimized Gaussian parameters are then quantized and compressed using JPEG XL.

To summarize, organizing Gaussian parameters into 2D representations provides a structured form that can be compressed using image codecs.

However, Gaussian optimization remains separated from subsequent coding, which limits the overall R-D performance.

III Methodology

To enable overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding, RDCompGS first introduces based on the distribution of transformed coefficients and their quantization probabilities.

Then, regulates the rate constraint across different compression conditions.

Finally, the estimated rate and rendering distortion jointly guide Gaussian optimization for subsequent coding.

Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed RDCompGS.differentiable rate estimationthe rate constraint adjustment model

To address the mismatch between Gaussian attribute optimization and subsequent coding and the limitation of using a single rate constraint across different coding conditions, we propose RDCompGS, as shown in Fig. .

RDCompGS introduces two main components. (a) Differentiable rate estimation constructs a differentiable rate term for Gaussian optimization (Section ).

(b) The rate constraint adjustment model regulates the influence of the estimated rate under different coding conditions (Section ).

The weighted rate term is then combined with the rendering distortion for Gaussian optimization (Section ).

The optimized Gaussian attributes are subsequently compressed using image codecs.

2

III-A

III-B

III-C

III-ADifferentiable Rate Estimation Model

Natural images generally exhibit strong spatial correlation, which is exploited by image codecs to reduce spatial redundancy. PLAS organizes Gaussian attributes into 2D grids and places Gaussians with similar attribute values at nearby positions.

As shown in Fig. , PLAS improves the spatial correlation of the Gaussian attribute grids, but a difference from natural images still remains. To further reduce redundancy for subsequent compression while maintaining rendering quality, RDCompGS performs overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding.

3

To incorporate the coding rate into the overall R-D optimization, we introduce differentiable rate estimation for the non-position Gaussian attributes.

The non-position attributes are first normalized and transformed using an $8\times 8$ block-based Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), while the position attributes are excluded to preserve scene geometry.

The statistical analysis in  motivates modeling the transformed coefficients using a zero-mean Laplace distribution. Fig.  further shows that the transformed coefficients exhibit distributions that are consistent with the Laplace model.[]

33

4

Let $x_{i}$ denote the $i$ -th DCT coefficient and $b_{i}>0$ its scale parameter.

The Laplace probability density function is

$p(x_{i}\mid b_{i})=\frac{1}{2b_{i}}\exp\left(-\frac{|x_{i}|}{b_{i}}\right).$ (1)

For a uniform scalar quantizer with step size $\Delta$ , the quantized

coefficient is

$q_{i}=\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{x_{i}}{\Delta}\right).$ (2)

The probability of obtaining $q_{i}$ is

$P_{i}=\int_{(q_{i}-\frac{1}{2})\Delta}^{(q_{i}+\frac{1}{2})\Delta}p(t\mid b_{i})\,\mathrm{d}t.$ (3)

Under the high-resolution scalar quantization approximation, the probability

density is approximately constant within each quantization interval.

Therefore, Eq. () can be approximated as

3

$P_{i}\approx\Delta p(x_{i}\mid b_{i}).$ (4)

Based on self-information, we define

$r_{i}=-\log_{2}P_{i}$ .

Using Eqs. () and

(), we obtain

4

1

$r_{i}\approx\log_{2}\left(\frac{2b_{i}}{\Delta}\right)+\frac{|x_{i}|}{b_{i}\ln 2}.$ (5)

Since the scale parameter $b_{i}$ is unknown during Gaussian optimization, we

eliminate it by minimizing Eq. () with respect to $b_{i}$ .

For $x_{i}\neq 0$ , the minimizing solution is

5

$b_{i}^{\star}=|x_{i}|.$ (6)

Substituting Eq. () into Eq. () yields

6

5

$r_{i}\approx\log_{2}\left(\frac{2e|x_{i}|}{\Delta}\right).$ (7)

To make the rate term differentiable and nonnegative during Gaussian optimization, we define

$r_{i}=\log_{2}\left(1+\frac{2e\sqrt{x_{i}^{2}+\epsilon}}{\Delta}\right),\qquad\epsilon=10^{-6}.$ (8)

The estimated rate is obtained by accumulating $r_{i}$ over the DCT coefficients

of the non-position Gaussian attributes:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}=k\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{i}=k\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log_{2}\left(1+\frac{2e\sqrt{x_{i}^{2}+\epsilon}}{\Delta}\right),$ (9)

where $N$ denotes the total number of DCT coefficients included in the rate

term, and $k$ is a conversion coefficient that scales the accumulated rate to

kbps.

III-BThe Rate Constraint Adjustment Model

During Gaussian optimization, the rendering distortion and the weighted estimated rate are jointly used to update the Gaussian parameters.

Since the gradient magnitude of the estimated rate varies with the quantization step, a single rate constraint cannot maintain an appropriate balance between the estimated rate and rendering distortion across different compression conditions. As illustrated in Fig. , using a single rate constraint provides only limited improvements in the high-bit-rate region. RDCompGS therefore introduces the rate constraint adjustment model to adjust the rate constraint according to the quantization step.

5

R-D performance comparison on the Truck scene under H.265/HEVC compression between Gaussian optimization without the rate constraint and with the rate constraint using $\lambda_{\mathrm{rate}}=1\times 10^{-7}$ at QP values of 4, 10, 16, and 22.Fig. 5:

We first analyze how the quantization step affects the rate gradient that is

backpropagated to the Gaussian parameters. According to

Eq. (), the gradient of the estimated rate with respect to the

$i$ -th DCT coefficient is

9

$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}}{\partial x_{i}}=\frac{2ekx_{i}}{\ln 2\,\sqrt{x_{i}^{2}+\epsilon}\left(\Delta+2e\sqrt{x_{i}^{2}+\epsilon}\right)}.$ (10)

For a fixed DCT coefficient $x_{i}$ ,

Eq. () shows that increasing the quantization

step reduces the gradient magnitude. When

10

$2e\sqrt{x_{i}^{2}+\epsilon}\ll\Delta,$ (11)

the dependence on $\Delta$ can be approximated as

$\left|\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}}{\partial x_{i}}\right|\propto\Delta^{-1}.$ (12)

Let $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ denote the Gaussian parameters and let $\mathbf{x}=F(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ denote the DCT coefficients obtained from the non-position Gaussian parameters. By the chain rule,

$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}=\mathbf{J}_{F}^{T}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}},$ (13)

where $\mathbf{J}_{F}$ denotes the Jacobian of

$F(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ .

Since the mapping from the Gaussian parameters to the DCT coefficients does

not explicitly depend on $\Delta$ , the dependence of

$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}$ on the

quantization step is introduced through

$\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}$ .

According to Eq. (), the rate gradient with

respect to the Gaussian parameters therefore approximately satisfies

12

$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\Delta)\approx\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\Delta}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}),$ (14)

where $\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ denotes a reference quantization step.

To characterize the magnitude of the rate gradient, we define

$G_{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\Delta)=\left\lVert\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\Delta)\right\rVert_{2}.$ (15)

The corresponding magnitude at $\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is denoted by

$G_{R,\mathrm{ref}}=G_{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}).$ (16)

Taking the $L_{2}$ norm on both sides of

Eq. () gives

14

$\frac{G_{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\Delta)}{G_{R,\mathrm{ref}}}\approx\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\Delta}.$ (17)

The same Gaussian parameters are also updated by the rendering distortion. We

therefore define

$G_{D}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\left\lVert\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{D}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right\rVert_{2},$ (18)

where $G_{D}$ denotes the magnitude of the rendering distortion gradient with respect to the Gaussian parameters.

To characterize the influence of the estimated rate relative to the rendering distortion, we define

$\rho(\Delta)=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{rate}}(\Delta)G_{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\Delta)}{G_{D}(\boldsymbol{\theta})},$ (19)

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{rate}}(\Delta)$ denotes the rate constraint at $\Delta$ , and $\rho(\Delta)$ represents the relative rate constraint strength with respect to the rendering distortion.

The reference value of the relative rate constraint strength is defined as

$\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}G_{R,\mathrm{ref}}}{G_{D}(\boldsymbol{\theta})},$ (20)

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ denotes the rate constraint at

$\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ .

Combining Eqs. (),

(), and

() gives

19

20

17

$\frac{\rho(\Delta)}{\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}}\approx\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{rate}}(\Delta)}{\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}}\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\Delta}.$ (21)

If the rate constraint is adjusted only to compensate for the reduction in the rate gradient magnitude as $\Delta$ increases, $\rho(\Delta)$ should remain approximately unchanged. However, this does not reflect the different compression requirements across quantization steps. A smaller $\Delta$ places more emphasis on rendering quality, whereas a larger $\Delta$ requires greater emphasis on reducing redundancy in Gaussian attributes. Accordingly, we let $\rho(\Delta)$ increase with $\Delta$ as

$\frac{\rho(\Delta)}{\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}}=\left(\frac{\Delta}{\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)^{\beta},\qquad\beta>0,$ (22)

where $\beta$ controls the sensitivity of $\rho(\Delta)$ to the quantization step.

Combining Eq. () with

Eq. (), the rate constraint is defined as

22

21

$\lambda_{\mathrm{rate}}(\Delta)=\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}\left(\frac{\Delta}{\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)^{1+\beta}.$ (23)

III-CTotal Training Loss

Following 3DGS , the rendering distortion is defined as[]

1

$\mathcal{L}_{D}=(1-\lambda_{\mathrm{dssim}})\mathcal{L}_{L1}+\lambda_{\mathrm{dssim}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{D\text{-}SSIM}},$ (24)

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{dssim}}=0.2$ .

The distortion considered in RDCompGS refers to the rendering distortion defined above, while the distortion introduced by compression is not explicitly modeled in the optimization process.

Before densification ends, the Gaussian representation is optimized using

only $\mathcal{L}_{D}$ . After densification, the estimated rate in

Eq. () is incorporated into Gaussian optimization using $\lambda_{\mathrm{rate}}(\Delta)$ in

Eq. (). The total training loss is

9

23

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{D}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rate}}(\Delta)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}.$ (25)

By jointly incorporating the estimated rate and rendering distortion, RDCompGS connects Gaussian optimization with subsequent coding to achieve overall R-D optimization for 3DGS compression.

IV Experiments

IV-AExperimental Setup

1 IV-A

We conduct experiments on three datasets: Tanks and Temples , Deep Blending , and Mip-NeRF 360 . These datasets contain diverse indoor and outdoor scenes with complex geometry and texture details. We evaluate rendering quality using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) , and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) . The encoded data sizes generated by H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL are used for compression evaluation. The coding performance is evaluated in terms of the Bjøntegaard delta rate (BD-Rate) .[]

34

[]

35

[]

36

[]

37

[]

38

[]

39

2 IV-A

The proposed method is implemented in PyTorch. Experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU. During training, PLAS is applied after Gaussian initialization and after each densification step to organize the Gaussian parameters into 2D representations. After the densification stage, differentiable rate estimation is introduced into Gaussian optimization.

Following the settings in V and SOG , Gaussian attributes are first quantized and then compressed using image codecs.

The position attributes are quantized to 16-bit values and split into high and low 8-bit components, which are represented as two three-channel RGB images.

The remaining attributes are quantized to 8-bit values.

Specifically, the opacity attribute and the $w$ component of the rotation quaternion are represented as single-channel grayscale images, whereas the scale attribute, the $xyz$ components of the rotation quaternion, and the SH coefficients are represented as three-channel RGB images.

These attribute images are then compressed using H.265/HEVC  (all intra coding) or JPEG XL , where the position attributes are encoded losslessly and the remaining attributes are encoded using lossy compression.3[]

32

[]

31

[]

40

[]

41

For H.265/HEVC compression, the quantization parameter (QP) values are set to 4, 10, 16, and 22. The corresponding quantization step size $\Delta$ is calculated following .

Higher QP values are not considered because they cause severe degradation in rendering quality. To determine the JPEG XL distance value, we select 260 3DGS attribute images from the three datasets. The position attribute images are excluded. For each H.265/HEVC QP, we use binary search to determine the JPEG XL distance value that produces the same bits per pixel. The resulting distance values are 0.1005, 0.2157, 0.4511, and 0.9363 for QP values of 4, 10, 16, and 22, respectively.

For SOG, the SH attributes are compressed using JPEG XL with quality levels of 95, 90, 70, and 50, while the default compression settings are used for all other attributes.

The coefficient $k=1/40$ is derived from the encoder frame rate of 25 frames per second.[]

Based on the parameter analysis conducted on the Truck scene from Tanks and Temples, we set

$\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}=8$ ,

$\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}=1\times 10^{-7}$ ,

and $\beta=0.2$ . Since the Truck scene is used to determine the reference parameters, it is excluded from all subsequent R-D evaluations to avoid potential bias.

The exceptions are the validation of the rate estimation model in

Section  and the analysis of the rate constraint adjustment model in Section , where the Truck scene is retained.

IV-BCompression Performance

We evaluate RDCompGS by compressing the optimized Gaussian representations using JPEG XL and H.265/HEVC, and compare the resulting R-D performance with SOG. Tables  and  report the results with JPEG XL and H.265/HEVC, respectively. The BD-Rate results show consistent R-D improvements across the three datasets. With JPEG XL, RDCompGS obtains BD-Rate reductions of 30.44%, 60.94%, and 56.55% on Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, and Mip-NeRF 360, respectively, corresponding to an average reduction of 49.31%. Similar improvements are observed with H.265/HEVC, where the corresponding BD-Rate reductions are 15.44%, 50.48%, and 47.61%, with an average reduction of 37.84%.

IV-CValidation of Rate Estimation Model

Having established the R-D improvements, we further evaluate the correlation between the estimated rate and the actual bit-rate. We use 260 non-position Gaussian attribute images generated after PLAS sorting. For each image, the estimated rate is compared with the actual bit-rate obtained by encoding the same image with H.265/HEVC.

As shown in Fig. , the estimated rate exhibits a strong linear correlation with the actual bit-rate across all tested QP values. At QP values of 4, 10, 16, and 22, the Pearson correlation coefficients are 0.997, 0.996, 0.990, and 0.973, respectively.

IV-DAnalysis of the Rate Constraint Adjustment Model

The parameter settings of the rate constraint adjustment model are analyzed in this section. The reference quantization step is set to $\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}=8$ . According to Eq. (), using a relatively large $\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ keeps the rate constraint small at small quantization steps, avoiding an excessive rate constraint in the high-bit-rate region.

The effects of $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $\beta$ are evaluated on the Truck scene, and the selected values are used in the subsequent experiments.

23

1 IV-D

Fig.  presents the R-D curves obtained with

different $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ values. As

$\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ increases, the compressed size generally decreases,

showing that a larger rate coefficient places a stronger constraint on the

estimated rate during Gaussian optimization. For relatively small

$\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ values, the reduction in compressed size is limited,

while the rendering quality remains relatively stable. Increasing

$\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ to $1\times 10^{-7}$ provides a more evident size

reduction without noticeable degradation in the three quality metrics.

Further increasing $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ results in only limited additional

size reduction, while PSNR and SSIM decrease and LPIPS increases more

noticeably. Considering these trends,

$\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}=1\times 10^{-7}$ provides a favorable trade-off

between compression efficiency and rendering quality and is therefore adopted

in the subsequent experiments.

IV-ECombination with Gaussian Pruning

Gaussian pruning can be incorporated into the 3DGS compression pipeline using image codecs.

To evaluate RDCompGS under this setting, we first adopt the pruning procedure in LightGaussian and optimize the Gaussian representation using RDCompGS.

In this process, pruning reduces the number of Gaussian primitives, while RDCompGS performs R-D optimization of the remaining Gaussian representation with respect to subsequent coding.

As shown in Table , the combination of RDCompGS with Gaussian pruning achieves consistent R-D improvements over LightGaussian on all three datasets. The BD-Rate reductions are 38.83%, 67.19%, and 54.54% on Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, and Mip-NeRF 360,

respectively, corresponding to an average reduction of 53.52%.

Across different QPs, RDCompGS substantially reduces the compressed size while maintaining comparable or slightly higher PSNR and SSIM, with LPIPS remaining generally comparable to that of LightGaussian.

These results demonstrate that RDCompGS remains effective when combined with Gaussian pruning, providing additional R-D gains for the pruned

Gaussian representation.

IV-FAblation Studies

We conduct ablation studies to evaluate the two main components of RDCompGS, including differentiable rate estimation and the rate constraint adjustment model.

Their effects are evaluated separately under

H.265/HEVC compression.

1 IV-F

To evaluate the effectiveness of differentiable rate estimation, we remove the estimated rate term from Gaussian optimization while keeping the other

settings unchanged. As shown in

Table , incorporating rate estimation consistently improves the R-D performance across all three datasets, with

BD-Rate reductions exceeding 50%. In particular, the reduction reaches 62.32% on Deep Blending, while positive BD-PSNR gains are obtained

on all three datasets. These results demonstrate that differentiable rate estimation effectively connects Gaussian representation optimization with

subsequent coding, leading to substantial R-D improvements.

2 IV-F

We further evaluate the rate constraint adjustment model while retaining differentiable rate estimation. Specifically, a single rate constraint with $\lambda_{\mathrm{rate}}=1\times 10^{-7}$ is used across all compression conditions instead of the adjustment model, while the remaining settings are kept unchanged.

As shown in Table , the rate constraint adjustment model

provides non-negative BD-PSNR gains on all three datasets and improves the

overall BD-Rate performance. Although the BD-Rate increases slightly by

0.77% on the Train scene, reductions are obtained on Deep Blending and

Mip-NeRF 360, with the latter reaching 5.46%. Averaged over the three

datasets, the adjustment model achieves a BD-Rate reduction of 1.76%. These results indicate that the adjustment model provides a more appropriate rate constraint under different compression conditions, leading to a more favorable overall R-D trade-off than using a single rate constraint.

V Conclusion

In this work, we revisit 3DGS compression with 2D representations from the perspective of R-D optimization, with the aim of better aligning Gaussian attribute optimization with subsequent coding.

We introduce RDCompGS, which combines rate estimation with the rate constraint adjustment model to balance compression and rendering quality under different coding conditions.

Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent R-D improvements across different codec settings, and RDCompGS remains effective when Gaussian pruning is incorporated into compression with image codecs.

Future work will further explore joint modeling of coding rate and compression distortion. Extending RDCompGS to dynamic scenes is also an important direction for future research.
