We propose an end-to-end pipeline for animating fluid regions in a static 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  reconstruction (cf. ).

In contrast to previous methods , our objective is a complete animated 3D scene observable from arbitrary viewing directions.

Besides its real-time rendering capabilities, 3DGS offers an explicit scene representation based on a set of points $\mathcal{G}$ with anisotropic Gaussian extent that are straightforward to animate.

Specifically, each Gaussian is described by its mean $\mathbf{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , 3D covariance $\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ , opacity $o\in[0,1]$ , and view-dependent color $c\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ computed from Spherical Harmonics coefficients $\in\mathbb{R}^{48}$ .

This representation is then optimized from multi-view RGB images $\mathcal{I}_{1,\cdots,N}$ with known camera poses.

To render an image, 3DGS linearly approximates the perspective projection onto the image plane at a point $\mathbf{x}$ (usually $\mathbf{\mu}$ ) :[]

0&\frac{f}{\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{3}}&-\frac{f\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{2}}{(\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{3})^{2}}\end{pmatrix}R_{n},\;\text{with}\;\mathbf{\hat{x}}=R_{n}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{t}_{n}$ (1)

where $\mathbf{\hat{x}}_{i}$ denotes the $i$ -th component of $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ , $(R_{n},\mathbf{t}_{n})$ the world-to-camera transformation of the $n$ -th view, and $f$ the focal length.

Optionally, $\mathcal{I}_{1,\cdots,N}$ can be extended by renderings from user defined camera poses.

For each pixel $\mathbf{p}$ in a rendered image $\mathcal{I}_{n}$ , color is accumulated by alpha blending Gaussian contributions:

$\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathbf{p})=\sum_{i=1}^{M}c_{i}T_{i}o_{i}g_{i}(\mathbf{p})\quad\text{with}\quad T_{i}=\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-o_{j}g_{j}(\mathbf{p})),$ (2)

where $g_{i}(\mathbf{p})$ is the $i$ -th Gaussian value at the pixel $\mathbf{p}$ .

Since our method assumes $\mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{I}_{1,\cdots,N}$ are provided as input, no training modifications and minimal renderer changes (see ) are required.

In the following subsections, we describe each step in our pipeline for animating fluids in such 3DGS models.

Sec.3.3.3

3.1

To construct a 3D motion field, we first estimate 2D optical flow $\mathcal{F}_{1,\cdots,N}$ for each input view.

Since the input images are static and non-time-consecutive, conventional optical flow methods  are not applicable.

Instead, following prior cinemagraph approaches , we employ a specialized neural network trained on fluid motion.

For improved controllability and cross-view consistency, the network is guided by user-defined motion hints and segmentation masks.[]

TD20

[, ]

HCSS21

MK22

We define a set of global 3D motion hints $\mathcal{H}=\left\{(\mathbf{p}_{l},\mathbf{d}_{l})\right\}_{l=1}^{L}$ interactively within the 3DGS scene using our GUI.

Each hint consists of a 3D position $\mathbf{p}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and a motion direction $\mathbf{d}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , where $\lVert\mathbf{d}_{l}\rVert_{2}$ controls motion strength.

Defining hints directly in 3D ensures consistent motion guidance across views.

The hints are projected into each camera view using the projection operator $\pi_{n}$ , resulting in sparse 2D flow hints $\mathcal{H}_{n}=\left\{(\pi_{n}(\mathbf{p}),\pi_{n}(\mathbf{p+d})-\pi_{n}(\mathbf{p}))\mid(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{d})\in\mathcal{H}\right\}$ that are converted to sparse flow maps:

$\mathcal{F}^{\text{sparse}}_{n}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}\frac{\mathbf{d}}{r^{\mathcal{H}}},&\text{if }\exists\,\mathbf{d}\text{ with }(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{d})\in\mathcal{H}_{n}\\

0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\,,$ (3)

with a regulation factor $r^{\mathcal{H}}=\operatorname{median}\left\{\lVert\mathbf{d}\rVert_{2}\mid(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{d})\in\mathcal{H}_{n}\right\}$ to limit the extent of projected motion hints in screen space.

To restrict motion to fluid regions, we additionally compute binary segmentation masks $\mathcal{S}_{1,\cdots,N}$ for all input images using the promptable segmentation model SAM3 .

These masks are used both to guide the motion synthesis network and to constrain subsequent 3D motion field fusion.

In practice, simple prompts such as “water” or “waterfall” are sufficient for robust segmentation in most scenes.

For cases requiring additional user control, we use an interactive segmentation tool .[]

Following Mahapatra and Kulkarni , the sparse flow maps are converted into dense flow maps $\mathcal{F}^{\text{dense}}_{1,\cdots,N}$ via distance-weighted interpolation within the segmented regions (see ).

Finally, a learned flow refinement network takes RGB images $\mathcal{I}_{1,\cdots,N}$ , segmentation masks $\mathcal{S}_{1,\cdots,N}$ , and dense flow maps $\mathcal{F}^{\text{dense}}_{1,\cdots,N}$ as input to generate high-quality fluid flow maps $\mathcal{F}_{1,\cdots,N}$ .

We adopt the SPADE-based U-Net architecture of Mahapatra and Kulkarni  using the implementation and pretrained weights provided by Li et al. .[]

In contrast to motion estimated from Gaussian self-similarity , which suits subtle motion such as swaying vegetation but not dense directional fluid flow, or to flow projected onto a single-view layered depth image , we project multi-view optical flow into the 3DGS scene to obtain a coherent 3D motion field $\mathcal{M}$ .[]

Depth Rendering.

In order to reproject 2D optical flow into the scene, depth information is required.

To this end, we render depth maps $\mathcal{D}_{1,\cdots,N}$ from the 3DGS model for all input views.

We compute the depth of each pixel via alpha blending as defined in , where the color of each Gaussian is replaced by its depth $\mathbf{\hat{\mu}}_{3}$ (cf. ).

Note that we divide by the final alpha value of the pixel to obtain meaningful depth for semi-transparent pixels.

We further highlight that using depth renderings of the underlying 3DGS model aligns the motion field with Gaussians that can be animated.

Eq.1

Multi-View Reprojection.

Our setup for the motion field fusion can be thought of as a multi-view reprojection problem , with $n$ known projections $v_{n}=\mathcal{F}_{n}(x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ of an unknown vector $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ .

This vector is anchored at $\mathbf{x}=\pi^{-1}_{n}(x_{n},\mathcal{D}_{n}(x_{n}))$ , which is the common point when unprojecting each $x_{n}$ into world space using depth information.

The goal is minimizing the geometric non-linear reprojection error:[, ]

HZ03

TIF24

$\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{v}}\displaystyle\sum_{n}\left\lVert\pi_{n}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{v})-(x_{n}+v_{n})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\,.$ (4)

As $v_{n}$ , i.e., the optical flow is usually small, it is reasonable to linearly approximate the perspective projection by first-order Taylor expansion $\pi_{n}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{v})\approx\pi_{n}(\mathbf{x})+J_{n,\,\mathbf{x}}\mathbf{v}$ , with $J_{n,\,\mathbf{x}}$ as defined in .

Since $\pi_{n}(\mathbf{x})=x_{n}$ is known, we can solve a simplified linear system of equations for $\mathbf{v}$ with the iterative Gauss-Newton algorithm:

Eq.1

$\underbrace{\left(\sum_{n}J_{n,\mathbf{x}}^{\top}J_{n,\mathbf{x}}\right)}_{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{v}=\underbrace{\sum_{n}J_{n,\mathbf{x}}^{\top}v_{n}}_{\mathbf{b}}.$ (5)

3.2.1

We implement the motion field $\mathcal{M}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$ as a regular voxel grid with fixed voxel size and store motion at voxel centers $\mathbf{c}\in C$ .

To enable querying for motion $\mathbf{v}$ at an arbitrary scene point $\mathbf{x}$ , we apply trilinear interpolation of the neighboring voxel centers of $\mathbf{x}$ .

The trilinear interpolation weights $w^{\text{tri}}$ define the motion contribution of each involved $\mathbf{c}$ , based on distance of $\mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ .

Every query for an $\mathbf{x}$ outside the bounding box of the grid results in $\mathbf{v}=\vec{0}$ .

The bounding box is initialized by the dimensions of the point cloud containing all reprojected dynamic pixels.

For fusion, we apply the concepts of multi-view reprojection and accumulate $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ (), per voxel over all views and solve for $\mathbf{v}$ afterward.

We leverage GPU-accelerated linear algebra to efficiently solve the Gauss–Newton system in parallel across voxels.

After fusion, $\mathcal{M}$ is converted into a sparse voxel grid, for memory efficient storage on disk.

Note that fusion is only performed once, since we use $\mathcal{M}$ as a static velocity field for all animation frames similar to Holynski et al. .

Eq.5

[]

HCSS21

In a first pass through the input data we approximate $\mathbf{v}$ at $\mathbf{c}\in C$ for all voxels based on $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{n}$ of the projected views $n$ .

Pixels within dynamic regions $x\in\mathcal{S}_{n}$ are reprojected with $\mathbf{x}=\pi^{-1}_{n}(x,\,\mathcal{D}_{n}(x))$ , and grouped to the corresponding voxels.

Grouping uses either hard indexing within the voxel bounds (each pixel has weight $1$ ) or trilinear splatting to neighboring voxels (weight $w^{\text{tri}}$ ).

Per view and voxel, the weighted flow values are averaged to obtain $v_{n}$ , and $w_{n}$ denotes the sum of weights.

With the Jacobian $J_{n,\,\mathbf{c}}$ evaluated at the voxel center, $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{c}}$ and $\mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{c}}$ are accumulated over all views, each view contributing once per voxel.

After accumulating all views, the per-voxel 3×3 linear systems $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{c}}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{c}}$ are solved and motion is stored such that $\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{v}$ .

For refinement, we also accumulate dynamic pixel hits $w^{\text{dyn}}_{\mathbf{c}}=\sum_{n}w_{n}$ and view hits $w^{\text{view}}_{\mathbf{c}}$ , i.e., how many views contributed motion to a voxel.

3.2.2

Wrong depth information from misplaced Gaussians causing wrong pixel reprojection, or voxels intersecting the boundary of static and dynamic regions, can lead to motion within static regions.

To this end, we refine $\mathcal{M}$ by deleting these incorrect voxels by performing a second pass through the input data.

Pixels outside the masked region $\mathcal{S}_{n}(x)=0$ are projected and grouped by voxels as before, but rather than performing reprojection, now only static hits are tracked as $w^{\text{stat}}_{\mathbf{c}}$ weighted by $w^{\text{tri}}$ if necessary.

Intuitively, a voxel observed more often as static than as dynamic most likely lies in a static region, and its motion is reduced accordingly:

$\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{c})=\left(1-\operatorname{min}\left(1,\,\frac{w^{\text{stat}}_{\mathbf{c}}}{w^{\text{dyn}}_{\mathbf{c}}}\right)\right)\cdot\mathbf{v}\,.$ (6)

We also find that the multi-view reprojection problem becomes ill-posed when there are limited observations, especially if the associated viewing directions are mostly collinear.

In practice, we therefore assume that a number of observations below a threshold is insufficient to reconstruct a plausible $\mathbf{v}$ .

Consequently, we set the motion of voxels with view hits $w^{\text{view}}_{\mathbf{c}}$ below this threshold $r^{\text{view}}$ to zero, further reducing the size of $\mathcal{M}$ .

We show pseudocode for our 3D motion field fusion approach and refinement techniques in .

AppendixB

3.3

We treat 3D Gaussians as Lagrangian particles that undergo deformation within Eulerian grids.

The majority of Gaussians reside in static scene regions and will therefore not be deformed by $\mathcal{M}$ .

This enables us to efficiently segment the scene into static $\mathcal{G}^{\text{stat}}=\mathcal{G}\setminus\mathcal{G}^{\text{dyn}}$ and dynamic Gaussians $\mathcal{G}^{\text{dyn}}=\{g\in\mathcal{G}\mid\lVert\mathcal{M}(\mu)\rVert_{2}>0\}$ by querying motion at their means.

3.3.1

To achieve volume-aware transformation of 3D Gaussians, we iteratively apply with velocities queried from $\mathcal{M}$ to transform mean and covariance of each $g\in\mathcal{G}^{\text{dyn}}$ .

The volume of a 3D Gaussian is approximated by seven sigma points:Unscented Transform[]

JU97

$\sigma_{i}(\mu,\Sigma)=\begin{cases}\mu&i=0\\

\mu+(-1)^{i}\sqrt{(3+\lambda)}\sqrt{\Sigma}_{\lceil{i/2}\rceil}&i=1,\dots,6\end{cases}\,,$ (7)

with $\sqrt{\Sigma}_{i}$ being the $i$ -th column of the Cholesky-decomposed covariance and $\lambda\!=\!3\alpha^{2}\!-\!3$ and $\alpha$ a parameter to control the spread around $\mu$ .

The sigma points have corresponding weights for mean and covariance defined as

$\displaystyle w^{\mu}_{i}=\begin{cases}\frac{\lambda}{3+\lambda}&i=0\\

\frac{1}{2(3+\lambda)}&i=1,\dots,6\end{cases},\;w^{\Sigma}_{i}=w^{\mu}_{i}+\begin{cases}3-\alpha^{2}&i=0\\

0&i=1,\dots,6\end{cases}.$ (8)

The Unscented Transform can be applied iteratively via Euler integration to acquire updated mean $\mu_{k+1}$ and covariance $\Sigma_{k+1}$ for any Gaussian $g$ and iteration $k$ .

The sigma points are displaced by the motion queried from $\mathcal{M}$ as

$\tilde{\sigma}_{i}=\sigma_{i}(\mu_{k},\Sigma_{k})+r^{\mathcal{M}}\mathcal{M}\left(\sigma_{i}(\mu_{k},\Sigma_{k})\right)\,.$ (9)

The recursion is initialized with the original Gaussian parameters $\mu_{0}=\mu,\,\Sigma_{0}=\Sigma$ .

We also apply a regulation factor $r^{\mathcal{M}}$ to manually control the motion extent in cases where $\mathcal{M}$ does not contain physically meaningful velocities.

The displaced sigma points $\tilde{\sigma}_{i}$ are used to update mean and covariance as

$\mu_{k+1}=\sum^{6}_{i=0}w^{\mu}_{i}\tilde{\sigma}_{i}\;,\quad\Sigma_{k+1}=\sum^{6}_{i=0}w^{\Sigma}_{i}\left(\tilde{\sigma}_{i}-\mu_{k+1}\right)\left(\tilde{\sigma}_{i}-\mu_{k+1}\right)^{\top}.$ (10)

3.3.2

Naturally, $\mathcal{M}$ contains motion sources, i.e., regions from which particles move away without new particles moving in, such as the top of a waterfall.

For a looping animation, we extend the symmetric warping technique of Holynski et al.  to 3D Gaussians by applying forward and backward transformations.

Each $g\in\mathcal{G}^{\text{dyn}}$ is forward transformed through $K$ iterations of into a keyframe-sequence $\mathcal{A}^{\text{fw}}=\big((\mu_{k},\Sigma_{k})\big)^{K}_{k=0}$ .

Analogously, a backward keyframe-sequence $\mathcal{A}^{\text{bw}}=\big((\mu_{K-k},\Sigma_{K-k})\big)^{K}_{k=0}$ is calculated using the negated motion field $-\mathcal{M}$ .

Although mean and covariance are calculated by forward propagating the transformation update from $0\rightarrow K$ , the order of keyframes in $\mathcal{A}^{\text{bw}}$ is reversed, such that $\mathcal{A}^{\text{fw}}_{0}=\mathcal{A}^{\text{bw}}_{K}$ .

Due to $-\mathcal{M}$ , $g$ moves backward within the motion field, which is reversed into forward flow direction.

Phenomenologically, this means motion sources from $\mathcal{A}^{\text{fw}}$ act as motion drains for $\mathcal{A}^{\text{bw}}$ .

Note that a general inverse motion field $\mathcal{M}^{-1}$ is not available but $-\mathcal{M}$ offers a reasonable approximation and ensures the required symmetry .

AppendixD

Opacity Blending.

While $\mathcal{A}^{\text{fw}}$ and $\mathcal{A}^{\text{bw}}$ internally offer a smooth animation, looping both will result in a visible cut when Gaussians snap back to their initial state at the end of the sequence.

Furthermore, two instances of each dynamic Gaussian double the local scene density.

To mitigate these effects, we multiply opacity $o$ of each $g\in\mathcal{G}^{\text{dyn}}$ by $w_{k}^{o}=\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\pi k}{2K}\right)$ .

Opacity for the forward and backward sequence is defined as $\mathcal{O}^{\text{fw}}=\big((1-w_{k}^{o})o\big)^{K}_{k=0}$ and $\mathcal{O}^{\text{bw}}=\big(w_{k}^{o}o\big)^{K}_{k=0}$ .

As $\mathcal{O}^{\text{fw}}$ decreases from $o$ to $0$ and $\mathcal{O}^{\text{bw}}$ increases from $0$ to $o$ , the backward instance fades in while the forward instance fades out.

This results in Gaussians being most visible in their original state while becoming less visible as they diverge due to applied transformations.

Note that $\mathcal{O}^{\text{fw}}_{k}+\mathcal{O}^{\text{bw}}_{k}=o$ for all $k$ ensures consistent local scene density and $\mathcal{O}^{\text{fw}}_{K}=\mathcal{O}^{\text{bw}}_{0}=0$ in combination with $\mathcal{A}^{\text{fw}}_{0}=\mathcal{A}^{\text{bw}}_{K}$ ensures a seamless transition between looping sequences (cf. ).

AppendixD

Randomized Animation States.

Loops can still be perceivable due to large repeating patterns, which 2D cinemagraphy mitigates by warping deep features and inpainting.

For 3D Gaussians, we instead randomly offset the global animation state $t\in[0,1)$ of each $g$ by an individual offset $t^{\text{off}}\in[0,1)$ .

The offset differs between Gaussians, but corresponding forward and backward instances are offset by the same $t^{\text{off}}$ to maintain the symmetric transformation of each individual $g$ .

Note that the looping dynamic is not disrupted; only the starting point of each $g$ along its transformation trajectory is shifted.

It may be infeasible to completely disrupt patterns in specific fluid regions, so a maximum allowed random offset can be used to restrict $t^{\text{off}}$ .

3.3.3

We implement our CUDA renderer on top of an optimized 3DGS implementation .

Our symmetric animation technique requires rendering multiple instances of each $g\in\mathcal{G}^{\text{dyn}}$ , each transformed by the keyframe of its own animation state.

For VRAM efficiency, these instances are virtual, i.e., share all animation-independent parameter buffers.

With the local animation state $\tau=(t+t^{\text{off}})\bmod 1$ , the keyframe of a virtual Gaussian instance is $k=\lfloor\tau K\rfloor$ .

For smoother animation, means, covariances, and opacities of neighboring keyframes can be linearly interpolated with weight $\tau K-k$ .

While linearly interpolating covariances is not exact with respect to rotation, the covariance difference between keyframes is typically small.

Consequently, it is a visually smooth and efficient alternative to proper rotation interpolation.[]

We evaluate our method and compare it to recent approaches with similar goals in a series of experiments.

We conduct all experiments on the same system using an RTX 4090 GPU.

Quantitatively evaluating synthesized fluid motion is inherently difficult: casually captured scenes provide no ground-truth motion, and static 3DGS represents moving water as a temporally averaged, blurred region whose high-frequency detail no method operating on a static reconstruction can recover without hallucination.

As our goal is visual plausibility rather than physical accuracy, and no suitable no-reference metrics for fluid motion exist, we assess motion quality qualitatively, primarily through our video, and evaluate efficiency quantitatively.

3D-Cinemagraphy produces visually compelling animations for viewpoints close to the input image, as it largely relies on high-detail 2D cinemagraph synthesis.

However, as the viewpoint deviates further from the reference pose, limitations of the underlying layered depth image representation become increasingly apparent, leading to geometric inconsistencies, animation artifacts, and missing content not observed in the reference view.

In contrast, Gaussian splatting-based approaches maintain viewpoint-consistent scene geometry, making visual quality primarily dependent on the reconstruction and animation of fluid regions.

Under casual capture conditions, 4DGS struggles to reconstruct high-frequency water dynamics, resulting in unstable and visually implausible motion.

As 4DGS models the entire scene as dynamic, it also fails to converge to the static solution in some regions (e.g., the darker rocks in ).

LoopGaussian preserves a temporally stable appearance, but its motion does not follow coherent fluid flow and instead exhibits locally inconsistent warping behavior (best seen in our video).

To further analyze this effect, visualizes the time-dependent motion of individual Gaussians by encoding projected motion direction as color.

LoopGaussian produces motion that varies both spatially and temporally within similar fluid regions, leading to incoherent flow patterns.

This behavior stems from its symmetric interpolation scheme, which blends forward- and backward-transformed Gaussian positions instead of rendering them separately.

In contrast, our method generates temporally consistent directional motion that more closely resembles plausible fluid flow.

Our video further compares our animation side by side with the drone-captured footage used for reconstructing the 3DGS model of the “Weir” scene.

Our method demonstrates that visually plausible fluid animation can be efficiently integrated into static 3DGS scenes without requiring a fully dynamic reconstruction.

While we primarily focus on water, the proposed approach also generalizes to other fluids such as lava ().

Fig.8

Our method generalizes to fluids other than water, such as lava. We show the animation from a novel camera trajectory in our video.

Figure 8:

Since the 3D motion field is precomputed only once and stored compactly, it could be distributed alongside static 3DGS scenes and rendered efficiently even on resource-constrained devices.

Furthermore, the optical flow estimation process is flexible with respect to the input views.

The RGB inputs $\mathcal{I}_{1,\cdots,N}$ may consist of original training images, renderings from user-defined viewpoints, or a combination of both, enabling targeted refinement of motion in challenging scene regions through our interactive GUI.

Despite these advantages, our approach is not without limitations.

First, the quality of the generated motion field strongly depends on the underlying 3DGS reconstruction.

Depth inconsistencies or reconstruction artifacts can lead to inaccurate motion fusion and visible animation artifacts ().

Fig.9

Failure case on “Weir”: inaccurate Gaussian geometry (depth, left) and a poorly reconstructed water surface (middle) lead to wrongly reprojected flow and thus an inaccurate motion field, visible as animation artifacts (right).

Figure 9:

Similarly, the method assumes that the fluid surface itself is reconstructed reasonably well.

This assumption may fail for highly reflective or visually ambiguous water surfaces, where the 3DGS reconstruction does not create enough Gaussians.

Our method also cannot recover fluid detail that is absent from the reconstructed 3DGS representation and, as depth stems from Gaussians at the visible water surface, motion is largely confined to this surface.

Future work could explore dynamic updates of the motion field to enable interactive or physically responsive fluid behavior.

This could allow animated fluids to react to user interaction or external scene events while maintaining real-time performance.

6

We presented a method for animating water in static 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes using cinemagraph-inspired motion synthesis.

Our approach lifts 2D fluid motion into a coherent 3D Eulerian motion field and applies it to Gaussian primitives to generate seamless looping animations that preserve real-time rendering and free-viewpoint navigation.

In contrast to dynamic reconstruction approaches, our method operates on casually captured static scenes and does not require dynamic multi-view acquisition or costly physical simulation.

Experiments on a newly captured dataset show more plausible water motion than prior methods at low computational cost.

We believe that combining static scene reconstruction with efficient motion synthesis opens promising directions for immersive, controllable, and realistic 3D content creation.

Appendix A

Following Mahapatra and Kulkarni , we derive dense flow maps $\mathcal{F}^{\textit{dense}}_{1,\cdots,N}$ from sparse flow maps $\mathcal{F}^{\textit{sparse}}_{1,\cdots,N}$ by spreading their sparse flow with weighted exponential pixel-distance functions defined as[]

MK22

$D(p_{1},\,p_{2})=e^{-\frac{\lVert p_{1}-p_{2}\rVert_{2}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}}\,.$ (11)

Here the L2 Euclidean distance is used in conjunction with a constant $\sigma=0.075H$ .

For each pixel $x$ , sparse flow $\mathcal{F}^{\textit{sparse}}_{n}(p)$ is weighted by $D(x,\,p)$ based on hint position $p$ .

Pixel values are summed up for all sparse hints and normalized to define dense flow maps:

$\mathcal{F}^{\textit{dense}}_{n}(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{H}_{n}|}D(x,\,p_{i})\cdot\mathcal{F}^{\textit{sparse}}_{n}(p_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{H}_{n}|}D(x,\,p_{i})},&\text{if }x\in\mathcal{S}_{n}\\

0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\,,$ (12)

with $p_{i}$ the $i$ -th hint position in $\mathcal{H}_{n}$ .

Note that dense flow is only defined for pixels within the segmentation mask of the view $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ .

item.title: 3DGS 实时场景重建综述：方法、系统与权衡 ｜ Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Scene Reconstruction: Methods, Systems, and Trade-offs
item.description:
一句话：把「只渲染」和「还要建图、更新、跟踪」两条成本线分开算，是选型时最容易被忽略的一点。

要点：

  • 把 GS 场景重建分成五个互相重叠的家族：单次生成、动态表示、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸式系统、GS SLAM
  • 明确区分仅渲染的吞吐与任务相关的构建、更新、跟踪、建图与优化成本——两者经常被混为一谈
  • 把受控的稀疏视角基准与各方法原生评测结合起来横向比较，并串成一条端到端管线

为什么值得看：选 3DGS 方案时只看单帧 FPS 会踩坑；这份综述给出的是按任务拆成本的对账方式。

中文摘要：3DGS 从 2023 年出现以来，凭借显式、高度可配置的场景表示，被迅速扩展到稀疏视角生成、动态重建、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸式系统以及 SLAM 等方向。这篇综述做的是把文献分类并串成端到端管线：把 GS 场景重建划分为五个互相重叠的家族——单次生成、动态表示、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸式系统、GS SLAM。作者特别强调一个常被混淆的区别：GS 可以提供实时渲染，但「渲染一个已有表示」与「构建、更新、维护场景本身」是两件成本结构完全不同的事，因此他们把仅渲染的吞吐与任务相关的生成、更新、跟踪、建图、优化成本分别度量。方法上，他们结合受控的稀疏视角基准与各方法的原生评测来做横向对比，给出面向实际部署的权衡清单。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2610.17513v1 [cs.CV] 13 Oct 2026

Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Scene Reconstruction: Methods, Systems, and Trade-offs

Ashim Dahal

Rabab Abdelfattah

Nick Rahimi

School of Computing and Computer Engineering, University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS, 39401, USA

Affiliation:

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis.

In this survey, we synthesize current literature, categorize them and provide a connection of current approaches and tools towards an end-to-end pipeline.

Since its inception in 2023, its explicit and highly configurable scene representation has been extended toward sparse-view generation, dynamic reconstruction, efficiency and compression, streaming, and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM).

Although Gaussian Splatting can provide real-time rendering, rendering an existing representation is distinct from constructing, updating, or maintaining the scene itself.

Explicitly, we categorize GS scene reconstruction into five overlapping families: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM.

We distinguish render-only throughput from task-specific scene generation, update, tracking, mapping, and optimization costs, and combine controlled sparse-view benchmarking with native evaluations to identify cross-family quality, latency, memory, and update-cost trade-offs.

Gaussian Splatting , 3D Scene Representation , Novel View Synthesis , Neural Rendering , Multi-View Geometry

Keywords:

1

Kerbl et al.  introduced 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) as an explicit scene representation capable of high-quality interactive novel-view rendering. Subsequent work rapidly extended this formulation beyond static per-scene reconstruction. Deformable 3DGS  and 4DGaussians  introduced temporal deformation and spatiotemporal representations, while later methods explored feed-forward sparse-view generation , efficiency and compression, streaming, and Gaussian-based SLAM. These developments increasingly shift the systems bottleneck from rendering an existing representation toward constructing, updating, transmitting, or maintaining the Gaussian scene.

This distinction is important for applications such as free-viewpoint video, immersive media, online mapping, and robotics. In these settings, interactive rendering alone is insufficient when scene construction, temporal updates, or map maintenance remain substantially slower than rasterization.

Several surveys have reviewed 3DGS from broader perspectives. Wu et al.  organize the field by 3D reconstruction, editing, and downstream applications; Fei et al.  use taxonomies based on characteristics and applications; and Bao et al.  examine optimization, applications, extensions, and recurring technical modules. More focused surveys address compression and compaction  and robotics . As summarized in Table , our focus is different: we organize Gaussian Splatting as a reconstruction pipeline and study which task-specific costs limit real-time deployment.

Section2.7

We formulate real-time Gaussian scene reconstruction from the pipeline perspective illustrated in . We organize the literature into five overlapping families according to the stage containing the dominant contribution: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. This pipeline-centric view exposes where geometry, pose estimation, temporal updates, memory, and rendering costs arise across otherwise different GS systems.

Figure1

: Figure 1Overview of a Gaussian Splatting–based reconstruction pipeline. Starting from images/video (optionally RGB-D/events), the system forms pose/geometry cues, initializes Gaussians (one-shot or MVS lifting), updates/optimizes the scene representation (per-scene, online, or temporal), and rasterizes/composites to produce renders, maps, and poses. Shaded containers indicate where the five taxonomy families primarily intervene (single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency/compression, streaming/immersive video, and SLAM with tracking–mapping).

We summarize the scope, organization, and contributions of this survey as follows:

Under this scope, the primary object is a (centers, covariances, opacities, and appearance parameters), and the key efficiency advantage comes from rasterizing a finite set of primitives rather than volumetric ray marching.

Unless stated otherwise, each primitive is represented by $(\mu_{j},\Sigma_{j},\alpha_{j},\mathbf{c}_{j})$ , where $\mathbf{c}_{j}$ may be RGB, spherical harmonics coefficients, or learned features depending on the method.

Table2

2.3

Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as $\mathcal{G}=\{g_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , a set of $N$ anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives in world coordinates. Each $g_{j}$ is defined by a mean $\mu_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , covariance $\Sigma_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ (commonly parameterized via rotation and per-axis scales for stability), opacity $\alpha_{j}\in[0,1]$ , and appearance parameters $\mathbf{c}_{j}$ . This explicit primitive-based representation enables high-throughput rasterization pipelines compared to radiance-field rendering .[]

19

Methods primarily differ in (i) which parameters are optimized vs. predicted, and (ii) how time is modeled. Static pipelines often optimize all parameters per scene with SfM/MVS/depth-based initialization; dynamic extensions introduce time dependence via explicit per-frame parameters, deformation models, or static/dynamic partitions. Online/SLAM-style systems additionally constrain updates to bounded latency and control representation growth via pruning, keyframes, and local refinement.

Representation complexity and real-time knobs

Runtime and memory are dominated by the number of primitives $N$ and the appearance bandwidth (e.g., SH degree or feature dimensionality). Dynamic/streaming settings add growth over time, so many systems explicitly regulate $N$ and appearance parameters to meet real-time targets.

Representation vs. serialization (file formats)

Gaussian scenes may be stored in different encodings (e.g., PLY-like formats or -style binaries). These typically change serialization/layout and attribute encoding (e.g., quantization, SH/features) rather than the underlying representation $\{(\mu_{j},\Sigma_{j},\alpha_{j},\mathbf{c}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N}$ ..splat

2.4

Given camera intrinsics $K$ and pose $T=(R,t)$ , each mean $\mu_{j}$ projects to

$\hat{\mu}_{j}=\pi\!\big(K,T;\mu_{j}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{2},$ (1)

and its 3D covariance $\Sigma_{j}$ induces an elliptical screen-space footprint (2D covariance) $\Sigma^{2D}_{j}$ . Rendering composites projected splats in approximate front-to-back order using alpha/transmittance blending . Modern implementations use GPU tiled rasterization and sorting so only splats overlapping a pixel/tile are processed, which is central to real-time performance . Approximate visibility/sorting can cause artifacts in dense or dynamic regions , motivating improved compositing and hardware/system optimizations .[]

2.7

The term real-time is used differently across Gaussian Splatting methods. Rendering, scene generation, streaming updates, and SLAM correspond to different tasks and should therefore not share a single throughput definition. We use approximately 24 FPS only as a reference for interactive playback, not as a universal threshold for reconstruction or scene updates.

Let all latency values be expressed in milliseconds. Render-only throughput is defined as

$\mathrm{rFPS}=\frac{1000}{t_{\mathrm{render}}},$ (2)

$t_{\mathrm{render}}$ where is the time required to render one frame from an existing Gaussian representation. For a reconstruction or update task, the pipeline latency can be written as

$t_{\mathrm{pipe}}=t_{\mathrm{pre}}+t_{\mathrm{pose}}+t_{\mathrm{depth/fusion}}+t_{\mathrm{init}}+t_{\mathrm{update}}+t_{\mathrm{render}},$ (3)

where only stages relevant to the evaluated task are included. The corresponding task throughput is

$R_{\mathcal{T}}=\frac{1000}{t_{\mathcal{T}}}.$ (4)

Accordingly, we report scene throughput for feed-forward reconstruction, update throughput for dynamic and streaming methods, and tracking or mapping throughput for SLAM systems. Offline optimization is reported using training or optimization time rather than scenes per second. These quantities are compared only when the task, unit of work, and timing boundary are aligned.

We prioritize recent work (2023–2025) while retaining foundational baselines needed for context (datasets, metrics, and core dynamic/NVS references).

We include methods whose is an explicit Gaussian-based model (or a direct extension) and that materially affect one or more stages of a GS reconstruction pipeline (initialization/generation, temporal modeling, map maintenance, streaming/delivery, compositing, or tracking-and-mapping).

We exclude NeRF-style methods as a primary focus, citing them only when necessary for context or when they explicitly bridge into Gaussian representations.

Literature was identified primarily through Google Scholar and the proceedings of CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, NeurIPS, and ICLR.

Seed queries included , , , , , and , together with closely related variants for dynamic reconstruction, streaming, compression, pose-free reconstruction, and real-time reconstruction.

We organize Gaussian Splatting work for real-time reconstruction into five pipeline-centric families, defined by the

primary stage a method intervenes in (capture/training, representation, rendering, system delivery, or online estimation).

Because many methods are multi-faceted, we allow secondary overlaps but assign each paper a single family

based on its dominant technical contribution.primary

Figure  shows the chronological development of representative methods across these families, illustrating how work following 3DGS progressively expanded toward amortized generation, temporal modeling, efficiency, streaming, and online mapping.

3

Single-shot / amortized Gaussian generation

Feed-forward construction of a usable Gaussian scene from one or few images, often using depth/MVS priors or learned

regularizers, optionally followed by brief refinement. Poses may be known, refined, or pose-free, but the defining feature

is replacing heavy per-scene iterative fitting with amortized inference from limited views.

Dynamic representations beyond 4DGS

Methods that treat time as a first-class variable in the scene model (e.g., time-conditioned parameters, deformation/warp

fields, key-time primitives, canonical-plus-delta factorization) or explicitly mitigate dynamic failure modes such as

ghosting, identity swaps, occlusion/disocclusion artifacts, and temporal flicker. The emphasis is temporal

change, not merely delivering or replaying content over time.modeling

Efficiency and compression

Works whose central goal is reducing compute, memory, or storage/bandwidth while preserving real-time operation, via levers

such as pruning/sparsification, quantization/packing, view-adaptive LoD selection, or system/hardware acceleration. We place

a method here when efficiency is the primary objective rather than a side effect.

Streaming and immersive video systems

Long-duration capture and interactive free-viewpoint playback under latency/bandwidth constraints, enabled by explicit

delivery mechanisms (progressive transmission, caching/tiling/segmenting, rate control, bandwidth-aware loading, or

continual update protocols). The core contribution is , not new temporal

scene parameterizations.system delivery and interactivity over time

SLAM with Gaussian Splatting

Online tracking-and-mapping where camera poses are estimated incrementally and the Gaussian map is updated under bounded

latency/compute, typically using keyframes, map maintenance/pruning, robustness to blur/occlusions, and (when relevant)

loop-consistency considerations. We place a method here when meeting tracking deadlines and maintaining a bounded-cost map

are central to the design.

MotionGS  modifies this formulation by adding explicit motion

supervision to the deformation field. Optical flow is decomposed as[]

79

$F^{M}_{t\rightarrow t+1}=F_{t\rightarrow t+1}-F^{C}_{t\rightarrow t+1},$ (12)

photometric reconstruction to explicitly matching projected Gaussian motion.

This supervision couples deformation accuracy to rendered depth and camera

pose: errors in either term perturb $F^{C}$ and therefore $F^{M}$ . In our

native DyNeRF run, the documented 20k schedule exhausted

an 80 GB A100 at iteration 7,600 (), showing that the

complete motion-guided pipeline can become memory-bound before convergence.

Streaming methods replace full per-frame reconstruction with a state transition

$\mathcal{G}_{t}=\mathcal{U}_{\theta}\!\left(\mathcal{G}_{t-1},I_{t}\right),$ (17)

where a compact Neural Transformation Cache predicts Gaussian translation and

Thus, IGS emphasizes learned motion transfer with periodic correction, whereas

WildGS-SLAM  addresses a different failure mode by making

the residual itself uncertainty-aware. Its mapping objective effectively weights

photometric and geometric errors as[]

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{map}}=\sum_{\mathbf{u}}\frac{\lambda_{I}\mathcal{L}_{I}(\mathbf{u})+\lambda_{D}\mathcal{L}_{D}(\mathbf{u})}{\beta(\mathbf{u})^{2}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{iso}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{iso}},$ (24)

where larger uncertainty $\beta(\mathbf{u})$ suppresses observations likely to arise

These differences lead to distinct deployment regimes. Feed-forward

single-shot methods are the strongest fit for rapid initialization and

interactive preview because they minimize scene-construction latency, although

the controlled results show a direct quality–latency–memory trade-off.

Per-sequence dynamic methods are better suited when temporal reconstruction

quality is more important than initialization time, since interactive rendering

can be achieved after a substantially heavier optimization stage. Compression

and LoD methods are most useful when storage, bandwidth, or rendering load is

the limiting resource. Streaming methods directly target temporal scene

delivery, but the measured update rates show that interactive playback and

real-time scene refresh remain different system requirements. Finally, Gaussian

SLAM is the natural family for robotics and online mapping because pose

estimation and scene reconstruction are coupled, but the wrapped rates in

show that joint tracking–mapping latency remains the

principal obstacle to video-rate operation. Thus, “real-time” Gaussian

Splatting is not a single operating point: the appropriate method depends on

whether the application must optimize reconstruction latency, temporal update

latency, map maintenance, memory/bandwidth, or render-only throughput.

This survey reviewed Gaussian Splatting (GS) for real-time scene reconstruction. Rather than only listing methods, we organized prior work into a pipeline-centric taxonomy and highlighted the trade-offs that determine whether a method is merely or deployable end-to-end.real-time in a submodule

The main strength of this work is its . We connect design choices (e.g., temporal parameterization vs. stability, pruning/quantization/LoD vs. fidelity, and rasterization choices vs. artifacts) to system-level outcomes such as latency, memory growth, robustness to pose/depth noise, and long-horizon stability. Strengths and value to the field.synthesis across components

The taxonomy, comparison framework, and failure-mode analysis help researchers position new contributions and practitioners reason about capture-to-render pipelines.

Our taxonomy necessarily simplifies a fast-moving hybrid space, where many systems combine amortized initialization with refinement or mix static and dynamic representations. Comparability is also limited: papers report speed and memory at different stages (e.g., per-image FPS vs. per-scene throughput), under different input-window sizes and hardware assumptions. Thus, end-to-end conclusions about “real-time” readiness should be read as pipeline-aware guidance rather than a standardized benchmark ranking.Weaknesses and limitations.

Future work.

The main remaining directions are task-specific standardized evaluation, deployment-aware scene generation, sparse-by-construction representations, long-horizon dynamic and streaming maintenance, and robust Gaussian SLAM. Together, these problems shift the focus from fast rasterization toward maintaining quality, bounded latency, and manageable state throughout the reconstruction pipeline.

为什么值得看：选 3DGS 方案时只看单帧 FPS 会踩坑；这份综述给出的是按任务拆成本的对账方式。

中文摘要：3DGS 从 2023 年出现以来，凭借显式、高度可配置的场景表示，被迅速扩展到稀疏视角生成、动态重建、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸式系统以及 SLAM 等方向。这篇综述做的是把文献分类并串成端到端管线：把 GS 场景重建划分为五个互相重叠的家族——单次生成、动态表示、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸式系统、GS SLAM。作者特别强调一个常被混淆的区别：GS 可以提供实时渲染，但「渲染一个已有表示」与「构建、更新、维护场景本身」是两件成本结构完全不同的事，因此他们把仅渲染的吞吐与任务相关的生成、更新、跟踪、建图、优化成本分别度量。方法上，他们结合受控的稀疏视角基准与各方法的原生评测来做横向对比，给出面向实际部署的权衡清单。

Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Scene Reconstruction: Methods, Systems, and Trade-offs

Ashim Dahal

Rabab Abdelfattah

Nick Rahimi

School of Computing and Computer Engineering, University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS, 39401, USA

Affiliation:

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis.

In this survey, we synthesize current literature, categorize them and provide a connection of current approaches and tools towards an end-to-end pipeline.

Since its inception in 2023, its explicit and highly configurable scene representation has been extended toward sparse-view generation, dynamic reconstruction, efficiency and compression, streaming, and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM).

Although Gaussian Splatting can provide real-time rendering, rendering an existing representation is distinct from constructing, updating, or maintaining the scene itself.

Explicitly, we categorize GS scene reconstruction into five overlapping families: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM.

We distinguish render-only throughput from task-specific scene generation, update, tracking, mapping, and optimization costs, and combine controlled sparse-view benchmarking with native evaluations to identify cross-family quality, latency, memory, and update-cost trade-offs.

Gaussian Splatting , 3D Scene Representation , Novel View Synthesis , Neural Rendering , Multi-View Geometry

Keywords:

1

Kerbl et al.  introduced 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) as an explicit scene representation capable of high-quality interactive novel-view rendering. Subsequent work rapidly extended this formulation beyond static per-scene reconstruction. Deformable 3DGS  and 4DGaussians  introduced temporal deformation and spatiotemporal representations, while later methods explored feed-forward sparse-view generation , efficiency and compression, streaming, and Gaussian-based SLAM. These developments increasingly shift the systems bottleneck from rendering an existing representation toward constructing, updating, transmitting, or maintaining the Gaussian scene.

This distinction is important for applications such as free-viewpoint video, immersive media, online mapping, and robotics. In these settings, interactive rendering alone is insufficient when scene construction, temporal updates, or map maintenance remain substantially slower than rasterization.

Several surveys have reviewed 3DGS from broader perspectives. Wu et al.  organize the field by 3D reconstruction, editing, and downstream applications; Fei et al.  use taxonomies based on characteristics and applications; and Bao et al.  examine optimization, applications, extensions, and recurring technical modules. More focused surveys address compression and compaction  and robotics . As summarized in Table , our focus is different: we organize Gaussian Splatting as a reconstruction pipeline and study which task-specific costs limit real-time deployment.

We formulate real-time Gaussian scene reconstruction from the pipeline perspective illustrated in . We organize the literature into five overlapping families according to the stage containing the dominant contribution: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. This pipeline-centric view exposes where geometry, pose estimation, temporal updates, memory, and rendering costs arise across otherwise different GS systems.

2.3

Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as $\mathcal{G}=\{g_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , a set of $N$ anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives in world coordinates. Each $g_{j}$ is defined by a mean $\mu_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , covariance $\Sigma_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ (commonly parameterized via rotation and per-axis scales for stability), opacity $\alpha_{j}\in[0,1]$ , and appearance parameters $\mathbf{c}_{j}$ . This explicit primitive-based representation enables high-throughput rasterization pipelines compared to radiance-field rendering .[]

19

Methods primarily differ in (i) which parameters are optimized vs. predicted, and (ii) how time is modeled. Static pipelines often optimize all parameters per scene with SfM/MVS/depth-based initialization; dynamic extensions introduce time dependence via explicit per-frame parameters, deformation models, or static/dynamic partitions. Online/SLAM-style systems additionally constrain updates to bounded latency and control representation growth via pruning, keyframes, and local refinement.

Representation complexity and real-time knobs

Runtime and memory are dominated by the number of primitives $N$ and the appearance bandwidth (e.g., SH degree or feature dimensionality). Dynamic/streaming settings add growth over time, so many systems explicitly regulate $N$ and appearance parameters to meet real-time targets.

Representation vs. serialization (file formats)

Gaussian scenes may be stored in different encodings (e.g., PLY-like formats or -style binaries). These typically change serialization/layout and attribute encoding (e.g., quantization, SH/features) rather than the underlying representation $\{(\mu_{j},\Sigma_{j},\alpha_{j},\mathbf{c}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N}$ ..splat

2.4

Given camera intrinsics $K$ and pose $T=(R,t)$ , each mean $\mu_{j}$ projects to

$\hat{\mu}_{j}=\pi\!\big(K,T;\mu_{j}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{2},$ (1)

and its 3D covariance $\Sigma_{j}$ induces an elliptical screen-space footprint (2D covariance) $\Sigma^{2D}_{j}$ . Rendering composites projected splats in approximate front-to-back order using alpha/transmittance blending . Modern implementations use GPU tiled rasterization and sorting so only splats overlapping a pixel/tile are processed, which is central to real-time performance . Approximate visibility/sorting can cause artifacts in dense or dynamic regions , motivating improved compositing and hardware/system optimizations .[]

2.7

The term real-time is used differently across Gaussian Splatting methods. Rendering, scene generation, streaming updates, and SLAM correspond to different tasks and should therefore not share a single throughput definition. We use approximately 24 FPS only as a reference for interactive playback, not as a universal threshold for reconstruction or scene updates.

Let all latency values be expressed in milliseconds. Render-only throughput is defined as

$\mathrm{rFPS}=\frac{1000}{t_{\mathrm{render}}},$ (2)

$t_{\mathrm{render}}$ where is the time required to render one frame from an existing Gaussian representation. For a reconstruction or update task, the pipeline latency can be written as

$t_{\mathrm{pipe}}=t_{\mathrm{pre}}+t_{\mathrm{pose}}+t_{\mathrm{depth/fusion}}+t_{\mathrm{init}}+t_{\mathrm{update}}+t_{\mathrm{render}},$ (3)

where only stages relevant to the evaluated task are included. The corresponding task throughput is

$R_{\mathcal{T}}=\frac{1000}{t_{\mathcal{T}}}.$ (4)

Accordingly, we report scene throughput for feed-forward reconstruction, update throughput for dynamic and streaming methods, and tracking or mapping throughput for SLAM systems. Offline optimization is reported using training or optimization time rather than scenes per second. These quantities are compared only when the task, unit of work, and timing boundary are aligned.

We prioritize recent work (2023–2025) while retaining foundational baselines needed for context (datasets, metrics, and core dynamic/NVS references).

We include methods whose is an explicit Gaussian-based model (or a direct extension) and that materially affect one or more stages of a GS reconstruction pipeline (initialization/generation, temporal modeling, map maintenance, streaming/delivery, compositing, or tracking-and-mapping).

We exclude NeRF-style methods as a primary focus, citing them only when necessary for context or when they explicitly bridge into Gaussian representations.

Literature was identified primarily through Google Scholar and the proceedings of CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, NeurIPS, and ICLR.

Seed queries included , , , , , and , together with closely related variants for dynamic reconstruction, streaming, compression, pose-free reconstruction, and real-time reconstruction.

We organize Gaussian Splatting work for real-time reconstruction into five pipeline-centric families, defined by the

primary stage a method intervenes in (capture/training, representation, rendering, system delivery, or online estimation).

Because many methods are multi-faceted, we allow secondary overlaps but assign each paper a single family

Figure  shows the chronological development of representative methods across these families, illustrating how work following 3DGS progressively expanded toward amortized generation, temporal modeling, efficiency, streaming, and online mapping.

3

Single-shot / amortized Gaussian generation

Feed-forward construction of a usable Gaussian scene from one or few images, often using depth/MVS priors or learned

regularizers, optionally followed by brief refinement. Poses may be known, refined, or pose-free, but the defining feature

is replacing heavy per-scene iterative fitting with amortized inference from limited views.

Dynamic representations beyond 4DGS

Methods that treat time as a first-class variable in the scene model (e.g., time-conditioned parameters, deformation/warp

fields, key-time primitives, canonical-plus-delta factorization) or explicitly mitigate dynamic failure modes such as

ghosting, identity swaps, occlusion/disocclusion artifacts, and temporal flicker. The emphasis is temporal

change, not merely delivering or replaying content over time.modeling

Efficiency and compression

Works whose central goal is reducing compute, memory, or storage/bandwidth while preserving real-time operation, via levers

such as pruning/sparsification, quantization/packing, view-adaptive LoD selection, or system/hardware acceleration. We place

a method here when efficiency is the primary objective rather than a side effect.

Streaming and immersive video systems

Long-duration capture and interactive free-viewpoint playback under latency/bandwidth constraints, enabled by explicit

delivery mechanisms (progressive transmission, caching/tiling/segmenting, rate control, bandwidth-aware loading, or

continual update protocols). The core contribution is , not new temporal

scene parameterizations.system delivery and interactivity over time

SLAM with Gaussian Splatting

Online tracking-and-mapping where camera poses are estimated incrementally and the Gaussian map is updated under bounded

latency/compute, typically using keyframes, map maintenance/pruning, robustness to blur/occlusions, and (when relevant)

loop-consistency considerations. We place a method here when meeting tracking deadlines and maintaining a bounded-cost map

are central to the design.

whereas InstantSplat uses 16.01 s for initialization followed by 35.02 s of

optimization. Hence the former admits a construction throughput, while the

latter is an optimization problem whose runtime depends on the refinement

budget. In both cases, the much larger decoder-only rFPS reported in

remains a separate quantity from the cost of

constructing $\mathcal{G}$ .

Recent feed-forward generalists broaden this regime to unconstrained input views

and unified geometry-to-Gaussian prediction, as exemplified by AnySplat and

YoNoSplat . These systems relax capture

assumptions, but move additional latency and memory pressure into their learned

geometry backbones and cross-view fusion.

MotionGS  modifies this formulation by adding explicit motion

supervision to the deformation field. Optical flow is decomposed as[]

79

$F^{M}_{t\rightarrow t+1}=F_{t\rightarrow t+1}-F^{C}_{t\rightarrow t+1},$ (12)

where $F^{C}$ is the component induced by camera motion and $F^{M}$ isolates

object motion. The predicted 3D Gaussian deformation is projected into Gaussian

flow $F^{G}$ and constrained by

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}}=\left\|\operatorname{sg}(F^{M}_{t\rightarrow t+1})-F^{G}_{t\rightarrow t+1}\right\|_{1}.$ (13)

This changes the optimization problem from learning motion primarily through

photometric reconstruction to explicitly matching projected Gaussian motion.

This supervision couples deformation accuracy to rendered depth and camera

pose: errors in either term perturb $F^{C}$ and therefore $F^{M}$ . In our

native DyNeRF run, the documented 20k schedule exhausted

an 80 GB A100 at iteration 7,600 (), showing that the

complete motion-guided pipeline can become memory-bound before convergence.

Other important dynamic formulations place temporal structure more explicitly:

4D-RotorGS and Ex4DGS encode time directly in the primitive representation,

whereas SC-GS uses sparse control points to structure deformation and support

motion editing . These alternatives reduce reliance on

one unconstrained per-Gaussian warp, but introduce their own temporal-parameter

or control-structure costs.

For a Gaussian scene

$\mathcal{G}=\{g_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , efficiency is governed by more than the primitive

count $N$ . A useful conceptual decomposition is

$B(\mathcal{G})\approx Nb_{g},\qquad t_{\mathrm{render}}\propto c_{g}N_{\mathrm{vis}}+c_{o}M,$ (14)

where $b_{g}$ is the storage per Gaussian, $N_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is the number of

Gaussians processed for the current view, and $M$ denotes their accumulated

screen-space overlap. The methods in and

act on different terms of this model: pruning reduces $N$ , quantization reduces

$b_{g}$ , LoD reduces $N_{\mathrm{vis}}$ , and renderer-level optimization reduces

the computational constants $c_{g}$ and $c_{o}$ . Their reported “efficiency” gains

are therefore not interchangeable.

scalable compression and transmission,

For 3DGStream, PSNR values correspond to stage 1 and stage 2, respectively.

GIFStream is an offline optimization result and is therefore not assigned a transition-update rate.

Streaming methods replace full per-frame reconstruction with a state transition

$\mathcal{G}_{t}=\mathcal{U}_{\theta}\!\left(\mathcal{G}_{t-1},I_{t}\right),$ (17)

so practical throughput is governed by the cost of $\mathcal{U}_{\theta}$ rather

than rasterization alone. IGS  reduces this cost with an

anchor-driven motion network: multi-view motion evidence is lifted into 3D and

used to predict the motion of the existing Gaussians, while selected key frames

are refined to limit temporal error accumulation. 3DGStream

instead represents the transition approximately as[]

65

[]

51

$\mathcal{G}_{t}=\mathcal{T}_{t}(\mathcal{G}_{t-1})\cup\mathcal{A}_{t},$ (18)

where a compact Neural Transformation Cache predicts Gaussian translation and

rotation and $\mathcal{A}_{t}$ adds Gaussians for newly appearing content.

Thus, IGS emphasizes learned motion transfer with periodic correction, whereas

3DGStream performs explicit per-frame transformation and structural augmentation.

The measurements in show that this update operator,

not rendering, is the dominant systems bottleneck. IGS reaches 126.74 rFPS after

the representation is updated, but its measured transition rate is only

0.116 s because the native schedule includes 100 refinement iterations

with densification. 3DGStream is slower at 0.079 transitions/s under its

150-stage-1 + 100-stage-2 schedule; the second stage raises mean PSNR from

27.34 to 28.18 dB, showing a direct quality–update-cost trade-off inside the

streaming loop. Hence

table10

-1

$t_{\mathrm{stream}}\approx t_{\mathrm{motion}}+t_{\mathrm{refine}}+t_{\mathrm{structure}}\gg t_{\mathrm{render}},$ (19)

for the measured online systems. Render FPS therefore measures playback capacity,

not the rate at which a new dynamic state can be incorporated.

GIFStream  shifts the objective from rapid online state

transition toward compact transmission of a time-varying Gaussian representation. GIFStream couples reconstruction with compression-aware optimization,

which can be summarized as[]

26

$\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{photo}}+\lambda_{e}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{entropy}}+\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}},$ (20)

with

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{entropy}}\approx-\sum_{t}\log p_{\theta}\!\left(\bar{V}_{t}\mid\bar{V}_{(21)

It uses a canonical Gaussian space with a deformation field conditioned by

time-dependent feature streams and applies temporal and spatial compression. This explains why its result in

should not be converted into transition throughput:

the measured 2023.62 s corresponds to offline optimization of a two-frame GOP,

while the resulting representation still renders at 89.75 rFPS. Streaming

therefore spans two different system problems: minimizing online update latency

and minimizing transmitted temporal representation cost.

Rate-aware and predictive temporal codecs such as 4DGC and P-4DGS further target

this second problem by exploiting inter-frame redundancy in Gaussian streams

; their compression gains

must therefore be assessed together with decoder latency and temporal artifacts.

RTG-SLAM  reduces this cost by partitioning the Gaussian map as[]

41

$\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{stable}}\cup\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{unstable}},\qquad\min_{\mathcal{G}}\mathcal{L}\;\longrightarrow\;\min_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{unstable}}}\mathcal{L}.$ (23)

Stable Gaussians that already explain previous RGB-D observations are largely frozen,

while optimization and rendering concentrate on unstable Gaussians and pixels with

new observations or large color/depth residuals. This converts map maintenance from

a dense update over $N$ primitives toward an active-set problem with

$N_{\mathrm{active}}\ll N$ . Its 884.60 ms wrapped time and 1.130 frames/s in

are consistent with this design goal, although the value is not

directly comparable with MonoGS because the wrapped runs differ in frame count and

stage composition. The important systems result is therefore the reduction of the

optimization domain, not the numerical FPS ordering.

table11

WildGS-SLAM  addresses a different failure mode by making

the residual itself uncertainty-aware. Its mapping objective effectively weights

photometric and geometric errors as[]

76

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{map}}=\sum_{\mathbf{u}}\frac{\lambda_{I}\mathcal{L}_{I}(\mathbf{u})+\lambda_{D}\mathcal{L}_{D}(\mathbf{u})}{\beta(\mathbf{u})^{2}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{iso}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{iso}},$ (24)

where larger uncertainty $\beta(\mathbf{u})$ suppresses observations likely to arise

from dynamic distractors. This changes robustness mathematically from treating all

pixels as equally valid map constraints to weighted estimation. In

, WildGS-SLAM processes the longer monocular Crowd sequence

at 1525.64 ms/frame and obtains a full-trajectory RMSE of 0.00665 m

(0.00371 m on keyframes). These values cannot be ranked against the Replica RGB-D

results, but they show that uncertainty-aware monocular estimation remains computationally

substantial even though it operates under a different dynamic monocular input regime. Thus, the three systems reduce different dimensions of the joint SLAM problem:

MonoGS restricts observation support, RTG-SLAM restricts active map variables,

and WildGS-SLAM restricts the influence of unreliable residuals.

Efficiency methods operate on a different axis. For

$B(\mathcal{G})\approx Nb_{g}$ , pruning reduces $N$ , quantization reduces $b_{g}$ ,

and LoD reduces the view-dependent active set $N_{\mathrm{vis}}$ , but none of

these implies a proportional decrease in $t_{\mathcal{T}}$ . The shared baseline

in makes this explicit: PUP 3D-GS

and Compact3D  reduce

serialized size by approximately 90% and 92.66%, respectively, while the

pruned PUP model does not render faster than the vanilla baseline in

. Memory is therefore an independent deployment

constraint rather than a proxy for speed; the failed MotionGS

execution on an 80 GB A100 provides the complementary

case where optimization becomes infeasible despite the efficiency of Gaussian

rasterization. A useful cross-family operating point is consequently

$\mathcal{P}=\left(Q,\,t_{\mathcal{T}},\,B(\mathcal{G}),\,t_{\mathrm{render}}\right),$ (26)

and methods should be compared through the resulting trade-off rather than a

single universal FPS or SPS value.

These differences lead to distinct deployment regimes. Feed-forward

single-shot methods are the strongest fit for rapid initialization and

interactive preview because they minimize scene-construction latency, although

the controlled results show a direct quality–latency–memory trade-off.

Per-sequence dynamic methods are better suited when temporal reconstruction

quality is more important than initialization time, since interactive rendering

can be achieved after a substantially heavier optimization stage. Compression

and LoD methods are most useful when storage, bandwidth, or rendering load is

the limiting resource. Streaming methods directly target temporal scene

delivery, but the measured update rates show that interactive playback and

real-time scene refresh remain different system requirements. Finally, Gaussian

SLAM is the natural family for robotics and online mapping because pose

estimation and scene reconstruction are coupled, but the wrapped rates in

show that joint tracking–mapping latency remains the

principal obstacle to video-rate operation. Thus, “real-time” Gaussian

Splatting is not a single operating point: the appropriate method depends on

whether the application must optimize reconstruction latency, temporal update

latency, map maintenance, memory/bandwidth, or render-only throughput.

This survey reviewed Gaussian Splatting (GS) for real-time scene reconstruction. Rather than only listing methods, we organized prior work into a pipeline-centric taxonomy and highlighted the trade-offs that determine whether a method is merely or deployable end-to-end.real-time in a submodule

The main strength of this work is its . We connect design choices (e.g., temporal parameterization vs. stability, pruning/quantization/LoD vs. fidelity, and rasterization choices vs. artifacts) to system-level outcomes such as latency, memory growth, robustness to pose/depth noise, and long-horizon stability. Strengths and value to the field.synthesis across components

The taxonomy, comparison framework, and failure-mode analysis help researchers position new contributions and practitioners reason about capture-to-render pipelines.

Our taxonomy necessarily simplifies a fast-moving hybrid space, where many systems combine amortized initialization with refinement or mix static and dynamic representations. Comparability is also limited: papers report speed and memory at different stages (e.g., per-image FPS vs. per-scene throughput), under different input-window sizes and hardware assumptions. Thus, end-to-end conclusions about “real-time” readiness should be read as pipeline-aware guidance rather than a standardized benchmark ranking.Weaknesses and limitations.

Future work.

The main remaining directions are task-specific standardized evaluation, deployment-aware scene generation, sparse-by-construction representations, long-horizon dynamic and streaming maintenance, and robust Gaussian SLAM. Together, these problems shift the focus from fast rasterization toward maintaining quality, bounded latency, and manageable state throughout the reconstruction pipeline.

item.title: 一套基就够动所有人：用高斯混合形状蒸馏做实时数字人 ｜ One Basis to Animate Them All: Gaussian Blendshape Distillation for Real-Time Avatars
item.description:
一句话：把每帧重型神经解码换成「浅层 MLP 预测系数 + 线性混合」，移动端跑到 60fps。

要点：

  • 发现预训练高斯数字人的动画可被与身份无关的 blendshape 线性组合紧密近似
  • 用浅层 MLP 预测 blendshape 系数再做线性混合，替换逐帧神经解码，且无需重训原始模型
  • 基用 block-local PCA 在渲染感知度量与显存预算下构建；宿主模型的 CPU 动画速度显著提升，移动端达 60fps

为什么值得看：数字人卡在每帧神经推理，线性近似把成本从「跑网络」降到「查系数」，是移动端可落地的那条路。

中文摘要：3D 高斯数字人能快速渲染，但实时动画常被昂贵的神经推理卡住。作者发现一个有用的结构性质：预训练数字人模型的动画结果，可以被一组与身份无关的 blendshape 的线性组合相当接近地近似。据此提出 GALA（Gaussian Animation via Linear Approximation）蒸馏方法：用一个浅层系数预测网络加线性混合，替代每帧的重型神经解码，并且可以直接作用在已有动画架构上、不需要重训原模型。为了兼顾保真度与显存，基的构建采用分块局部 PCA，在渲染感知的度量下、受显存预算约束地挑选。实验验证了这种共享线性结构确实存在，并把宿主模型的 CPU 动画速度大幅提升，使移动端设备上跑出 60fps 的写实 3D 动画成为可能。

Abstract

3D Gaussian avatars support fast rendering, however, their real-time animation is often challenged by the costly neural inference. We address this bottleneck and show that the animation of pretrained avatar models can be closely approximated by a linear combination of identity-independent blendshapes.

Building on this finding, we introduce (aussian nimation via inear pproximation), a distillation method that replaces per-frame heavy neural decoding with a shallow coefficient predictor and a linear blend.

To improve fidelity and reduce memory requirements, we propose to construct the basis using block-local PCA under a rendering-aware metric and a memory budget. Our method learns a shallow MLP network to predict blendshape coefficients and applies to various animation architectures without retraining original models. We validate GALA by accelerating the inference of three distinct avatar models for 3D animation of facial expressions and full-bodies with clothing dynamics. Across these models, our distillation generalizes to held-out identities and reduces CPU animation cost by up to three orders of magnitude while preserving most of the rendering quality. Excellent results of our method confirm the shared linear structure of learned avatar representations and enable highly efficient and accurate animation at frame rates reaching up to 60fps on mobile devices. GALA enables efficient, high-fidelity animation across diverse Gaussian avatar models. By introducing shared blendshapes and a lightweight coefficient predictor, GALA accelerates CPU animation by up to three orders of magnitude and enables real-time deployment on mobile devices.

Recent advances in neural avatars have substantially improved the generation, reconstruction, and animation of photorealistic digital humans. Representations based on 3D Gaussians are particularly attractive because their explicit primitives support efficient rendering , and they underlie models for head generation, reconstruction from a single image, and full-body animation with clothing dynamics . However, efficient rendering does not imply efficient animation. Many models evaluate a substantial neural network at every frame to update Gaussian attributes from expression or pose parameters, and this per-frame computation, which we call the model’s , can dominate inference cost and limits deployment on CPUs and mobile devices.()

The cost of neural animation raises the question of how much of the computation performed by a pretrained avatar model is necessary at inference time. The complexity of its nonlinear decoder does not establish that its outputs require an equally complex representation, and deformations across identities may share a compact linear structure even when the architecture and the training objective do not impose one. In this work, we show that the animation outputs of diverse pretrained Gaussian avatar models can be closely approximated by an identity-specific neutral avatar and a linear combination of identity-independent , which we obtain by analyzing Gaussian attribute residuals relative to the neutral state across identities and driving signals. Crucially, a basis extracted once from a model also captures the animation of identities excluded from basis construction, since identity-dependent motion is retained through the blendshape coefficients while the deformation basis is shared.blendshapes

Linear representations have a long history in face and body modeling . More recently, Gaussian blendshape methods have demonstrated efficient photorealistic animation with bases fitted to individual subjects , while systems such as LAM adopt a predefined animation rig . Our work investigates a different setting, extracting a reusable basis from a trained model that represents many identities (Table ). The basis approximates deformations learned by the original network and can be reused for new subjects without reconstructing it, where identity independence refers to sharing within one pretrained model.(; )

Building on this finding, we introduce a Gaussian blendshape distillation strategy, which we call (aussian nimation via inear pproximation). Our method constructs separate bases for Gaussian attribute groups and spatial regions using block-local principal component analysis under a rendering-aware metric, which prioritizes deformations that matter for visual fidelity, and allocates components within a memory budget according to their estimated image-space error reduction per stored byte. A shallow coefficient predictor, conditioned on identity and driving signals, then learns to control the extracted basis, so that animation requires only coefficient prediction and a linear blend added to the cached neutral avatar. The procedure requires no retraining of the original model.GALAGALA

We apply our approach to three existing models with distinct architectures and training objectives, the of our distillation: AGORA  for head generation, FlexAvatar  for one-shot head reconstruction, and DynaAvatar  for full-body reconstruction with clothing dynamics.

GALA closely approaches animation accuracy of approximated host models and consistently outperforms other baselines on respective benchmarks.

Crucially, our method increases CPU animation speed of host models by up to and enables on-device photorealistic 3D animation at 60 fps.

Recent work on photorealistic avatars explores several approaches. 3D-aware GANs trained from unstructured images collections generate heads as triplanes  or Gaussians , and their animatable versions condition generation on the parameters of morphable models through deformation fields or expression branches .

One-shot reconstruction methods regress an animatable head from a single image, either by using 3D GANs during training  or by direct supervised reconstruction from tracked video , and diffusion priors pursue the same goal with synthesised supervision .

Per-subject methods optimise Gaussian avatars from videos of particular people . Work on full-body animation follows similar approaches.

One-shot full-body reconstruction methods  articulate Gaussians by SMPL-X skinning , while DynaAvatar  adds pose-dependent clothing dynamics using a transformer conditioned on pose history.

We apply our approach to two recent host models for head animation AGORA , FlexAvatar  and one host model for full-body animation DynaAvatar , and demonstrate significant improvement of their inference speed.Animatable avatar models.()

Linear representations have a long history in modeling human shape and appearance. Eigenfaces represent facial images in a low-dimensional PCA subspace , while active appearance models capture variations in shape and texture . Three-dimensional morphable models extend this principle to facial geometry and appearance learned from scans .

For animation, blendshape models express deformations as weighted combinations of offsets from a neutral shape , and multilinear models disentangle identity and expression variation .

Modern parametric models, including FLAME  and SMPL-X , combine learned shape and corrective blendshapes with articulated skinning to represent expressive faces and bodies; see  for a review of 3D morphable face models.

These representations provide the driving parameters for the avatar models considered in our work. We show that the resulting neural animation outputs themselves admit a compact linear approximation: an identity-shared blendshape basis over Gaussian attributes, extracted from a pretrained network without direct fitting to scans.Linear face and body models.(; )

Recent work extends blendshape representations to photorealistic Gaussian avatars. Methods such as 3D Gaussian Blendshapes , HeadGaS , Gaussian Déjà-vu , RGBAvatar , GEM  and WebAvatar  learn bases over Gaussian attributes or latent features from monocular or multi-view observations.

RGBAvatar predicts blending coefficients from tracked expression parameters, while GEM extracts a basis from a trained subject-specific avatar network and predicts its coefficients from images.

Similarly, SqueezeMe  distils per-subject full-body Gaussian avatars into linear corrective bases for efficient headset rendering. These methods establish the effectiveness of linear representations for individual avatars, but require a separate basis for each subject.

Fixed-rig approaches such as LAM  instead support efficient animation through a predefined FLAME-based articulation model.

Differently from previous work, our method extracts a shared identity-agnostic blendshape basis from a pretrained neural model. The basis captures deformations learned by that model and is reused unchanged for identities unseen during extraction, extending Gaussian blendshape distillation from individual subjects to models of diverse identities.Photorealistic blendshape models.()

Our goal is to accelerate pretrained Gaussian avatar models () by replacing their per-frame neural decoding with a fast inference based on linear blendshape representations. We first introduce a generic host model and its animation parameters in Section . Section  then presents main parts of our method, namely the construction of identity-shared basis

and prediction of its coefficients from animation parameters.host models

3.1

3.2

3.1

We consider avatar models that represent a subject using $n$ 3D Gaussians rendered by differentiable splatting . Each Gaussian is described by a $d$ -dimensional attribute vector, which includes position, scale, rotation, opacity, and appearance, with additional skinning weights where required.

Avatar animation is controlled by parameters derived from parametric face or body models such as FLAME  or SMPL-X .

We denote the animation driving input by $\theta$ and its neutral setting by $\theta_{0}$ . For models with temporal conditioning, $\theta$ includes the required motion history. An identity descriptor $w$ , either supplied directly or extracted from an input image, remains fixed throughout an animation sequence.

We define pretrained host models as $A(w,\theta)\rightarrow G\in\mathbb{R}^{nd}$ , where the output concatenates the attribute vectors of the $n$ Gaussians.

Importantly, Gaussian indices in the model output $G$ must have consistent correspondence across variations in identity and animation parameters. This constraint is typically satisfied by existing models which initialize Gaussians on a shared UV grid or template-anchored point .()

3.2

In this section we present our method that aims to approximate the costly neural animation of the original host model $G=A(w,\theta)$ by a simpler model

$\hat{G}=A(w,\theta_{0})+Uc(w,\theta),$ (1)

where $A(w,\theta_{0})$ is the representation of a neutral avatar estimated only once per animation sequence, $U$ is a linear basis and $c$ is a vector of basis coefficients. The rest of this section explains our approach to construct the basis $U$ and to efficiently estimate its coefficients $c(w,\theta)$ . Figure  gives an overview of our method.

2

Overview of GALA. Residuals $r_{i}$ of the host model $A$ with respect to the neutral avatar $A(w_{i},\theta_{0})$ (Section ) are decomposed by a spatially local, rendering-aware PCA under a memory budget $\mathcal{B}$ into the block-diagonal basis $U$ (Section ). A coefficient network $f_{\phi}$ is trained to regress the projected coefficients $c^{\star}$ (Section ). At inference, the neutral avatar is computed once per subject, and every frame costs one evaluation of a shallow network $f_{\phi}$ and a linear blend.Figure 2:
